Mr, J. A. FRASER (Cariboo):	I should
like to ask a question of the Minister of the Interior relating to the administration of water in the railway belt in British Columbia, based on the following information:
- In 1912 a Railway Belt Water Act was passed-amended in 1913-under which the Dominion practically transferred to the province the administration of water in the railway belt.
The 1913 act provided that all water within the railway belt should, during the pleasure of the Governor in Council, be administered under the water acts of the provinces in force at that time and it was further provided that the Governor in Council might direct that any act or portion thereof passed by British Columbia after March 3, 1913, relating to water in the province should apply to the water in the railway belt as if such act were enacted by the parliament of Canada. However such order in council had to be published for four consecutive weeks in the Canada Gazette and laid before both houses of parliament within the first fifteen days of the session next after the date thereof and such order in council was to remain in force only until the day immediately succeeding the prorogation of that session of parliament, unless during the session it was approved by resolution of both houses of parliament.

I desire to draw the attention of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs to the contents of a communication I have received from the residents of my constituency concerning conditions in the White Bear Indian reserve, near Areola. This is written by the secretary of the Areola presbytery of the United Church of Canada, and with the permission of the House I will read the communication. It is as follows:
To the Honourable,
the House of Commons, Ottawa.
We the presbytery of Areola, in the United Church of Canada, deeply concerned about the physical condition of the Indians, on the White Bear reserve, wish to draw the attention of your honourable House to these conditions, that they may be materially improved. A31 told there are some 235 persons on the reserve, a large number of these are suffering from physical ailments, such as discharging ears, inflamed eyes, diseased tonsils and adenoids, and especially tuberculosis, and while the medical officer is doing all he can to minister to the bodily needs of the ailing, much more needs to be done.
There is quite a number of Indians on the reserve who are tubercular some of these quite advanced, and there is practically nothing being done for them, or to prevent the spread of that scourge. On a recent visit, by some members of this presbytery it was found, that several persons, advanced in years, werein the last stage of consumption, and they had neither suitable food, or nursing, or dwelling place, and know nothing of the precautions necessary to prevent the spread of the disease.
We are aware that there are four government hospitals in the province for the care of diseased Indians, and four nurses to attend to the physical well being of the people. Anji while appreciating the occasional visits of Nurse Colvin to the White Bear reserve, we desire to point out, that the tie which binds Indian parents and children together is 60 strong that the [DOT]former will not permit the latter to enter a hospital, or sanatarium, and all indian adults have such a dread of chloroform, that they are evidently unwilling to enter a hospital for treatment.
We are strongly of the belief that the Indians on the White Bear reserve need in the worst way, a resident nurse, to see to it, that those suffering from any disease have the treatment which the medical officer prescribes, so that they may have a Chance to get well. At the present time, as things are, many of them are doomed to die for lack of a trained nurse, to administer medicine and give necessary nursing.
rMr. Lapointe.]
Of the 64 houses on the reserve, ten have a shingle roof, others have sods or clay, which cannot keep out rain.
He goes on to tell about the tubercular patients sleeping on the floor under these conditions. He then says:
In several of these one-roomed houses, two families or more try to live together. Only two families on the reserve keep pigs or poultry, only one man keeps cows, and the children being raised without milk suffer seriously from malnutrition.
I would ask the minister, first, whether he is aware of the existence of these conditions and if so what explanation he can give. Secondly, if he is not aware of this state of affairs, can I have his assurance that he will properly investigate the subject and, in the event of the conditions being found to be as outlined in this communication, that some steps will be taken immediately to afford the necessary relief?

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Edmonton, Superintendent General of Indian Affairs):

speechtext: I have no doubt that the allegations contained in the letter my hon friend has read are correct so far as tuberculosis is concerned. This is a disease which is very prevalent amongst the Indian tribes, and it is one which it _ is difficult to combat for the very reason outlined in that letter, namely, that the Indians will not leave their homes to go to the hospitals provided for the care of such patients. To establish on each reserve a hospital for this special purpose is out of the question; it would be too expensive. I think I can assure my hon. friend that the commissioner at Regina is fully aware of the conditions on these reserves particularly in Saskatchewan. Recommendation for a nursing staff was made some three years ago, and four nurses are now travelling through the provinces examining Indian children and giving such relief as they can. I am informed that this work has been very beneficial to the Indians, and good progress is being made. It would be idle to deny that there is a great deal of tuberculosis among the Indians, not only in the western provinces but throughout Canada. It is a very serious problem for the department. That, I think, is all I can say in reply to my hon. friend.
Mr. Speaker-

I desire to call the attention of the government and particularly of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald, Antigonish) to a condition in the city of Quebec to which reference has been made in the press. It is alleged that the walls and fortifications of Quebec are in imminent danger of falling and of causing, in such a fall, serious damage to life and property. It is also alleged that the walls under the care of the federal government are in a filthy, disreputable and dangerous condition. I would ask the minister if he has any knowledge of these conditions and if he has any intention of effecting a remedy.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
The situation in regard to the walls of the citadel at Quebec is this. From a military standpoint the citadel has become entirely obselete and the department has no great interest in maintaining it as a matter of defence. The ground, however, is of great historic value and we feel that the *city and province of Quebec might well share in whatever the Dominion government might do in the way of preserving the citadel as a spot of historic interest.
Conferences have been held with that end in view and estimates have been obtained as to what the cost would be of restoring the citadel and maintaining it in a proper state of repair. Those estimates show that the cost would run in the vicinity of $425,000 so that a very costly proposal has to be considered. The department at all times has been ready to confer with the city and province of Quebec as to what steps might be taken towards the preservation of this very interesting, memorial of the past.
My attention has been called to a statement in the press with reference to the condition of a portion of the ramparts and what is known as Rampart street. I desire to say in answer to my hon. friend that the records of the department show that that particular street and its condition are entirely under the control of the city of Quebec which took the street over in 1922 and assumed the responsibility of looking after it in all respects. If anything is wrong in connection with that street the fault is that of the city of Quebec.
There appears in the estimates of this year an item of $10,000 which was rendered necessary in order to prevent the falling of a portion of the citadel walls which would have imperilled lives and property, and tenders have now been called for the purpose of carrying on this work as quickly as possible.

I have not the figures for 1921. My hon. friend did not ask for that the other day.
That is quite true.
I am informed that the cost is about the same and the work is about the same as it was in 1921.

I have some
difficulty in accepting my hon. friend's answer and when I say some difficulty I mean considerable difficulty. In 1921 the department was actively engaged in looking after the National railways. It had its solicitors to look after it; there was this thing and that thing to be done all the time; the officials were checking accounts and the like. To-day all they are doing, as I understand the matter, is looking after the accounts of the canals. My hon. friend says that the work is about the same.

Yes. The last time the estimate was before the committee I mentioned the fact that during the time the department directly administered the railways the cost to which my hon. friend has reference was charged to the railways directly. In the old Intercolonial days, as will be remembered, that portion of the staff was very largely at Moncton. The same charges relating to accounting are made to-day with respect to the Department of Railways as were - made prior to 1921. The items to which my hon. friend refers were always chargeable to railway accounts, so I am informed. The staff to-day is 103; in 1921, it was 104.

What are the
items that now refer to the department?

This is a general
summary of the work it is doing now which will probably satisfy my hon. friend:
The details of operation of the Canadian Government railways and the field supervision of construction and betterments were never matters dealt with in their detail by the departmental staff.
That was the point I was making.
The placing of the Canadian government railways under the National board of operation and management has occasioned no change in the administration of the Canadian Government Railways Act and the other acts prescribing the administration of similar property. The Canadian government railways continue to be operated under the government railways act, the only difference in relation to the departments being that a board of directors of the Canadian National Railways now perform the duties previously assigned to a general manager.
That is the only difference.

My hon. friend has not grasped my question. My question is:	What railway work has the department
now to do? What is left?

Railway matters dealt
with by the department. I have a partial list of them before me. Those matters are: Obtaining authority of the Governor General

Supply-Railways and Canals
in Council for entering into contracts for work to be carried out on the Canadian government railways, executing such contracts and recording in connection with them-

Suppose we just stop at the very first one. When the matter is left entirely in the hands of the board of directors, what is the necessity of having them do their work through this department instead of through the organization which is doing so much more?

My hon. friend is well
aware of course that although the Canadian National Railways is a system, the different parts of it still maintain their individual entities. The title to the former Canadian government railways is still in the crown. The crown must provide the necessary funds. The same recording is necessary in the department now that the work is being carried on by a board of directors as was necessary when the same work was being performed by a general manager; the relationship of the department to the board of directors is identical with its former relationship to. the general manager of the system; and financing, recording and accounting in the department is necessary just as much to-day as it was then in connection with expenditures of that kind.

It is quite true, Mr. Chairman, that the country still owns the national railways. It is equally true that it owns the Canadian Northern railway, the Grand Trunk railway and the rest of them; it is also equally true that so far as the Grand Trunk is concerned, its identity has to be maintained by reason of certain contractual obligations which are still outstanding. But the minister is not getting sent in particulars of Grand Trunk finance, nor particulars of all the other properties that are kept distinct, and there is no reason in the world why it should be done here. Look at the farce of the thing, Mr. Chairman, in this case the minister has absolutely nothing more to do with the contracts of the Canadian National system, having regard to the Intercolonial railway, than he has with anything else.

My hon. friend is wrong
there.	[DOT]

Technically so.
But is my hon. friend going to say he is interfering in the busines management of the Intercolonial? If he is not so interfering, all this so-called work is unnecessary. The thing is perfectly plain and simple. We have separate identity in connection with this property; granted. We have got it separate in connection with the different component companies, many of them, and we have got it separate in connection with the Intercolonial railway. But there is no more reason why the department should be interfering with the Intercolonial-if it is interfering-than with any other part of the system. And if it is not interefering, wherein has it any more work to do in connection with contracts for the Intercolonial than it has in connection with contracts for what used to be the Grand Trunk?

I am a little surprised
that my hon. friend does not know the situation much more intimately. As a matter of fact, while not interfering in any way with the management of the former Intercolonial railway, the Minister of Railways does have a definite responsibility with regard to that road which he does not have with respect to other parts of the Canadian National system. It still remains the property of the crown. The Minister of Railways is still responsible for its operation, and he discharges that responsibility by ituming over matters Of operation to the board of directors of the Canadian National Railway system. He cannot, however, dissociate himself from responsibility for capital or other expenditures on the property. Under the law they must be made by the Department of Railways and Canals, and the minister is responsible in a different way in connection with that system as compared with other portions of the present National system. I agree with my hon. friend that as soon as we can get refinancing of the whole property, including the old government system, it will be desirable to have the same conditions apply to all of the different entities now comprising the National railways; but until that time comes the Minister of Railways must sign all contracts for work done on the former Intercolonial, on the former Transcontinental and on the former Prince Edward Island railway. His relationship is entirely different to the former government roads from what it is to the companies which were taken over as part of the Canadian National system. I intend, of course, as Minister of Railways, to endeavour to work towards the elimination of those conditions. But so far as the Intercolonial and the Transcontinental are concerned, may I say to my hon. friend that, since he raised the point the other day, I have looked into it, so far as my time would permit, and I find that the work ol the department in relation to those roads has not changed by reason of their becoming part of the Canadian National system. The relationship is only

Supply-Railways and Canals
changed in the particular to which I referred, that the former general manager is now replaced !by the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways.

Mr. Chairman,
the minister is very happily confusing matters of form with matters of substance. In matters of form he is perfectly right-if he wants to go on duplicating work he can do so. He has already turned around and said to the management that they can run this government railway. And he can let them run it; or, on the other hand, he can keep up this unnecessary organization and do just what he is doing. There is no more reason in the world why there cannot be agents for the making of a contract for that purpose than there are agents for running the railway and coming to a hundred and one decisions all the time. Then my hon. friend says that there is responsibility here in the crown for capital account. Of course there is; but there is responsibility for everything in the crown. Is my hon. friend going to tell me that in connection with capital account this government has nothing to do with it, whether it be for the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Northern or any other part of the system? He will not tell me that. If he does, he is making a most extraordinary statement. The government is responsible for every single dollar of capital account. My hon. friend knows it, and he himself has said on other occasions that so far as capital account is concerned that is something this parliament is responsible for. Well, if he was right then, it is responsible for capital account in connection with Grand Trunk extensions and contracts just as much as it is here. My hon friend can say: The department takes contracts in my name. So it does. But he knows he can take contracts in the name of his agents just the same. Just simply for the purpose of keeping on this vote of $81,000 he is treating the board of directors as agents only for certain purposes, and for all other purposes he is carrying on the old machinery.

My hon. friend is unfair -I am sure quite unconsciously so. The $81,000 for the controller's office is for the controller and the work of his office in connection with the whole Department of Railways and Canals. If I might be permitted to say so, the argument my hon. friend last Advanced, if sound, is surely an argument for an increase in the staff. If I am responsible as Minister of Railways for all the capital expenditures of the Canadian National, then
(Mr. Dunning.]
naturally I require a larger staff than in former Intercolonial days when the minister was responsible only for the Intercolonial and the National Transcontinental. However, that would be a quibble.

Worse than a
quibble-nonsense.

Then the nonsense is
his.

No. My hon.
friend admits that it is a quibble. I say it is worse.

There is a statutory
duty here, and as long as the Minister of Railways feels the responsibility which he ought to feel in relation to a statute he will feel a more detailed responsibility with respect to contracts for work done on the former government railway system than he will feel with respect to those portions of the present National system which were formerly operated under private companies. I may say to my hon. friend that formerly he operated for two years or more under the system which still obtains, because it was recognized there, as it is recognized to-day, that until we can put this system together financially, these distinctions must be maintained. We must know how that property stands against which there are no mortgages and no securities, and we must know how each of the various constituent companies stands in relation to the whole. I can assure my hon. friend, however, that I will look carefully into the necessity for this in the future; he knows that I have been but a short time in the department. Since he first raised the matter, a few days ago, I have satisfied myself that this is needed for the present at least. I can further assure my hon. friend that if I find it not needed I will undertake not to spend the amount, and to reduce the staff if a reduction is possible. Further than that I cannot go at present.

My hon. friend says my argument was one for a larger staff instead of a smaller staff, and then he was good enough to say that his statement was a quibble. He might have gone still further and said that his statement was pure nonsense as well. The minister says that if he is responsible for the capital accounts of all these different lines he will have to add to the staff.

No, no.

Supply-Railways and Canals

Well, the nonsense is admitted, so we will get rid of that. Then the question arises of any responsiblity for capital as to one part of the system or the other; it arises in the minister's own admission. He now shakes his head; he thinks he has it both coming and going, but things do not work that way. With regard to capital expense the government has the responsibility of seeing to it that the public moneys are not pried loose without parliamentary authority. I think my hon. friend will absolutely agree with that; capital expenditures cannot be made except by the vote of the representatives of the people, and new obligations cannot be so taken up. Does my hon. friend agree with that, or is it his view that new capital obligations can be taken on without reference to parliament? The minister has not yet made up his mind; I think we should know before this item passes, because it is a very simple thing. down the way made a speech he was going to make another speech, I say also that it will not be long before I shall repeat what I have said in trying to emphasize the necessity of putting a stop to the present unnecessary duplication of transportation services by consolidating our two great railway systems.

Item agreed to.
Hudson Bay railway-construction and 'betterments, $3,000,000.
My hon. friend is not taking that up to-day, is he?

Well, I advised many
members who asked me as to the time and date that I would take this vote up to-day. Many are here who are interested in it.
Go ahead.

There are very few here at present who are interested in the vote, and perhaps that is the reason why my hon. friend wants to go ahead' with it. But I venture to suggest to him it is generally poor policy to do that. This supply was put on at the very tail end of a long order. At least I think it is the last. I should like to be right so I will look it up.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You are right.

Usually the
government are supposed to pay some attention to the order in which they announce the business of the House. I think my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) will agree with me there also. This is what we were told yesterday we were to do to-day:
Third readings of Bill No. 114 to amend the Customs Tariff 1907,-
I think that bill has been passed.
-and Bill No. 115 to amend the Special WaT Revenue Act;-
I do not think that has been touched.
-second reading of Bill No. 116 to amend the Income War Tax Act 1917;-
A long measure.
-second reading of Bill No. 150, respecting the Chicoutimi Harbour Commissioners; second reading of Bill No. 152, to amend the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act; second reading of Bill No. 153, to amend the Criminal Code; consideration in committee of Bill No. 91, to amend the Immigration Act.
Then merely as a possibility, not as an indication, we were told:
If we go into supply we will take up the estimates of the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Public Works.
Instead of that we are going straight ahead. I did not object to the introduction of the
other item because. I did not think many gentlemen wanted to speak to it, but I know a great many hon. members will speak on this item, and the notice given was merely an alternative that if this long list of business was finished and supply reached, we might go into the estimates of this department.
I do not think the Hudson Bay railway vote should be proceeded with.

I find nothing inconsistent in our procedure to-day with the statement of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) on Wednesday evening; there was certainly liberty given to go into supply. My hon. friend reads a meaning which is not in the words:
If we go into supply we will take up the estimates of the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Public Works.
It was in no way contingent upon the other matters referred to going through. I did give an assurance more than a week ago to a number of hon. members on both sides of the House that to-day was arranged on this side for the debate on the Hudson Bay railway, and I am sure that hon. members interested were so advised. I think my hon. friend opposite (Mr. Hay) and others spoke to me, and I am now all prepared to deal with the matter.

I do not know whether the word "if" is a conditional word or not; I had the idea that it was generally so intended. But I am not standing on anything except the ordinary usage of this House. I do not know what the practice of the hon. member may have been in Saskatchewan, whether when he gave a list he stuck to it or whether he always took the end first and otherwise tried to mislead the oposition.
I must protest; that is grossly unfair and unwarranted on the part of my hon. friend.

There is nothing at all unfair. I read this list as it is printed, and I suggest that if my hon. friend's practice in Saskatchewan was to take the tail and make it the head in order to mislead the opposition, that has not been the practice in this House.
Again I must protest; it has not been my practice to mislead the opposition at any time.

Then my hon. friend should withdraw his statement and go on.

Supply-Railways and Canals

I think it is my hon. friend who should withdraw. Surely when a list is presented it is not obligatory upon the government to follow it in every detail. The question asked is as to the business for the next day; the business is stated in any order, and I venture to say that if I looked up Hansard I could find where my 5 p.m. hon. friend has answered such a question in exactly the same way and then, on the succeeding day, taken up the business in whatever order suited him as the minister concerned.. To attribute deceit is surely not fair.
The list is exactly as I read it, with the word "if" included.

Yes; "if" we go into supply. We are in supply.
Sir HENRY DRA"i TON: I understood you were trying to clean up this order paper; the order paper is pretty well set out here, but it may be that I am wrong in my idea. I simply point out what I read before and what I read fairly, as it is printed, without anything in addition, but so far as I am concerned it is a matter for the government to do as they please.

With respect to this item, I think the minister gave notice about a week ago in answer to a question from some hon. member -deeply interested in the question; the minister said this particular item would be taken up when his estimates were next under discussion. Consequently I cannot see how the House has been led astray. I see no reason why this item should not be taken up, since a good many of those chiefly interested in it are present, and I can see no cause for delay at present.

Perhaps we will be able to get some particulars here. In the first instance the country is entitled to have -whether some members and their constituents who are particularly interested in this question think so or not-a full discussion of this item, and there will be a full discussion, regardless of any efforts made to force the item through this House. We are entitled to know exactly what the governmental programme is; we are entitled to know exactly how this money is to be applied. The country is also entitled to know how much money is to be spent in carrying out the project as a whole. We have now before us a vote which, as I understand it, is for the present-I will not say requirements, because I do not know what they are, but this vote 
will be used during the current jmar. Then I think we are entitled to know whether it is contemplated to do more than complete the railway, for example, whether in the opinion of the government it will be necessary to supply boats for the service; whether, in case boats are supplied or in any event, it is in the opinion of the government necessary to protect, lighthouse and generally look after these seas in the same way other approaches are protected. We should know what the cost will be, and whether terminals are to be erected at this point. In other words, we are entitled to know the complete particulars of the full commitment. '

If my hon. friend had put his request for a postponement of this discussion on the ground of courtesy and having regard to the fact that only some ten members of the Conservative party are present in the House on the occasion of a discussion of such importance, I would have been glad to accede to his request. But he put his request on the ground that deception was being practised, and I again call to his attention the fact that more than a week ago, when I was asked a question by an hon. member opposite, I indicated that on the next occasion we were in supply on railway estimates this matter would be taken up. In addition to that, a number of members on both sides of the House spoke to me privately about the matter, and I indicated that it would come up to-day. I quite appreciate that the empty chairs opposite do not mean that hon. gentlemen are not interested in this project and do not desire information regarding it, but they do mean that a certain meeting in Montreal is probably of more importance to them at this juncture. I am not blaming them at all, but if my hon. friend makes his request in his usual courteous manner for a postponement of this item I will be glad to report progress.

My hon. friend has a way with him, but I thought in the first instance that I made a very quiet request. Then I was told afterwards that I was misinterpreting the English language. I am quite content to throw myself on my hon. friend's mercy and possibly in view of the situation to-day he might adjourn the consideration of this matter.

We can take another
item.

I am quite
content. You can take another item.

Any other item but this.

Supply-Railways and Canals

Any other item but this.
Item stands.
WelJand ship canal construction (revote, $3,000,000)- $14,000,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

I fail to understand why
an item of $3,000,000 is of such importance that its consideration must be adjourned, and a vote of $14,000,000 is to go through without any discussion whatever. Possibly some hon. members can understand the matter-I cannot. If the Hudson Bay railway vote, in view of its great importance, must be adjourned in order that it may be discussed in detail, surely the House is entitled to a full explanation of a vote of $14,000,000.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is there anything we may take up?

Of course it is rather
embarrassing to find that the whole proceedings of the House must be held up in order to enable a political meeting to be held in Montreal. The government 'has some sympathy with the point made by my hon. friend opposite that if a vote of $3,000,000 is important one of $14,000,000 is surely of greater importance. I am quite willing to permit this item also to stand until it suits the convenience of my hon. friends in Montreal.
Item stands.
Chambly, improvements (revote, $7,500)-$55,000.
This item calls for an explanation.

The items in this vote
consist of the following:
Machinery	$ 2,500
Riley Bridge (Revote)	 3,000
Survey (Revote)	 2,500
Wharf	 45,000
The upper western bank of Chambly canal within the limits of the city of St. John's forms a landing wharf, a portion of which was rebuilt in concrete in 1919. The 800 odd feet of wall piling with sheating, immediately above the Canadian Pacific Railway bridge is now in a very dilapidated condition, old piles and facing having rotted and portions having been carried away. As the foundation is uneven and relatively soft at certain places, it is proposed for the present to sink a stone filled timber crib which, later, after settlement, may have,the portion above water renewed in concrete.

Item agreed to.
St. Ours lock, improvements, $50,000.

We did not
abject to any of the other votes because they are old and the country is committed to them. But this is a new item and perhaps my hon. friend will explain What is contemplated.

The amount required here is to rebuild in part the old lock at this place, which was built during 1847-1848, the intention then being to provide for 7-foot navigation. However, during low water periods, this navigation is not available, and at times boats drawing more than 5 feet 6 inches cannot pass the lock. In 1907, the walls and mitre sills of this lock were found to be seriously undermined, and during the three following years the sum of $75,000 was expended in making repairs. At present this lock is in a worse condition than it was at that time and a certain amount of reconstruction is imperative.

How much navigation is
there through this particular lock?

I have not the exact
figures but it is used very extensively for the transportation of lumber, coal and hay. It is on the Richelieu river.

Has the minister any idea
what the revenue from this source was last year?

AVe do not have any
revenue from our canals; they are free.

Item agreed to.
Baker's dam improvements, $30,000.
This is a new item also. What is the vote for?

To renew with concrete
the cribwork facing on the east side of the channel. What is called Baker's dam, in reality guide piers on each side of Baker's channel below Ste. Anne lock, is the only passage for boats of nine feet draft plying between the St. Lawrence and the Ottawa rivers. The inner faces of the cribs, which were built in 1875, are decayed and falling down into the channel, the eastern wall being the worse of the two. It is thought necessary to rebuild immediately this eastern wall.

Item agreed to.
Ontario-St. Lawrence canals, improvements (revote $7,000), $7,000.

That is the
usual vote?
Supply-Railways and Canals
This relates to the improvement of the upper entrance to Rapide Plat canal, and is to pay off the contractors.

Item agreed to.
St. Peters canal, improvements, $6,300.
That also is to cover finishing up?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Trent canal, improvements (revote, $155,840), $395,100.
I think we ought to have a little explanation from the minister in regard to these improvements.

I may say for the information of hon. members from other parts of the country that the Trent canal extends from Georgian bay to Trenton; it will provide a short cut for navigation. The amount required is $44,400 less than was provided last year, and the following are the items
for which the vote is to be used:
Construction lock gates	 $20,000
Dredging and drilling	 25,000
Extension to lock aprons	 5.000
Dam, Elliott's Falls-Gull river	 10,000

Eel's lake dam	 11,500

Severn Division
Staff on construction	 55,000
Young's point section (revote, $35,000)..	..	80.000
Dam at lock 23 (revote, $59,340)	 68,000
Bridge at Atherley Narrows (revote, $40,000).	40.000

I can give details of every one of the items to which I have referred if any member of the House desires it.

Can you give us any
idea of the tonnage?

In the past we have had to spend a great deal of money on this project, and I am afraid that in future we will have to spend more. What was endeavoured to be done by the former administration in the same circumstances was to make no expenditure except for the 'purposes of safety. We had to make necessary expenditures to obviate the danger of a flood breaking out here or a wall going there or a lock breaking. We had a responsibility there which we had to look after.

We have adopted the
same policy exactly. I can on another occa-

sion get the figures regarding the tonnage for all the canals. I am sorry I have not them here, but inasmuch as the expenditure on the Welland canal will come up on future occasions, that will open up a discussion on the tonnage of any of the canals.
What is the principal commerce carried on this canal?

There is no large traffic on the Trent canal, because it is not finished in a manner capable of carrying through traffic, but there is considerable local traffic, and a very great many steamers plying for hire and pleasure.

I understand the traffic is
mostly that of pleasure steamers. Does the minister think it is proper for us to keep up an annual expenditure for pleasure steamers? I understand there are about half a dozen a day for commerce. This seems to be a large expenditure.

My hon. friend is referring more to the lower end. I have seen very little mercantile traffic there, but it so happens that at other portions of the system there is some traffic of a business character. I do not think my hon. friend, any more than myself, would to-day go into such a venture. I think he would find himself just as I found myself when I was asked to provide money for works of this kind. The situation is that the works are there. They have been in existence for many years, and there are property rights and that sort of thing. It is an artificial structure for which the country is responsible. My hon. friend's policy apparently is the same as mine was, that is never to spend money except to maintain these public properties in safe condition. There might be loss of life if we did not do that and damage might occur. If the minister follows that course, that is all he can be expected to do.
That is all. To cut out this expenditure would be to pave the way for a greater expenditure as a result of abandoning the property. I do not think it would be practical to do that.

I was considerably more
anxious to ascertain what the hon. member for West York thought about it than to get the minister's views. Is he willing to go to an expenditure of almost half a million a year to maintain a waterway which is used principally for pleasure craft, and yet when it comes to a commercial venture like the Hudson Bay railway, to hold the House up

Supply-Railways and Canals
and not permit us to go forward with that vote, which is not greatly out of proportion to this vote, when we consider the object in view.

My hon. friend is wrong. Nothing depends upon the size of a vote one way or the other, but a great deal depends on whether it is right in principle or not. The Hudson Bay railway may be shown to be perfectly right in principle. I myself doubt it. I think I gave a pretty fair offer to the westerners when I was asked what I would do with it, and if the offer had been accepted it would have gone a long way. However, that is a matter of the past. Certain hon. members, before going away, asked me especially to have this item stand. Some of them are very much in favour of the railway, but my hon. friend is not right when he thinks it is held up because it is not taken up to-day. That is not the case. We generally make very much better progress with estimates when members are given an opportunity to state their views. I do not like this item. My hon. friend is hopelessly and entirely wrong. I hope he will not make a habit of that sort of thing. I tried to make it clear that the only reason I was in favour of a vote of this kind was that I could not get out of it, and I ask the minister whether he was holding it down to exactly the same thing, namely, putting in such improvements from time to time, really betterments, as would keep the banks up and prevent flooding of farms and property, and perhaps loss of life, for all of which we would be liable. The structure is there. There is a great deal of difference between that and some other items. The hon. member can see, if he wants to be fair, that there is a great deal of difference in connection with a vote you cannot get out of and one you can get out of.

I do not see any difference in principle at all, because from my point of view and the view of my hon. friend's own leader, the vote on the Hudson Bay railway is one we cannot get out of. I do not want to have any misunderstanding with the hon. gentleman himself. If this request to have this Hudson Bay railway vote held over is merely that it might be the more adequately reviewed, I hays no objection whatever, but I must remind him that for the last four years in this House, the subject has been discussed as no other subject has. Every detail has been brought to light as far as I know, and perhaps one is inclined to be a little too provoked when hon. members hold up this very much overdue item. Those of
us who are interested feel that the summer is coming on, and, unless the Hudson Bay item is dealt with pretty soon, very much of its effect will be lost. That is all. I am very much in sympathy with hon. members who sit behind my hon. friend, and who, like myself, are interested in the item, and I just raise the point on this item, because on the face of it the position seems contradictory, that the hon. member can sit there passively allowing this item to go through-this item for a work which it seems to me is a white elephant-and yet pertinaciously block the more important item of the Hudson Bay railway.

I do not know that I should try to explain to my hon. friend, but I am going to take another shot at it.
I think the Minister of Railways understands it, and I shall try to make my hon. friend understand it. Does my hon. friend think there will be any loss of life if the Hudson Bay railway is not built, and if there is danger of very heavy damage claims being made against the country?
The political aspect-

My hon. friend should be above political considerations. He ought to be, but I am afraid he is becoming a very practical politician, and his politics is the Hudson Bay railway. He is perfectly right in looking after it, but I want to point out that the item which has just gone through, as stated by the Minister of Railways himself, is an absolutely inescapable item. We have had to do (the same thing time and again in connection with inescapable items, and the hon. member who is most insistent that the Hudson Bay item should not go on to-day is a gentleman who is going to vote for it-at least he says so.

In view of the statement
of the minister that the vote is merely for improvements or keeping in condition the portion of the canal already completed, and in view of his further remarks, I understand there is no intention of completing the portion necessary to make the canal navigable from Georgian bay over the summit. At the present time there is a marine railway over the summit in order to permit boats to be transported over the portages, as we call them in western Canada. I suppose that is the name used in the east as well. There is no intention of making further capital expenditures looking to the completion of the canal to the continuous water.
Item agreed to

Supply-Railways and Canals
Welland canal improvements, $395,100.
In view of the other item in regard to the Welland canal standing, I would ask that this one stand also.

I would be willing to
allow this to stand but I might explain to the hon. member that this is in connection with the existing canal. The item in regard to the new Welland canal is already standing.

Item agreed to.
Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, maintenance and operation, $250,030.

What is the
reason for the increase? There seem to be continuous increases.
There is an increase of
What are the details?

This is altogether for the staff of the board, clerks of various kinds, and the list is a lengthy one. There are ninety in the service of the board as against eighty-six last year. That is, there is provision for four more. There has been quite a little reclassification by the Civil Service Commission during the last year and it is difficult to see where the extra four come in.
Is the increase due to increases in salary under the civil service list?
Yes, with the exception of what I have previously mentioned.

I think there is a little more than that. I am again looking to the time when my hon. friend rwould have said in the first instance that we were so frightfully extravagant when as a matter of fact we were so much more economical in 1921.

I did not say that at
all.
I thought the hon. member did.
The hon. member must have a guilty conscience.

Not at all.
There is nothing like knowing that you were much more economical than the other fellow. In 1921 this vote was $190,000 as against $190,150 the year before.

Salaries to-day amount
to $206,000.
[Mr. Murphy. 3

I really thought I had a big enough staff when I was running that organization. I have never been turned down by the government in a single request for expenses. I thought I had enough people working there and it was costing the country quite enough money. The then government never stinted the board in an improper way while I was a commissioner.

Does the hon. gentleman
take into consideration the superior talents of the gentlemen, who now compose the board?

If the minister will take the position suggested by my hon. friend apparently the difference in the cost under different chief commissioners is $60,000 a year. Can we seriously take the suggestion of the hon. gentleman and have the whole of this extravagant increase blamed on the new chairman as is suggested by the hon. member?

The explanation asked
for by my hon. friend with respect to the question of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) is precisely the answer required to his own question. There are no less than forty-six statutory increases and increases due to reclassification in this list this year as compared with last, totalling in all over $6,000. Those come about automatically.

I suppose the
minister has not the number of officials for 1921?

No, but I shall be glad
to get the information for my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When the minister has
been so nice?

I think the
committee will admit that we have been making very good progress. We should continue just in this frame of mind and the item will stand.

I think my hon. friend
will admit I have been more than fair to him this afternoon and unless there is some better reason than merely a desire to secure the number of employees in 1921, I should like to make some progress.

The minister is making good progress. He has been good but he is good only in spots. He has a way of jumping from one extreme to the other. 1 think we had better call the next item.

Supply-Railways and Canals

At this end of the
chamber we can hear nothing at all. I would suggest that the Minister of Railways and the hon. member for West York go outside and settle the question and come back again.
Mr. O'NEILL: While we are on this topic there is one branch more or less overlapping in connection with the handling of explosives. I understand we have an Explosives branch in the Department of Mines but the matter of transporting explosives is under the Board of Railway Commissioners. How much does that service cost? It would seem to be a part of the duties of the Department ol Mines.

There are in the department officers in charge of safety and mechanical appliances as well as of fire prevention, but I do not see anything relating to explosives.
Mr. .O'NEIL:	There must be some staff
to see to the proper transportation of ex-: plosives, to prevent for example the coupling of a special explosive car with a passengei train. What does it cost the railway to carry out this service?

The Board of Railway
Commissioners lay down certain rules governing the transportation of explosives.
Mr. O'NEIL:	But who sees that they are
carried out?

There is no officer known especially as inspector of explosives but 1 presume that some of the officials I have mentioned would see that these regulations were carried out. There are many orders of the Board of Railway Commissioners which are not enforced directly by the railways as my hon. friend implies. They become a part of the laws of the country and persons disregarding them are prosecuted in the usual way. I cannot say definitely offhand that there is any officer especially deputed to look after the matter of explosives, and I am very doubtful whether this would be practicable.

There is a highly competent body in the United States known as the Bureau of Explosives which is at work more or less all the time on this very question. This bureau devises means for the transportation of dangerous commodities and we have largely availed ourselves of its work. We have also experts of our own in our Mines' branch. There are rules and regulations drawn up by the Board of Railway Commissioners with regard to the carrying
of explosives, and while inspectors are engaged supervising the way in which various articles are carried it would be impossible to say just how much it costs to inspect explosives here and explosives there.

speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Carried.
Carried? I am afraid it will be carried on division, and the matter will be opened up again at a time not so convenient to the minister.
I have sent for the Minister of Finance.
I will not delay the passing of the item but it will be carried on division if it is carried at all, and it will be opened up again at a time not convenient to the government.

Canada Highways Commission: to provide for payment of staff of Canada Highways Commission including A. W. Campbell, C. E., Chief Commissioner of Highways, at $5,000 per annum, $32,000.

In what way does the Canada Highways Commission co-operate with the provincial commission in Ontario, let us say? What is the extent of the Dominion commission's jurisdiction over provincial highways?

The provisions of the
Canada Highways Act involve what is known as federal aid to the construction of main highways in the provinces. The work of the commission is gradually drawing to a close. The legislation covered a stated sum of money over a period and as the work is diminishing the staff is being reduced. Next year we expect to complete the work.

Item agreed to. '
To provide for the payment of salaries and expenses in connection with the St. Lawrence ship canal surveys and investigation, including the Canadian National Advisory Committee, and its employees and including E. B. Jost, $2,500, as assistant to Chairman of Engineering board, and G. W. Yates, $1,200, as secretary, $130,000.
What is the personnel of the committee?
What are the names of these engineers?

One is General Mitchell; the other is a French-Canadian whose name I do not know at the moment. Mr. McLachlan of the Department of Railways and Canals is the chairman. He comes under the next item. It 'is estimated he gave 200 days to the work. The balance of the items are travelling expenses.
Where does Mr. McLachlan come in?
Mr. McLachlan gave 17 days per month to this work. That is equivalent to 200 days a year, and at $50 a day it represents $10,000.
What are the different committees we now have on the job?
There is the national committee to which I made reference-
Excuse me, the national committee is composed of Mr. Me-Lachlan, Mr. Mitchell and somebody else.
Those compose the engineering board.
That is what I thought.
The national committee consists of-I will get the names for my hon. friend; I cannot think of them all now. The Right Hon. Mr. Graham is chairman of the national committee.
Not now, is he?

He is still chairman. Then Sir Clifford Sifton, Dr. Mc-Dougald, Mr. Ahearn of Ottawa

and there are several others. I will get a complete list for my hon. friend.
Then there are some other committees?

The inter-departmental
committee-
Who compose the inter-departmental committee? *

A member from each of the following departments:	Militia, Railways and Canals, Public Works, Interior, Justice and External Affairs. I am speaking from memory. The purpose of the committee is to iron out the inter-departmental aspects of the St. Lawrence investigation, as it touches so many of the departments of government.
Can my hon. friend tell us what reports have been made, to whom, and what action, if any, has been taken on them?

This is some of the work completed:
The survey of the St. Lawrence river from Lachine to Montreal, begun in the former year has been completed.
Additional borings have been made along a proposed
route for a canal between Lachine and Nuns island.
Additional borings have been made along the location of a proposed dam across the river at the foot of the Lachine rapids.
A group of 14 borings to rock along the line of the proposed navigation and power channels have been made at the head of lake St. Louis.
Topographical surveys have been extended on both sides of the river between Lachine and Monti eal, particularly in the stretch of the country between Highlands an Verdun, on the north side, and between Cauglinawaga and La Tortue on the south side of the river.
Ten additional borings have been completed along the route of a proposed canal between Hungry bay and the St. Lawrence river.
A number of borings have also been completed along the south shore of the St. Lawrence river, near Cedars, and in addition a line of 12 borings has been completed along the site of a proposed dam across the river at the head of Cedars rapids.
A number of borings were made along the south side of Co tea u rapids.
A number of borings have been made on the site of a proposed power house at the head of lake St. Louis at Cascades point.
The topographical information obtained in the section between lake St. Louis arid lake St. Francis was extended on both sides of the river, and also extended so as to include the islands in the river.
Many additional meterings of flow of the St. Lawrence river at Iroquois point have been made, and a number of precise lines of water levels have been run, and also continuous water elevation records have been secured at control points in the river.
In the international section of the St. Lawrence river, the American section has completed a survey of the river from Kingston to Iroquois, and also between Barnhart island and Cornwall. They have also undertaken a very extensive boring programme which is partly completed. Has the Canadian case

I indicated1 a while ago, possibly while my hon. friend was out of the chamber, that we hoped to have a report from our engineering board to the national board for Canada some time this fall. Then it will be for the similar American board to arrange to meet with our board. Then the thirty-foot Welland canal stands on its own bottom, and I think can be justified in view of the

The reason I asked to-day whether we would be likely to come to a joint decision on this matter was the fact that in the United States at the present time there is a very strong agitation to dig an all-American canal, and as far as one can judge from the newspaper reports that project is receiving a great deal of support. If that canal is ever built co-operation between Canada and the United States for the construction of the St. Lawrence canals would of course be ended. For that reason I think it is of the utmost importance that our case should be prepared, and that we should call upon the United States to come into conference with us and reach a decision whether we are going to carry out this work or not. I regard it as one of the most important moves ever made by the Dominion of Canada. It would give to the cities of Montreal and Quebec, I think, supremacy as the grain exporting ports of the world, because this canal would drain not only our own northwest but a very large part of the northwest and central west of the United States; and if there was the necessary depth to accommodate vessels of large draft we would have a volume of commerce going down practically all the Great Lakes and through the 'St. Lawrence, probably, to Quebec. That would make that route perhaps one of the most important in the entire world. The benefit I anticipate would be this: I do not think very many tramp steamers would come from the ocean to the head of the lakes, although there might be some. I imagine the economical method of handling grain would be to load boats at the head of the lakes with 500,000 bushels, as there are vessels with that capacity. Those vessels would proceed to the city of Quebec or Montreal and break bulk there, filling perhaps three or four tramp steamers that were ready to take the cargoes. There would be some volume-perhaps a considerable volume -of package freight going up the lakes if you will visualize the possibilities of this route as I have hastily tried to sketch it I think it will be admitted that this is the greatest project Canada ever faced for the development of her own trade and for the draining of trade from our neighbours to their advantage' and to our profit. The estimated cost of this work is about $250,000,000.

No.

What is it?
Do you mean the whole cost?

I understood the estimated cost was $250,000,000. I am not including the Welland canal in that 'but I am including the other work on the lower St. Lawrence. It has been pointed out by Mr. Gardener, of Chicago, who has given a great deal of study to this question-has the minister got the figures of the total cost?

When I said, "No" I
had in mind that my hon. friend was not including the Welland canal.

No, I was not including
the Welland canal.
The preliminary estimate of the cost of the portion from Kingston to Montreal is $252,000,000.

That is what I had in
mind. Now, Mr. Gardener points this out- I met him here a little more than a year ago and had a long interview with him. The plan he suggested for financing the enterprise is a joint commission of United States and Canada that would construct the work and operate it afterwards without profit. The commissioners would have to be paid, and no doubt there would be a considerable staff to operate the canal and keep track of all the accounts; but if this work can be constructed by the two governments jointly and operated at cost we would have not only an ample waterway but one that could be used under the very best conditions. Looking at it in this way, in the broad view as it affects every province, with perhaps the exception of British Columbia, enabling us, as it would, to draw so much trade and traffic from our neighbours, I say this is the most important project Canada has ever faced in the way of transportation. I would urge the minister therefore to press upon the commissioners the necessity of bringing the other nation into conference and of reaching a conclusion from our standpoint as quickly as possible. I think the conclusion would ibe in favour of the canal; at any rate I hope so. We ought to know before the agitation for the allAmerican canal through the State of New fork is carried very much further.

I might repeat what I
said this afternoon with reference to the time the Joint Engineering Board will probably report. With regard to the all American project, I am informed the initial estimate of cost for the all American canal is in the neighbourhood of $600,000,000, so that there are a few discouraging factors.

A few hundred million
does not mean very much over there.

Perhaps not. There is
no power development possible on the all American route. I do not want to enter into a discussion now of what the possible benefit of the St. Lawrence ship canal might be. The national advisory committee will investigate that point and obtain the information, and I do not want to anticipate by any too-glowing prophecies what the detailed result of the examination will be. It is very important we should know all that it is possible to find out about it before a decision is reached.

What is the
date of the report of the International Joint Commission? I think the commission made a report some time ago recommending the adoption of the scheme.

December 19, 1921. I
will read an extract from the recommendation which will show that we have given attention to that and followed it up. The quotation reads:
In a matter of such unusual magnitude, involving engineering factors that are more or less debatable, and affecting the interests of many millions of people, too much care cannot be taken to ensure the adoption of plans that will be beyond reasonable criticism, both as to the general scheme of development and the working out of its details. It is therefore desirable that before any steps are taken to carry out the commission's recommendations, the plans of the engineering board, together with such comments or criticisms or alternative plans as have been filed with the commission by other engineers, should be referred back to the board enlarged by other leading members of the engineering profession, to the end that the whole question be given that further and complete study that its magnitude and importance demand.

How many
years will the consideration be held up?

Then it will be a question of the National Committees giving consideration to that report from the point of view of the nation appointing it. International action of course will result.

In connection with this
project, I am not at the moment going to offer any opinion as a private citizen whether or not Canada should adopt the scheme and go ahead.

not the time or the place, in the absence of information, to do it. The time is close at hand, if it has not already arrived, when something of a fairly definite character should be determined. The minister read an extract from the report of the International Joint Commission in 1921 which indicated that a reference of the problem, which had already received very considerable study, should be made back to an enlarged or extended group of the engineering profession.
I think that proposition is perfectly sound.
I am not going to offer a single criticism of the members of the engineering profession forming that board, but I do wish to offer a criticism as to the wisdom of the appointment of the additional board, superimposed upon the engineering board. There is another board composed of Sir Clifford Sifton, Dr. McDougald, of Montreal, and the other gentlemen named, some of whom I think are very estimable gentlemen and probably highly qualified, and some much less qualified. The impression has been in my mind for some time, and has been emphasized somewhat to-night, that this board is a sort of tactical board, a board of policy-
Strategy.

No, that is a sacred term which should not be dragged into these sordid matters. I would say a board of policy, a board of tactics, a board which-if I am doing the minister an injustice he will I am sure hasten to correct me-would meet and consider the problem. It was no doubt felt that when the engineers or technical men got through with their part of the work and passed their report to this superimposed board, there might be, in the study of it, indefinite and interminable delay for years to come. Frankly I think this matter is of such great importance that the complete technical information of the department should be placed before this House as early as possible. I understand the care that is necessary, but the International Joint Commission report was made about four and a half years ago, and the study for that period of four and a half years by this engineering board is almost sufficient to supply us with the necessary technical information. I should like to suggest that parliament should be placed in possession at an early date-I would say at the next session of parliament-with the fullest possible draft of all the engineering problems solved, so that they might judge of the merits of the matter from a national standpoint. I am not prepared to offer any
opinion. It would be utterly futile for me to attempt to suggest it, but I think we should have before parliament this information. I agree with my friend from Toronto (Mr. Ilocken) that this is perhaps one of the most important matters that has been brought to the attention of, not the House, but the country, for many years. It is going to be difficult to work it out from a constitutional and economic standpoint. The expenditure of this money from year to year is warranted and desirable only if there is a definite objective in mind and I hope the. engineers' report or reports, because I apprehend it would not be necessary for them to. complete and exhaust every problem before, bringing in some report-
Would my hon. friend advocate an interim report from the engineers?	.

I am not advocating it; so far as I can recall, I have not spoken to an engineer on this subject except last year to one or two who were not on the board, very eminent men. If the engineers said that it was inadvisable I would not offer my opinion against theirs. But if the engineers are prepared to make an interim report on any branch of the whole problem it is important that parliament be seized of that information. I again wish to place before the minister my suspicion that the national advisory committee is the fifth wheel to the coach. I do not want the minister to give me that betraying smile again, but I think he has suspicions of the same character.
Perhaps my hon. friend will let me state my own suspicions and not put them into my mouth.

It is rather friendly and brotherly assistance I am giving to the minister, because I know it would be awkward on that side of the House to express such a suspicion and I would not expect the hon. gentleman to do so. This fifth wheel to the coach, this advisory board, may be the medium through which this problem will be delayed. There are large interests in Canada opposed to this; there are others very strongly in favour; but parliament should at the earliest possible day have the fullest information so that parliament itself may determine the wise course to pursue.

In the meantime we have to carry on what we have in hand, namely, a deeper waterway from the upper lakes to the St. Lawrence. That includes what is now under way, the deepening of the Welland canal to a depth of thirty feet-and we

Supply-Railways and Canals
have been told this evening that this is to be completed within five years. This is an important work and it must be carried on. There is, so I understand, a proposal under consideration to get deeper water for larger vessels carrying grain as far as Prescott and I would be glad if the minister would say something about that. We ought to continue until we get twenty or twenty-five feet of water right into the port of Montreal. I understand the cost would be greater to get the required depth below Prescott. Hav'ng the information that it will take a long time to frame a policy in regard to the St. Lawrence deep waterways; \ye must go on with and press for an extension and a deepening of the Canadian waterways which can be used in the meantime jointly by the United States and ourselves, the United States to be contributory to the cost of keeping them up.

With regard to the
question of the hon. member for South York, the canal works are being put down to a depth of thirty feet, but the maximum depth of the reaches will be twenty-five feet. As I indicated this afternoon, the work on the Welland canal will be completed in four or .five years. I can assure the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) that whatever smile I had on my .face was not at the advisory board but at the board of strategy on that side of the House to which reference has occasionally been made. I can understand my hon. friend being rather suspicious of boards of strategy after the experience of a little while ago. The national advisory committee has a serious purpose. As regards the suggestion which my hon. friend made that possibly the engineering reports would be sufficient and that we should got no further, he ignores the fact that technical men working on the engineering end of the problem cannot be expected to take into account all the economic factors resulting from the operation of such a waterway. Neither can they be expected to be able to give adequate consideration to the international political questions involved and there are many questions of that nature.
The terms of reference in the order in council which I read just after we resumed at eight o'clock give an idea of the work of the national advisory committee. Further, the whole of Canada will become responsible to this great work if it is undertaken, and therefore the national advisory committee contains representative men from other sections of Canada than the section in which the work is contemplated. For instance the Maritime provinces will have to bear their

share of responsibility of this large sum of money and there is a representative from the Maritime provinces. There is a gentleman from Vancouver. The port interests of Montreal, Quebec and Toronto are also represented.
Who represents Toronto?

Sir Clifford Sifton. In the United States there is a similar body whose duty is to deal with this matter. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre appears to doubt the bona tides of a national advisory committee in connection with this matter. Frankly I think it is absolutely necessary that a body of representative men who are willing to devote their attention to this matter and to consider in detail all the reports should advise the government with regard thereto after studying the various phases of the question. The United States have found the same course advisable; the distribution of the members of their national committee is almost similar to the distribution of our own, and the national advisory committee has a serious purpose in view.

Another reason why we should speed this up- is that at the present time the city of Chicago and some of the states between that city and the Mississippi are agitating for enough water to operate a barge canal. There is great resistance to that from Michigan, Ohio and some of the other states.

matter. That is the belief to-day. The government have appointed different committees to make sure that nothing shall be done at the moment. This matter has been in the hands of the government ever since they came in; the report is dated December, 1921. The engineer can tell the minister whether I am wrong.
I am getting the information.
Am I wrong?

My hon. friend is not
correct.

Possibly by hon. friend
does not know that the construction at Morrisburg is on the international section of the canal and without the co-operation of the United States government development is not possible.

I did not say it was. The fact of the matter is that everything is being done to prevent co-operation with the state of New York, which is actively interested in this undertaking. If there is a clash of interests, ought not the government to look into the matter? This is nothing new. The newspapers have made the same charge and it has never been denied. There is a direct interest on one side, absolutely opposed to the interest of the people in securing development of power on the St. Lawrence. Sir Clifford Sifton, we understand, controls or is interested in the Georgian bay ship canal project. Why? The Minister of Justice will correct me if I am wrong when I say the company claims that, while it was incorporated originally for the purpose of improving waterways, it has the right to all water powers on the river and particularly to such water powers as are generated in the improvement of any waterway. There is therefore a direct relation between the delay in this matter and the interest of the company. [Sir Henry Drayton.)
end the development of electricity, just as much perhaps as navigation itself, ought not to be those who are directiy interested in seeing that that development does not take place. We have had no action yet at all.
That is not so.

I will reply when my
hon. friend has finished.

Very well, I
should like to have the information now.

Oh yes, that!

That! That is one
of the most important things to be done. I do not know;

The contractors for sections Nos. 3 and 4 are obligated to supply all crushed stone needed for sections Nos. 1 and 2 under contract with Mr. J. F. Porter, and this supply has precedence over any rock needed for sections Nos. 3 and 4.
When the contract for sections 3 and 4 was awarded in June 1922, no excavation had been started in section 4, but excavation in section 3 was well under way and the rock excavated therein, containing no clay or other objectionable matter for concrete, was all sent to the crusher. In none of our borings in section 4 did we find rock of a character different to that found in section 3, and it was no doubt on this assumption that the contractors put in their unit tender prices.
Acting on this assumption we did not force the contractors to reserve all stone excavated from sections 3 and 4 for sections 1 and 2 and we allowed them to use a large portion of it for concrete work.
Contrary to all anticipation, it is now found that the southern end of section 4, from Stations 360 to 397, has a rock formation intermixed with thick vertical and horizontal seams of brown clay and silt rendering necessary the washing of the greater part of the rock before allowing it to proceed to the crusher.
A very close tab has been kept of the extra cost to the -contractors of this washing, as detailed in division engineer Lazier's report of August 25th. 1925 and engineer in charge Grant's report of September 25th, 1925.

I realize of course that there are important ports in Canada which are managed without the assistance of harbour commissions, and I may assure the hon. gentleman that if a request comes from any such port there will be no resistance on the part of the government. In this case the people are satisfied that the business of the port can be carried on to better advantage if a commission is appointed. speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
These two sections which we intend to repeal were added |to the Criminal Code in 1919. I do not say that they were placed in the act on account of events in Winnipeg, although it was done after those events. But it was explained at the time that owing to the period of unrest through which the world was passing it would be important to place those sections in the act which, if not enlarging the powers already given under the clauses relating to sedition, would at least make them more definite in certain ways. It was further explained that they were intended to replace to a large extent, certain provisions which had been made during the war under the War Measures Act by way of orders in council. Since that time labour in general, but especially organized labour, has continually and strongly complained about these two sections. Every year since I have been a member of the government representatives of the Trades and Labour Congress, when they came annually to present their suggestions to the government, have asked that these two sections might be repealed, leaving the situation as it was prior to 1919. They have always feared that the sections in question would be directed against the activities of labour unions, although those who are responsible for the insertion of the sections in the code always claimed that such was not the intention. At all events we have already in the code sufficient protection as to everything against which we should be protected in the matter of sedition. We have those precautions in section 87 and also provisions concerning unlawful assemblies. We find provisions in section 130 regarding sedition, oaths or engagements in societies; in section 132 against seditious words, seditious libel and seditious conspiracy, in section 135 against any libel on a foreign sovereign, and in section 136 against publishing false news. Sedition under the British law, of course, is an old offence, but there has never been a strict definition of sedition. I think it was in 1880 that the British commissioners who. were entrusted with the work of drafting the English code inserted a clause defining seditious intention. That clause read as follows:
An intention to bring into hatred or contempt or to excite disaffection against the person of Her Majesty, or the government and constitution of the United

Criminal Code Amendment
Kingdom or of any part of it as by law established, or either House of Parliament, or the administration of justice; or
to excite Her Majesty's subjects to attempt to procure, otherwise than by lawful means, the alteration of any matter in church or state by law established; or
to raise discontent or disaffection amongst Her Majesty's subjects; or to promote feelings of ill will and hostility between different classes of such subjects.
This was not made part of the British code; parliament rather preferred to let the tribunals decide as to sedition under the common law as the practice had always been in the past. The same thing happened in Canada. When our Criminal Code was introduced in parliament there was a clause similar to the one which had been drafted by the commissioners of the English code. Here also, after a good deal of discussion and criticism, both in committee and in the House, the clause was not accepted, and we were left with the old British law concerning sedition and governed by the common law of England. This has always worked well in Canada, as well as in Great Britain, and I am firmly convinced that the sections which were added in 1919, on account, as was said at the time, of the unrest which prevailed in the world, are not at all necessary. I asked the officers of the Department of Justice to ascertain whether any prosecutions had ever been made under these sections, and I was told that they could find no record of any.

speechtext: Well one of the grounds of their fears was the use of the word "force", coupled with the word "industrial or economic change."
