speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend may
be sure that the Criminal Code as it was and as it will be left- will be sufficient to protect the citizens of Canada in that respect. I am far from being sure that these sections have improved our code. I think the British system with regard to this is better than the United States system. These are really copies of the United States law in this matter and I am in favour of the British system.

If I may supplement what the minister has said with regard to the objections of organized labour, I should like to quote a paragraph or two from the 1920 report of the proceedings of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada. They had taken the advice of Mr. J. G. O'Donoghue of Toronto with regard to the bearing of certain of these sections. He gives his reasons for his objection to these two words "force" and "terrorism" which had been made use of in connection with the Winnipeg trials.
Judge Metcalfe's charge to the jury in the Russell case contained the following:
Mr. Russell gave us his idea of a sympathetic strike. He said, "When a dispute originates between an employer and his employees, and when the labour organizations see that organization being beat, they come to their assistance by calling a strike to force their employers to bring force to bear upon the original disputants to make settlement." That is Russell's definition given in the boa. . . . Force, force, force.
The comment is made:
A court would be quite justified in interpreting the word in its natural or dictionary sense.
As for the word "terrorism", some light can be thrown upon the interpretation of it by that given in the Winnipeg case of Rex vs. Russell. There Judge Metcalfe says:
"To walk around about, for instance, to a place where people are employed in large numbers, and to 'boo', gentlemen of the jury, as much terror may be inspired through that as by two or three fighting ohaps coming along with bludgeons. Take it from me, in strikes you can incite terror without hitting a man over the head. You can incite terror of starvation; you can incite terror of thirst. Is not that quite as effective as inciting by bodily violence? Your stomach will bring you quicker than a crack on the head sometimes. If it is possible that picketing can be done in this country, then the lawful method of picketing is so ineffective that it is a reasonable inference that in strikes of this class, unlawful means would be intended to be applied. Sometimes it has a deterring effect upon people's minds by exposing them to have their motions watohed, and to encounter black looks."
The last couple of lines show the possibilities of the word "terrorism."
But apart from the question of altering these two words, I should like to call attention in the sections to be repealed to several phrases which I think any hon. gentleman will come to realize are not such as we would like to leave in the laws of this country. In defining an unlawful association one section speaks of any society that advocates the use of force. Again that word is used, but force may be economic force. What do we mean by force? Further, there is this provision with regard to the property of such unlawful association:
Any property, real or personal, belonging or suspected to belong to an unlawful association. . . may, without warrant, be seized or taken possession of. . . and may thereupon be forfeited to His Majesty.

A trades union is not

As the minister

The janitor of a hall in which was held a meeting of an association which was suspected to be unlawful might be charged with being associated with that organization and liable to imprisonment. If it be proved that the person charged has (a) attended meetings of an unlawful association. . . it shall be presumed, in the absence of proof to the contrary that he is a member of such unlawful association.
That seems to me a most outrageous clause. If an association is holding a street meeting and someone comes along to listen to what has been said, he is then presumed to be a member of such association and the burden of proof lies with him. We used to be taught that a man ought to be regarded as innocent until he was proven guilty. According to this legislation the thing is reversed and the very fact that he attends a meeting is presumptive evidence that he belongs to an association. Further, any owner of any theatre or other building in which a meeting is held, although he may know nothing about the matter, may be dragged in because there has been this meeting of an unlawful association.
It reads "who knowingly permits", which is contrary to what the hon. member has just said.

What I meant to say was that the owner of a hall may know the name of an organization, but it is very difficult for him to determine whether or not that organization is unlawful. He may rent his hall or he may be afraid to rent it for fear of being dragged in. A little further down section 6 reads:
If. [DOT] * . any justice of the peace is satisfied. . . that there is reasonable ground for suspecting that any contravention of this section has been or is about to be committed, he may issue a search warrant-
And so on, to seize and carry away books. That is going still further. How any justice of the peace can be more of a mind reader than anybody else, and can determine beforehand whether a crime is going to be committed, I do not know.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We really do not need these sections in the code.

Suppose that as
between different nationals in this country or as between religious bodies prejudice ran high: you can understand how readily some petty police magistrate might get the idea into his head that someone was about to do something dreadful. Would it be reasonable that he should have power immediately to order seizure of property in such a case? In this connection I might quote from a judgment of Lord Camden, who held that search warrants were contrary to the fundamental

Criminal Code Amendment
Anglo-Saxon rights of personal security and property:
Where is the written law that gives any magistrate such a power? I can safely answer there in none, and therefore it is too much for us without authority to presume a practice legal which would be subversive of all the comforts of society. . . If suspicion at large should be on a ground for search especially in the case of libels, i.e., seditious publications, whose home would be safe?
We may well take the judgment of Lord Camden on such a point. It is provided further in the code that any person who imports into Canada from any other country any such literature shall be liable to twenty years. I remember an instance several years ago in which a friend of mine wrote to me with regard to a book which he had ordered from England and which had been seized in the customs. On inquiry of the customs officer I found that this book was regarded by the postal authorities as seditious, notwithstanding the fact that it was published in England and that copies of it were on the shelves in some of our public libraries. I wrote back to my friend and told him that he might consider himself lucky that he was not serving twenty years in the penitentiary inasmuch as action could have been taken against him under this legislation in the Criminal Code.
To a large extent our policy after the Great war and subsequent to the Russian revolu-toin, when people were very much afraid of what might happen throughout the world, was almost as repressive as the legislation which was adopted in Great Britain a hundred years previously after the Napoleonic wars. In this connection I would quote from May's Constitutional History of England touching the legislation of 1792. At page 33 he says:
The influential classes, more alarmed than the government, eagerly fomented the prevailing spirit of reaction. They had long been jealous of the growing influence of the press and popular opinion. Their own power had been disturbed by the political agitation of the last thirty years, and was further threatened by parliamentary reform. But the time had now come for recovering their ascendency. The democratic spirit of the people was betraying itself, and must be crushed out in the cause of order. The dangers of parliamentary reform were illustrated by clamours for universal suffrage, annual parliaments, and the rights of man; and reformers of all degrees were to be scouted as revolutionary. . . It was a crisis of unexampled difficulty, needing the utmost vigilance and firmness. Ministers, charged with the maintenance of order, could not neglect any security which the peril of the time demanded. They were secure of support in punishing sedition and treason; the guilty few would meet with no sympathy among a loyal people. But, counselled by their new chancellor and convert, Lord Loughborough, and the law officers of the crown, the government gave too ready a credence to the reports of their agent: and invested the doings of a small knot of democrats-chiefly working men- *with the dignity of a wide-spread conspiracy to
overturn the constitution. Ruling over a free state, they learned to dread the peo-ple, in the spirit of tyrants. Instead of relying upon the sober judgment of the country, they appealed to its fears; and in repressing seditious practices, they were prepared to sacrifice liberty of opinion. Their policy, dictated by the circumstances of a time of strange and untried danger, was approved by the prevailing sentiment of their contemporaries: but has not been justified in an age of greater freedom, by the maturer judgment of posterity.
That summary of conditions which prevailed in that time of unrest may well suggest to us that possibly we have been carried away by some such fear and that the time has come for us to follow more nearly the practice that obtains in Great Britain.

I should be the last to
suggest that there should be any restriction in the operations of properly organized trades unions. The trades union has in the social system a place which is firmly established, and he would be a judge of very tyrannical and questionable judgment who would read into trades union disputes anything of the character suggested in what the hon. gentleman has quoted. He has cited the conditions that prevailed after the Napoleonic wars. But are we not in a somewhat different position to-day? There is at this time a nation of between 130.000,000 ' and 150,000,000, the purpose of whose government is to upset the government of all other nations. A world revolution is the policy of the Russian government; there can be no doubt of that. This they declare to be their policy, and instead of applying their own resources to the improvement of internal social conditions they send vast sums of money to other countries to stir up strife with the end in view of precipitating revolution. In the strike which has just concluded in England large sums of Russian money were offered, and in one or two instances accepted, and the offer was not made to assist in winning the strike. I do not think anyone would suggest that.

speechtext:
We are running away from the bill.
Mr. H0CKEN: I know we are, but I am coming back to it. I want to show why I think there is necessity for some part of that clause. There cannot be any doubt about that, and my argument is, Sir, that while we have 130,000,000 people controlled by revolutionists, who, not satisfied with that they have accomplished in their own country, are keenly anxious to upset constitutional government in all other countries, we must have some law on our statute books to protect us from their activities. The Soviet emissaries are found not only in Great Britain, but in this country, in the United States, in China, in Japan and in India, in fact they are scattered all over the world, and when this Dominion may be made the special object of their attack nobody can tell. I am one of those who believe we are bound continually to have reform, to advance in our social life; but eveiy proposal to that end should be tried and its merits proven before it is put into operation. This is the very opposite of revolution. There has been evolution in our social and industrial life during my time that is really remarkable. When I contrast the conditions under which we now live with the conditions under which I grew up as a boy, I find they are immensely improved to-day. All this goes to show that the process of evolution is proceeding in industry as well as in all other spheres of human activity. I think that is the proper form of procedure. But when we find men who are determined to bring about world revolution and to establish what they call the "rule of the proletariat" in every country of the world, and using the resources of the national treasury of Russia to bring about that violent change, then I say every country that desires to preserve its institutions is warranted in enacting the necessary protective legislation-not to apply such legislation against its own citizens who

may be conducting an industrial strike, but to keep out aliens whose only desire is to create dissatisfaction and stir up discord in an effort to upset the government of the country.
Would not our immigration laws prevent them getting in?
No. I am entirely sympathetic towards trade unions and the orderly development of our industrial system, but I am absolutely opposed to anything in the shape of revolution.

speechtext:
May I tell my hon.
friend that this bill is not desired by the extremists to whom he is referring but by the Trades nad Labour Congress, which has been asking for such legislation as that which I am now presenting to the House. As my hon. friend says, we must encourage legitimate labour organizations.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When speaking on the Winnipeg strike some years ago, I took the opportunity of saying, that the extremists do not like the legitimate labour organizations, because they do not want any agreement with capital. Mr. Chairman, I should like to say to my hon. friend who is directing this bill-and I am speaking entirely for myself; I have not consulted by colleagues other than to speak to those immediately adjoining me to-night-that I would be quite agreeable to the repeal of these two clauses, particularly in view of the assurance that he gives, in which I am quite certain he is sincere, that the offences covered by them are fully covered in the general law which has been on the statute books for many years. Now, I address myself more directly to the observations of my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and the school of thought he represents, because we might as well talk frankly about these things; and I concede he has the right

to hold whatever views appeal to him-what alarms me is this: but before expressing my views let me quote subsection (1) of section 97A, which it is intended to repeal:
Any association, organization, society or corporation, whose professed purpose or one of whose purposes is to bring about any governmental, industrial or economic change within Canada, by use of force, violence or physical injury to person or property, or by threats of such injury, or which teaches, advocates, advises or defends the use of force, violence, terrorism, or physical injury to person or property, or threats of such injury, in order ,to accomplish Such change, or for any other purpose, or which shall by any means prosecute or pursue such purpose or professed purpose, or shall so teach, advocate, advise or defend, shall be an unlawful association.
Now, my hon. friend extracts from the old sections a paragraph here and there. Prior to his rising to his feet I had marked certain clauses and I was going to suggest to him that certain portions which I think extreme should be changed. But I direct his attention and the attention of the House to this point:	You have got to read that
section in its entirety, for what it is intended to deal with is the heart and kernel of the attempt that was made not only in Winnipeg, but also in Vancouver, in Calgary and in other centres of Canada where it did not really come to light. The section was drafted to cover the type of organization actually in existence in the form of corporate bodies, deliberately intending to wreck the governmental institutions of this country by violence. There is no question of that.
I want to register an objection to that. May I say a word here ?
I do not think it quite the courteous thing to interrupt.
Very well, I will wait until the hon. gentleman is finished.

I always give way to anyone who wants to interrupt, but I think one might be allowed to finish one train of thought. At that time organizations-yes, an organization of a nation wide character- physically visible in Winnipeg, Calgary and Vancouver and known in other sections of the country, was in existence with the deliberate intention of wrecking our constitutional, democratic form of government by violence. There is no doubt of that.

I am not going to be drawn into an argument; I do not think anyone will question it.
I question it.

My hon. friend will
surely not suggest for a moment that he does not know what I have said to be absolutely correct.
I certainly deny it in toto.

I am sorry my hon. friend does so, because I had a fairly high regard for him, though differing from his economic views and from his socialistic views. There are a great many persons for whom I have a personal regard but who hold these extreme views, honestly I believe. But that does not prevent me from expressing my absolute abhorrence of the process or processes which they purpose to adopt, and there can be no doubt but that that condition existed in Canada when this law was passed. Fortunately for Canada, for Germany, for Austria and for the Balkan states which change so frequently; fortunately 11 p.m. for old England and for the United States, though to a less degree, and fortunately for many of the principal countries of the world, the time has passed for the moment when this force or association of forces is very serious or menacing. Yes, and it may be again.. Now, Mr. Chairman, we have on our statute books and in the Criminal Code very many sections which I might say are useless and unnecessary so far as the average life of the ordinary citizen is concerned. But why are they there? They are there to meet a possible contingency which may arise; some evil-designed person or group of persons may set out to perpetrate a crime against society, and therefore we protect society by these provisions in the Criminal Code. That leads me to the suggestion that the very language marked here for opprobrium and condemnation will be found in other sections of the Criminal Code. Although I am not a lawyer and may be entirely wrong, I will hazard the guess that one of the expressions used a moment ago-"or is about to be committed''

which was used as a reason whv this clause should be wiped out, will be tound in other sections of the Criminal Code; it must necessarily be there. I will appeal to my friend the Minister of Justice, and I am sure he will sustain me. If one suspects that the crime of murder or arson or grand larceny or something else is about to be committed-

Or smuggling.

Criminal Code Amendment

Yes, or smuggling-there rests upon that person a duty to do whatever may be in his power to prevent it, and he may get a search warrant through the proper processes. I noted in my bill certain words; one of the things I cited was this phrase, "without warrant", in one section. I have always been very strongly opposed to giving wide license-I did not use the word "liberty" -to peace officers to make searches without warrant; I think we cannot be too careful in that regard. But because I support that principle, and have done so during the fifteen years I have been in this House, I do not want to be classified as one who condemns the structure of society as we now have it, and the institutions we have to-day. I do not want to associate myself, for instance, with a wholesale condemnation of the intent of this legislation, which was passed in a time of stress.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I don't want to, either.

I am sure my hon. friend does not. That is one reason why I find myself in a somewhat difficult position. I know that my good friend (Mr. Heaps) who is extreme in his views in regard to this and kindred matters will, when this is repealed- and I am prepared to support its repeal on the grounds advanced by the Minister of Justice-go through this country and acclaim it as a victory for the school of thought which he represents in this House. That is one of the reasons I find a dislike, if I may use the word, to support it. If my hon. friend and those associated with 'him would take the stand taken by the Minister of Justice; if he would take the moderate stand he adopted in his language to-night I would gladly associate myself with him in bringing about the repeal of this measure. But I am apprehensive that its very repeal will be used throughout Canada within the ambit of those who follow the Third Internationale, if I might use that name in a broad sense, as a victory and an encouragement to them to carry on their agitations.
I have one other thought .'before I sit down. The experience since 1918, the year of the second revolution in Russia; the experience which is not limited to Russia but which centres there because Russia was chosen as a plastic and suitable place to bring their schemes into existence; the experience the world has had of that doctrine, warrants us in setting our faces unswervingly against this propaganda and its extension here or wherever an effort may be made to spread it. It should also be 'borne in mind that the doctrines of the Third Internationale, against 
which this legislation was directed, are not the doctrines of the masses; they are not the doctrines of democracy or the proletariat. They are the doctrines of a very narrow group of highly educated but wholly unscrupulous individuals who are seeking for power and who exercise in Russia a more rigid and more arbitrary power than has ever been exerj cised within the last hundred years by afiy government on the face of the earth.
I am quite aware that in answer to this statement it will be advanced that the government of Russia to-day is moderate, and that it has qualified its former drastic measures. That is true. Why? Because in the face of an overwhelming world-wide antagonism, not in the ranks of a few capitalists or others but among the rank and file of the people of a dozen countries, in the face of an overwhelming influence from that source they were forced to abandon their extreme economic standards and views and come in large measure back to the normal economic views held in other countries. Yet the avowed intention of the Third Internationale, which still stands behind and whose hand still overshadows the Russian government, is still there. I have a great faith in the people of Canada and have often stated that I do not think such a doctrine can ever find root and succeed in this country; but there were times and there were places where it had such a measure of success that it made a great many of us falter in our confidence in its inability to succeed. So while I personally feel inclined to accept the very moderate and, I think, very reasonable view advanced by the Minister of Justice, I do not wish to allow myself to be associated with the suggestion that this legislation was evil or that its intent was evil; and it is only with the assurance that our liberties are safeguarded in other ways that I would consent at all to agree to its removal.

I do not wish to
delay the passing of this section by speaking at any length, but as the last speaker has directed his remarks to me rather than to the bill, I cannot allow his statements to pass without adding a few words. I would say distinctly that I am not under trial or on the defensive at all. It always amuses me to find the assurance with which some hon. members of this House undertake to lecture other members. Some of them are apt to get very hysterical about Russia. I do not know why Russia should be introduced into this discussion. While the hon. member for Toronto West Centre was speaking I recalled that I had seen in the Graphic a few days ago a rather interesting

Criminal Code Amendment
illustration showing that in England, they do not get quite so excited about these things. This was an illustration of the unfurling of the Soviet flag at the Shakespeare celebration at Stratford-on-Avon. Evidently the Russian officials, one of whom was the official trade representative of Russia for some time in Montreal, were participating in a tribute frohn that country to the great British poet. I do not know why in Canada-other than because we are so near to the hysterical United States-we have to become so excited about Russia. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) spent the greater part of his speech in denouncing the Third Internationale which, according to him, is wholly unscrupulous, one of the worst institutions that has ever existed on the face of the earth, and incidentally he tried to associate me with that body. Well, I may say very frankly, without criticizing the Third Internationale or defending it, that I belong to an organization that has no affiliation whatever with the Third Internationale, and if the hon. member would take a little trouble to read the labour papers he would find that the organ of the Third Internationale sometimes criticises very severely the organization which my comrade and I represent because we are so far from being in harmony with their position.
What organization do you represent?

The Independent
Labour Party of Manitoba. We were both elected on its platform, and as my comrade (Mr. Heaps) suggests, we have had the opposition of the communists in the political field. So it is always just a little bit amusing to those of us who have been at all near the inside of the labour movement to hear the perfectly wild statements made by some honourable members-statements which they would be ashamed to make if they had any real knowledge of the situation. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre seeks to associate me with the Third Internationale after he has denounced it in round terms and states that I belong to a certain school of thought, that I am extreme in my views. Well, I have tried to express myself as clearly as possible during the last five years in this House, and I have said here the very self-same things that I have been saying up and down the country.
No, only a part of them.

No, the self-same
things. I will allow the hon. member for Vancouver Centre to read the very charges

The other night when I suggested a capital levy for the extinction of the war debt, which is a part of our programme, one hon. gentleman stated that it savoured of Moscow. It is the first time in my life I have ever heard that the extinction of the war debt by means of a capital levy was ever advocated in Moscow. As a matter of fact we took the proposal from the programme of the British Labour party.

In Russia they took it
all.

Quite so; there
they did not wait for a capital levy,

from those who became millionaires during the war?

I do not blame the hon. member. I know how widely such statements were circulated by the press at the time. But I should like to suggest to him that I was as closely connected with that strike as most men. I was not officially connected with it, I did not arrive in Winnipeg until the third week of the strike. But I knew the labour situation intimately at the coast; I knew intimately the men in Winnipeg, and I want to say that there was not one scrap of evidence adduced during the six weeks of the trial that showed there had been any preparation whatever to overturn the government by force of arms. One other word on this subject and I am through. The hon. gentleman would try to make out that I am advocating the use of force. I would say to him and the House very frankly that on principle I am opposed to the use of force. The political organization which I represent is opposed to the use

of force. That is one reason why we are criticized some times by the representatives of the Third Internationale. We carry our views in that regard to this extent:	We are
opposed to military force in settling disputes as between nations just as we are to its use in the settlement of disputes as between classes. And the irony of the whole situation is that some of us who during the years of war were accused of everything under the sun that was bad because we opposed force in settling international disputes, have later been accused of the advocacy of force in the settlement of class disputes. I repeat that personally I am opposed to force and further that in advocating the wiping out of th:s legislation I am not urging or defending the use of force for the attainment of the objects of labour. I would say to the hon. member opposite that if the labouring people are agitating as some of them do, sooner or later force will have to be used; why are they doing it? Because they have learned the use of force from those who control our government to-day. They say that if force was used in whipping the Germans, force is also justified in securing our rights. I think their logic cannot very well be disputed.
You are advocating force.
No.
What are you doing then?

I think any hon. member who has listened to my speech will say that I have not advocated force. I would say that many of the labour people have learned the use of force from those who employed it during the war.
That is the government.

Yes, and having
learned the lesson, they say that if the only way of defeating the Germans was by mean3 of force, and if the only way of settling other international disputes is by force, then the means of settling class disputes is by force.
You believe that?
No, nor do I believe it is the way to settle international disputes. That is why I am voting for disarmament all along the line.

Will my hon. friend dispute the fact that the strike in Seattle, the possession of that city for several days by a certain group, the general strike in Vancouver and the general strike in Winnipeg, were car-

ried on by the application of force, without quibbling as to what form of force? My second question is, was not my hon. friend in favour of and supporting ali three strikes?
I am afraid we are digressing from the bill before the committee, but with regard to that word "force" there was no armed force-
That is a different thing. '
No armed force in the Winnipeg strike.

There was a concerted effort on the part of the labour people in general, or a sympathetic strike.

No.
Absolutely.
No.

physical control of the management of the community.
Since my hon, friend has asked me the question, I do not believe there was any real connection between the Seattle strike and the strikes in Canada.
Oh yes there was, directly.

I would admit that at that time there was a good deal of general unrest all over and there was a feeling after the war that we had come to the time when we should settle things on a new basis. The manufacturers and others were talking of reconstruction and the labour people were talking of reconstruction, only-I will adfndt this- that the word they most commonly used was "social" or "economic" revolution, which is a technical phrase in all socialist literature, and which means that since a hundred years ago we had an industrial revolution which changed production from individual to collective production, it had to be followed by another revolution, economic and social which would give democracy in industry. Does that answer the question?
No.

I am very much in
the same position as my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre. I am prepared to accept the assurances of the hon. Minister of Justice that there are provisions in the Criminal Code that take care of the situation that this

enactment was designed to take care of, and that words and phrases in this enactment which were prepared perhaps hurriedly and which are too strong should be eliminated. For instance, in the very first paragraph the word "force", which is used in two places, could have very well be left out, and the clause would have carried identically the same meaning and served the same purpose. The positions of the labour organizations, and particularly the railway brotherhood, have been referred to, I would like to point out that the movement that this enactment was designed to correct had for its purpose the destruction of these very organizations. I am not going to follow my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre. I read into the record a couple of evenings ago a statement, in which it was clearly set out that the first purpose of that movement was the destruction of organized labour. Those who wanted to bring that about recognized that organized labour stood as the main barrier in their road to the progress they desired to make, and the whole movement, originating as it did in the western and northwestern United States and in western Canada was designed-for what? To seize the railways, to seize industry and municipal government, and eventually to seize the government of this country, following _ out their nurpose. Now it is true the agitation has to some degree quieted down, if I may use that expression, but let us not lose sight of the fact that, although it has quieted down, it nevertheless exists. There are so-called Sunday schools in this country, in many towns in northern Ontario and in our cities. They are taking the boys and girls from these towns, wherever they can get them, into these so-called Sunday schools, to teach them the doctrine of the destruction of the present system of government in this country, and these organizations are being financed to a very considerable degree by the Third Internationale and the Soviets in Russia. My hon. friend has frequently referred to what the labour movement desires, and in that regard I take it he presumes to speak for the labour people in this country.

No, I represent
primarily a certain group in "Winnipeg; I do not claim to speak for all the labour people.

Just in a few words I wish to associate myself with the members who have been single-handed in advocating this measure. It would be a pity for us to leave those gentlemen to fight this battle alone, because after all it is the battle of all of us. this measure which is giving us an amount of liberty which is long overdue. I totally dissociate myself from the sentiments as expressed by my hon. friends to the right. The regrettable thing about extremes is that one extreme begets another.
. Curing war time there was a vast upheaval in people's ideas; democracy kicked over the traces, and there was an explosion here and there throughout the civilized world. Most people took it calmly because such thkws . had happened before; but people of a certain timidity of disposition, of a certain conservative cast of mind, immediately became hysterical, went to the other extreme and wanted to divest the people of the liberties which they had. I thought we were so far removed from the disturbing scenes of war time and the aftermath of war as to be able to look at these things calmly, but I am afraid the hon. member for Vancouver Centre and the hon. member for East Algoma are still under the influence of that .period. I was struck by the paralled1 which the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken) drew with the period just after the Napoleonic wars. He said:	"In those times there was
no international organization trying to overthrow governments and constitutions." But he was altogether wrong. At that time minds just like his were putting forward exactly the same plea that he has to-night, that we must curb liberty, the time-honoured liberty of the people, because they have conjured up some imaginary force that is undermining democracy.

I call to mind an incident which illustrates my point. The government of that time in England actually hired spies to dog the steps of, not communists, not bolsheviks, but respectable and prominent citizens. I remember the story of one spy who had a big nose and who was detailed to watch the movement of no less persons than the poet Woods-worth and the poet Coleridge. One summer day these two innocent gentlemen were engaged in the open air in a discussion of the works of the philosopher Spinoza. The spy crept up close to them and heard them talk about Spinoza. He went right away to the authorities and said that those men were guilty, they were talking about "Spinozy." You may read the records of that time and you will find that in England there were certain people who displayed the same hysteria, the same extremity of feeling, that has been manifested by our hon. friends to-night. They conjured up the same imaginary forces gnawing awa3' at the foundations of society, and in every forward step of the slow advance of the people's liberties you have had unfortunate people of this extraordinary timidity of mind. Sometimes it is inherent; sometimes it is acquired through enjoying a position of special privilege-because the privileged classes have never taken kindly to revolutionary ideas; they have always tried to isolate them as fast as they have appeared, to wall them around, to put them behind bars. But they have never succeeded, because thosq ideas are essentially dynamic and sooner or later they burst forth again.
I stood up more particularly to put myself squarely alongside our friends who are advocating this measure of liberty, and I think the government can be congratulated on coming out straightforwardly and espousing it. After all they are doing justice to the principles of Liberalism for which they stand, as I understand its history and its meaning. In the last few days we have witnessed a deluge of contempt aimed at our hon. friends opposite from Winnipeg. I for one resolved that I would take the first opportunity of associating myself with those members of parliament. In other words, no new offence is being created.

If we are to discuss the bill
for the rest of the night I want to say a word or two, not from the constitutional view but from the point of view at least of a loyal citizen. Like the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), I can see no good reason whatever, and certainly no good reason has been advanced by any hon. members who have spoken, why these sections of the Criminal Code should be repealed. It is not often that I take up the time of the House and I trust that the committee will bear with me while I quote these sections. The matter is more important than many of us realize and we should be careful before altering the code or substituting for the existing sections any others that may be proposed. The first clause quoted by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, 97A, reads:
(1) Any association, organization, society or corporation, whose professed purpose or one of whose purposes is to bring about any governmental, industrial or economic change within Canada, by use of force, violence or physical injury to person or property, or by threats of such injury, or which teaches, advocates, advises or defends the use of force, violence, terrorism, or physical injury to person or property, or threats of such injury, in order to accomplish such change, or for any other purpose, or which shall by any means prosecute or pursue such purpose or professed purpose, or shall so teach, advocate, advise or defend, shall be an unlawful association.
I cannot see why that subsection should be removed from the statutes. I think it is perfectly proper, for it is a safeguard to constituted authority. I would also quote section 97B, and ask the Minister of Justice to give some reason for its repeal:
(1) Any person who prints,, publishes, edits, issues, circulates, sells, o-r offers for sale or distribution any book, newspaper, periodical, pamphlet, picture, paper, circular, card, letter, writing, print, publication or dooument of any kind, m which is taught, advocated, advised or defended, or who shall in any manner teach, advocate, or advise or defend the use, without authority of law, of force, violence, terrorism, or physical^ injury to person or property, or threats of such injury, as a means of accomplishing any governmental, industrial or economic change, or otherwise, shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for not more than twenty years.
I cannot imagine why the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) should advocate the repeal of that provision. To my mind it is a perfectly reasonable section and should not be repealed. There is no doubt that some changes might be made in the act so long as the sections to which I have referred are not altered.
A minute ago the hon. Minister of Justice said that the repeal of these sections was not advocated by extremists. I must disagree with

him, because from my own personal experience I am satisfied that he is mistaken. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Kennedy) read an article last night, which was published in one of the Winnipeg papers shortly after the strike, stating that the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), who was an alderman at that time, acted as chairman of a meeting in Winnipeg at which the Union Jack was deposited under the rostrum and the red flag hoisted in its stead. Now, Mr. Chairman, I believe anyone who could be a party to sueh a proceeding is an extremist. And the hon. gentleman is one of those advocating the repeal of these sections. Therefore when the Minister of Justice says this amendment is not advocated by extremists, I cannot agree with him. In this connection may I read a report from the Manitoba Free Press of March 1, 1921, of a meeting held in the city of Winnipeg? I am sure that after hearing what was said at that meeting the Minister of Justice will agree with me that the speaker referred to was an extremist. This is the report:
Before W. A. Pritchard had launched upon his address, a group in the audience struck up the strains of the "Red Flag", the rest of the audience rising and joining in the song.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said he was opposed to force, and yet these are the words used by Mr. Pritchard, a gentleman closely associated with him:
"Quite a lot of water has passed under the bridge since the benign old man said 'One year' " was Mr. Pritchard's opening remark. "The scrap of 1919 was of a considerable magnitude, and if I read the signs of to-night, there seem to be more scraps to come.
I want to tell you that the real enemies of labour are the traitors within our ranks. Declare war upon these skunks and tell them that it is a war to the knife, and knife to the hilt. When we kill them we will dispose of the finest weapon that the master class has ever employed."
Now, surely the Minister of Justice will agree with me that some at least of those who are advocating the repeal of these two sections are extremists of the very worst kind. My hon. friend from Nelson (Mr. Bird) a short time ago said he was proud to line himself up beside these men who have been fighting "the age-long battle for labour and liberty." What kind of liberty were they asking for? What kind of liberty do these sections curb? Simply the liberty to destroy That is the purpose of the law which it is sought to repeal. As representatives of the Canadian people are we willing to repeal this law which safeguards the loyal citizens of this Dominion? While I would not object to the law being amended in some form, I believe that these two sections should stand on the statute book.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In 1910 there was a conflict in the province of British Columbia as to who had jurisdiction in the railway belt with respect to water rights. That was settled by an appeal to the Privy Council, and in 1913 legislation was passed by this parliament, bringing the whole matter into conformity and empowering the province of British Cohmrbia to supervise the granting of these rights. Since that time amendments have been made to the British Columbia Water Act. One of the provisions

of the Railway Belt Water Act was that water rights in the railway belt could be placed by order in council under provincial administration. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I should like to have an opportunity of conferring with my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) before committing the government on the question. I would point out however that the time has already been extended by a year, at least once, so that civil servants have had two years within which to decide whether or not they wish to avail themselves of the provisions of the act. It seems strange that they should be unable to reach a decision in the matter. However, I wiill undertake to see that the representations which the hon. member has made are carefully looked into.

I am aware that in rising to speak again I am trespassing somewhat on the rules, but I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that in view of the importance of the matter the House will bear with me. Without going into details I may observe that there are certain groups of civil servants who do not come under the act at all, and who have asked to be given that privilege. One of these groups includes, for instance, Income Tax employees, and there are the employees mentioned by my hon. friend (Mr. Manion)-the weighers. This is a very important question which vitally affects some who cannot come under the act. I really think the wisest course would be to extend until 1927 the privilege of election and in the meantime properly amend the Civil Service Act. I am neither criticizing nor blaming the government, for I realize that this is a large and intricate question and one that must be carefully considered.

The Minister of Finance has just handed me a report on the matter submitted to him by the Superintendent of Insurance. I might read for the information of my hon. friend one paragraph which bears upon the point he has raised:
I think the recommendation to the government should be that the tune be not further extended, or if at all, for a period not exceeding three months, that the act be amended as heretofore suggested in order to cover causes of obvious omissions an the original act, and that no further enlargement or increase in benefits be considered 'until after the period for election has expired and the fuilil effect of the transfers and appointments uip to that date has been ascertained.
I think it well to put that expression of view on record.

I would call the attention of the Prime Minister to the point in that letter which suggests that the act be amended. If the government is prepared to deal with the whole question, the recommendation of the superintendent is sound.

Can the Prime Minister give the House an assurance that the appointments to the Civil Service Commission will be made before prorogation this
session?

The government is anxious, in whatever appointment it makes to the Civil Service Commission, to secure persons whose suitability for the post will commend itself to the people of the country. It is not easy to secure such a person to fill a position on the Civil Service Commission, and I may frankly admit to my

Cicil Service Superannuation
hen. friend that it may be necessary for the government to ask parliament to amend the Civil Service Act in order to facilitate the appointment of the type of man who will be regarded as well qualified to fill this position of great responsibility. The original act provided that the commissioners should be appointed for life, but subsequent appointments were limited to ten years, and there is no provision for a pension at the end of that time. The position carries with it a salary of $6,000 per annum. It is difficult to induce an individual of the standing and personality the government is seeking, to assume the position at a salary of $6,000 for ten years in the absence of any provision for a pension subsequently. The government is considering the advisability of asking parliament to provide for a larger salary and to arrange, if possible, for a pension in the event of the position not being made permanent. I emphasize the desire of the government to appoint as commissioners only such persons as will readily commend themselves to the judgment of the country, and naturally it will require some time to secure the right individual or individuals. My colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) reminds me that at the moment the service is not being embarrassed inasmuch as the Department of Justice has given a ruling that the chairman of the Civil Service Commission has full power to act for the commission as a whole. It has been suggested that the commission might be confined to one individual. We shall be giving that phase of the matter a trial while we are endeavouring to secure the other two officials.

In answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) regarding jobber broker combines, I promised to make a statement not later than to-day. With the permission of the House I submit the following statement:
Following a formal complaint under the Combines Investigation Act, a commissioner was appointed in July 1924 to investigate an alleged combine in the distribution of fruits and vegetables in western Canada. The commissioner reported on the 18th February, 1925, to the effect that a combine-called for convenient reference a jobber-broker combine- was operating in western Canada, and that its operations were against the interest of the public.
It appears that the supplies of Canadian grown fruit and vegetables consumed in the four western provinces come principally from the province of British Columbia. The grower, living in British Columbia and disposing of his products all the way from Calgary to Winnipeg, must have agents at the various centres to receive the fruit and vegetables, inspect them for quality and condition, and sell them to the jobbers, as the wholesale fruit houses are called in those provinces.
In 1906 and for some few years thereafter the system of distribution in Canada was from the grower, through his broker, to the different jobbers who sold to the retail' trade, which in turn distributed to the consuming public. The jobbing houses, of which there were two or more in each town of any size, were for the most part independent of each other and in more or less friendly competition. Speaking generally' and surveying western Canada as a Whole, distribution was made through many independent and competing jobbers. There was a free and uncontrolled outlet for supply.
The Nash organization of Minneapolis, which first entered Canada in 1906, and now operates a chain of jobbing houses throughout the west, introduced the principle of the jobber-owned broker about 1913. The Canadian jobbers, who have admitted the harmful' nature of the principle, say that in self-defence they had to follow suit.
By reason of the introduction of the jobber-broker principle, the Whole aspect of the distribution of fruit and vegetables in western Canada changed. Instead of distribution being through many unallied houses, it is now principally through two chains of jobbing houses, namely the Nash organization, and

Fruit Combine
the remaining Canadian jobbers. Each of these has its chain of brokerage offices, that of the Nash being known as the Mutual Brokers Limited and that of the independents, as the Canadian houses are called, being known as the Growers Sales Agency, Limited.
The commissioner reported against the principle of the jobber-owned broker on the ground that it was an attempt to join in the one organization two opposing	interests-the
broker, whose interest should be solely that of the grower and to sell at the best price obtainable, and the jobber whose interest was to purchase at the lowest price and so make the largest profit and therefore was opposed to that of the grower; and he set out in his report instances in which the combine had operated detrimentally to the interest of the grower and others. Certain of these instances, which are set out on pp. 22 et seq. of the Report may be summarized under the following heads:
(a)	Failure of the broker to sell to the jobber at the best price.
(b)	Attempts to keep the growers in the dark-(1) as to the prices at which their goods were sold; (2) the persons to whom they were sold; and (3) the allowances made to the jobbers on account of the alleged condition of the fruit on arrival.
(c)	False returns.
(d)	Secret profits.
(e)	Special rebates to Nash Jobbing houses which were not given to Canadian Jobbing houses.
(f)	Attempts to break up growers' cooperative organizations.
Following the report of the commissioner, indictments were laid against certain persons and individuals, charging inter alia (a) conspiracy to defraud; (b) offences against the Secret Commissions Act; (c) offences against Section 498 (The Combines Section) of the Criminal Code; (d) offences against the Combines Investigation Act. The trial of the accused took place under counts (a) and (b), the counts under (c) being traversed to the next assizes, and those under (d) being withdrawn.
The trial resulted in the conviction of four individuals and four companies. The individuals were sentenced to one day each in jail and to a fine of $25,000 a piece. The corporations were sentenced to fines of $25,000 each. Both individuals and corporations appealed from their conviction and the crown appealed from the sentences, suggesting that they should be more severe. Before the appeals were argued the defendants withdrew their appeals and the crown accordingly withdrew the aopes'
Numerous representations have been made to the government from time to time by growers' organizations and others, to the effect that the jobber-broker combine operates injuriously not only to the grower but also to the Canadian jobbing trade and to the consuming public; and that it should be done away with.
Following the verdict in the recent trial, the so-called Independent Jobbers, that is to say those Canadian firms which are not in what is known as the Nash organization, decided to cease the operation of the brokerage houses which they have been operating in conjunction with their jobbing business. These firms were not among those indicted. As the result of this action of the Independents, the jobber-broker connection is now operated only by what is known as the Nash organization. Since the trial counsel for the Nash interests has made representations to the government that they would like the view of the government on this question.
The matter is of considerable public importance, and in view of the fruit season having commenced before the appeals were disposed of and of the desire of all parties for an expression of the attitude of the government on this question, this statement is made.
It is not the duty of the government to advise corporations, as to how they should conduct their business, nor is it the intention of the government to do so. But the government has found that the question of the jobber-broker combine method of doing business is of such public importance that all parties concerned are entitled to know the government's attitude toward its continuance.
The jobber-broker combine is an attempt to join in the one organization and under the same control, the broker, whose interests should be solely that of the grower, and the jobber, whose interest is opposed to that of the grower. This puts the broker in a position in which his interest conflicts with his duty. Where there is such a conflict of interest and duty it is impossible to guarantee by any external supervision that the thousands of annual shipments of the growers will be handled honestly. Such a relationship is against the established principles of our few, and it is difficult to see how the grower could hope to obtain proper returns for his goods under such a system.
The government has taken steps to ascertain the opinion of those who have a practical knowledge of the operations of the jobber-broker combine. While some growers defend them they have found pretty general condemnation. Responsible officials in govern-rr nt. employ condemn it; growers' organ!-
Nova Scotia Steel Industry

zations controlling the vast majority of the crop of British Columbia condemn it; and there is testimony from Canadian jobbers to the same effect.
In view of all! these considerations, the government has decided that it must treat the jobber-broker connection as against public policy; and this announcement is made so that all parties may be aware of these views. If the law as it stands is sufficient to deal with this question, resort will be had to it should there be any disregard of its provisions. If the law as it stands is not sufficient, such appropriate legislation within the legislative competence of the Dominion will be introduced as may be necessary to give effect to this decision.

That lit is expedient to provide for the extension of the provisions of chapter 11 of the statutes of 1918 (relating to guarantee on removal or postponement of indebtedness of the Canadian Northern Railway system), to the Canadian National Railway Company and to any company referred to on the Canadian National Railway Act, 1919 (1919, c.[DOT] 13), and in the act relating to the Grand Trunk Railway system (1920, c. 13), and to enable each one of such companies to issue its notes, obligations or other securities, hereinafter called "substituted securities," for the purpose of acquiring, by application of the proceeds thereof, or by exchange therefor, the notes, Obligations or other securities or indebtedness of any other or others of such companies, and to authorize the Governor in Council to guarantee the substituted securities.
In adopting the motion, it is understood that we are not adopting the principle at all?

minister will have a request from the company in connection with this matter. He probably will have a report from the financial department showing where this is wanted. If he would read that report it will help.

at hand. I have the substance of what, is required. It is very easily available. The act which is being amended by this proposed legislation applies to the Canadian Northern Railway system, and did not apply to the old Grand Trunk system, nor to the Grand Trunk Pacific. The purpose of the present amendment is to add two sections, enabling an adjustment to be made of the indebtedness of the three systems, the Canadian Northern, the Canadian National, formerly the Grand Trunk, and the Grand Trunk Pacific. The wording is broadened to enable compromises or adjustments to be made of existing indebtedness, and also to enable one of the companies, such for instance as the Canadian National, to issue its notes or obligations, instead of the obligations of the subsidiary company which is being substituted.

component parts before the amalgamation, the amounts shown as received by each of the groups, or at least the amount shown as advanced by the government, including the issue of bonds does not correspond with the amounts of which we have been given any record, as having been expended. I would be very glad
to try to facilitate my hon. friend's efforts to find that hundred odd million-

might suggest that a better and easier course would be for my hon. friend to go before the special committee-and as a member of the House my hon. friend has that privilege- and before that special committee the actual officers of the road who are engaged in making up the account can be examined regarding the matter in detail and at any length.
