My hon. friend is entirely wrong when he speaks in that way. In the first instance there is a great deal of difference between the Grand Trunk case and this. We did not like the Gtiand Trunk case. There is no question about that. But the fact that people went out, bought on the market, ran up the price and got control of the ktock did not add five cents to the obligation of the government. But in this particular case, if we have any advertising-and this particular discussion is an advertisement, because it is advertising to everybody that particular securities are good ones to get hold of-that is the way to run up the price and the only way you can run it up successfully. That is going to be done if we adopt this proposal. I think the minister should withdraw the proposition or have a conference. I do not think we should countenance such a proposition at any time.

It seems to
come down to the question of the subsequent approval of parliament. Would my hon. friend be \yilling to let the resolution pass, with the distinct understanding that we are not committed to anything more than that the government should get certain powers that are suggested here, either with the approval of parliament or without the approval; but that that matter should be settled before any bill is passed? I have a great deal of sympathy with the point of view that the approval of parliament should be obtained. If it is possible to do what is here suggested with the approval of parliament, I would be entirely in favour of the proposal for the approval of parliament. But listening to the discussion this afternoon, I confess, not having the knowledge of finance which my hon. friend opposite has, I am not sure that the object aimed at by the minister could be attained with the provision for the approval of parliament.

I would agree
with my hon. friend's suggestion except for this reason: If the approval of parliament is

C.N.R.-Substituted Securities
necessary there is no object in the legislation at all. We might just as well make up our minds one way or the other. If the approval of parliament is to be required, we gain nothing by passing the legislation now.
My hon. friend made a remark which I think has a bearing on this question, namely, that in the public interests it is advisable that there should not be too much publicity at this stage.

That is why
I wanted to hold a conference.

If that is true, and my hon. friend agrees to it, would it not further the situation if the resolution were allowed to pass, it being understood by both sides that the bill will not be proceeded with unless we have some agreement and understanding between the two parties in regard to it?
Let us agree to have the conference first.
If the resolution is passed and the bill is introduced, before the second reading is proceeded with we could have a conference.

I think it would be more
satisfactory to have the conference first.

As my hon. friend has
so little confidence in our good faith, I am prepared to move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.

Motion agreed to.
Progress reported.
The House resumed from June 2, consideration in committee of Bill No. 91, to amend the Immigration Act-Hon. Mr. Stewart-Mr. Duff in the chair.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Edmonton, Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
When this bill
was in committee last week, there was some question as to whether the Criminal Code would cover section 41 of the Immigration Act. I think we were all in agreement in regard to the provision of the amendment, namely, that it was taking out of the hands of the Department of Immigration the right to bring before a board of inquiry and deport aliens under section 41. That is all that was involved; the offences contained in section 41 are dealt with under the Criminal Code.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I was led
into error by the fact that I was not aware that sections 97 and 97 (b) of the Criminal Code had been repealed. That matter was taken up on Friday when the amendments to the Criminal Code were passed. I understand that sections 132 and 141 of the Criminal Code do cover, or can cover, practically all that is provided for in section 41. Section 41 is merely removing from the Department of Immigration the right to bring before a board of inquiry and to try individuals suspected of certain offences. What we are doing in effect is simply to provide that a trial should be had before a judge and jury, and then we step in and enforce deportation afterwards.

This gives the minister
the right to determine whether or not the man/ should be deported.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

Section 41 says that the
officer of the municipality shall report the case to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
And what does the minister do?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The officer
reports to the minister only in case of conviction. The provisions in section 41 were that if those offences were proven before a board of inquiry deportation followed as a matter of course. Now it cannot follow-, unless it is reported that a conviction has been registered.
What does the minister do?
The minister sees that the man is deported if he receives a report from the judge that the man has been convicted.

Under what authority is
he deported?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Under section 40. The minister still retains power to deport under section 41. As a matter of fact,
I would very much rather the Immigration department was relieved of the deportation proceedings altogether, and that officers of the crown who are charged with other duties might perform that duty, but we are retain-

Immigration Act
mg it under section 41, I presume for offences of this character, and to offences under the Narcotic Drug Act the same procedure applies. Where convictions are made we register deportation. Apparently that is our business. We are police officers to that extent.

As I explained when we were last considering this amendment I was not concerned then nor am I so much concerned now with anything except the question whether the amendment will cut out from what I may call deportable offences, any offences for which deportation now lies. The Minister of the Interior first told us that the offences would be the same under the present act and under the amendment. On further advice he altered his statement and said: No, there would be some offences for which deportation lies under the present act for which deportation will not lie under the new legislation.
When the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) was speaking in committee on this matter on the last occasion he admitted that there would be certain acts for which deportation now lies for which deportation would not lie under the amendment. I would like to know what these are. The minister now states that he thinks that notwithstanding the repeal of sections 97A and 97B of the Criminal Code, notwithstanding those amendments that were made the other day, there will be no change. I want to call attention to this. Section 41 of the act as it now reads states:
Every person who by word or act in Canada seeks to overthrow by force or violence the government of or constituted law and authority in ... . Canada.
Perhaps that is covered by the offences that are mentioned in section 134 of the code where it is an indictable offence to speak seditious words or to publish seditious libel or to be a party to a seditious conspiracy. But further down there is this offence:
Or advocates the assassination of any official of any of the said governments or of any foreign government, or who in Canada defends or suggests the unlawfull destruction of property or by word or act creates or attempts to create any riot or public disorder in Canada.
I very much fear if those cases for which deportation now lies are covered by the code with 97A and 97B repealed. If there is any doubt about the matter we should not leave those offences as acts which can be committed without liability to deportation. The man in Canada who defends or suggest the unlawful destruction of property-where is that offence covered by part II of the code? I cannot find it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend cannot find the exact words in the Criminal Code, but those matters all come under some sections of the code relating to sedition, seditious intention, seditious words and seditious libel. The only difference will be that those people will have to be convicted first before being deported.

I am not talking of that at all. The only section that could possibly refer to this is section 134 where it is made an indictable offence to speak seditious words or to publish a seditious libel or to be a party to a seditious conspiracy. I suggest to the Minister of Justice that those words are not sufficient to cover the offence described in the present section 41 of the act, namely, the offence of defending or suggesting the unlawful destruction of property.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is sedition under the common law.
Have there been any complaints against the department in connection with the deportation of people who have come under the provisions of this section which is being repealed?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot
say directly under those particular provisions but we have difficulties in connection with almost every deportation. In very many cases there are people who object to the deportation and who try to fight us on the ground that it is illegal and to hold up the deportation if they can.

Under the proposed legislation those advocating sedition or anarchy or a state of affairs of that kind are to be given the dignity of a public trial before a judge and jury whereas under the old act the minister and his officials had the authority to take such people in hand and bundle them out of the country in a hurry.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is a fair interpretation.

Under present conditions, with a situation such as exists throughout the world, I do not think it is advisable to make the change in our law unless there is some pressing need for it and a demand on the part of people who are not in sympathy with those subject to this section of the act. I protested the other day against it and I do so again because I am satisfied that the change is being made largely through the influence of undesirable people in this country.
Immigration Act

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I hardly
think that is a fair statement because three different attempts have been made to amend section 41 of the Immigration Act, not for a moment in order to wipe out the offences but to take out of the hands of the Department of Immigration and the minister the right to seize and deport people without trial except trial by his own officials who constitute a board. That is all that we are attempting to do. My hon. friend says that if these people are anarchists they have no right to any consideration. After all the common law provides that a court is the judicial body which decides matters of this kind.
This amendment was inserted at a time when affairs were somewhat strenuous in the country but frankly I would much prefer that the court should deal with this matter than that responsibility should be upon the minister. It has been stated that this is too much power to put into the hands of the minister and I have agreed with that on every occasion when the question has been brought up in the House. I know the objection taken is that individuals guilty of some of these offences are not worthy of trial. All'I say is: Do not ask the minister to decide upon the worthiness or unworthiness of the person concerned; let the court decide that, and afterwards we will perform the duty of getting him out of the country.
Under section 40 are there not certain offences the determination of which still remains in the hands of the minister and as regards which he still retains the power of deportation without trial?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
The minister is now proposing to make a distinction between those mentioned in section 40 and those guilty of sedition or anarchy.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not necessarily anarchy, but sedition is one of the offences. A very wide interpretation can be put upon the word "sedition." My hon. friend will agree that it may be difficult to prove prostitution, but at the same time it is an offence for which the minister has power to deport.
I can see no good reason why this legislation should be amended. From what direction is the pressure coming for it? By whom has it been recommended?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Trades and Labour Council, which is a very respectable body in this country, has repeatedly requested the government to amend this legislation and it did so again this year. Tom Moore is president of the organization which I think truly represents labour in this country.
Is the Trades and Labour Council pressing for an amendment which would prevent deportation of those who advocate anarchy?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Trades and Labour Council does not advocate that at all. There is no request for stay of deportation. What is asked for is trial.

The effect of
this legislation will be undoubtedly that many guilty men will escape. We all know how difficult it is to secure conviction in the trial of offences of this kind, and if the minister and the board of inquiry 'which is already provided, are thoroughly convinced that a citizen is undesirable!, even though he may not be convicted in any criminal court, surely there should be reserved to the department the right to deport such a man without going to the expense of securing conviction criminally, with the uncertainty that must attend any such trial. There might not be evidence enough to bring about a conviction, and yet there might be sufficient evidence to warrant the minister in considering an individual an undesirable. He might be stirring up trouble and should be deported. But it will be impossible to secure his deportation under the legislation now proposed.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen
to the left are laughing. I do not see anything to laugh at, especially when we recall the experience we have had in Canada with some of this class of people. It costs thousands of dollars to secure a conviction and the result is that many of them escape.

Who is better qualified
than the courts to decide whether or not a man is undesirable?

The court's
business is to ascertain merely whether a crime has been or has not been committed. A man might be a very undesirable citizen and yet not be guilty of any particular crime.
Undesirable in what sense?

In every sense.

Immigration Act

In what sense specifically
-because he eats peas with his knife?

When we are
selecting immigrants in the Old Country we do not act on the principle that merely because a man has not been guilty of any crime he is therefore admissible.

No, we have regulations
governing his entry.

Exactly. Why
not therefore follow that principle right through?

And abolish the courts
altogether?

No, I do not
suggest that.

To whom would the hon.
gentleman leave the discretion of deciding whether anyone was desirable or undesirable? Would he leave that discretion to members of parliament?

Leave it to the
board of inquiry as in the past. Surely it is safe to leave the matter in the hands of the board. And, besides, it is cheaper.
Who would make accusation against the undesirable?
The same person who would make it in a court. Someone must start the machinery, whether in the court or before the board.

Did the hon gentleman
ever read section 41 of the part which is being repealed?
Yes.

Does he know that under
that section the board of inquiry could have excluded from this country almost every man who has even been of any benefit to the human race in the fight for liberty in foreign countries? It could have excluded nearly all the great patriots during the last century. Anyone who had opposed organized government in his own country could have been kept out under the legislation as it has existed heretofore. For example, as my friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) suggests, Lord Carson could have been refused entrance into the country.

You would 'not
want him anyway.

Neither I would. But the
law would have excluded him at any rate, just as it would have excluded Michael
Collins, Mazzini, Garibaldi, Kossuth and practically all those who fought against organized government in one country or another of Europe. Does the hon. member w'ant that state of affairs to continue, or does he want this to be a fairly free country?
Mr.	STEWART	(Leeds):	Have those
people or any of them ever come here to reside?

No, but they could have
been excluded if they had come.
Mr.	STEWART	(Leeds):	You cannot
deport a man until he is here, and has made himself a nuisance in Canada.

There would have been any number of people who would have concluded at once that some of these men I have mentioned were nuisances. Would my hon. friend suggest that a court would not be competent to inquire into the conduct of such persons?
Mr.	STEWART	(Leeds):	A board of
inquiry set up by the minister and under his control and responsibility would be just as capable of determining a matter of that kind as a court of justice ,and perhaps more so.

It is a question of taste,
as I suggested in regard to the peas.

The minister will hardly
suggest that any injustice has been done in the past. I do not accuse him of cowardice nor do I think he is a coward, but the only reason he has given so far for wanting to repeal the law is the fact that he does not want to assume the responsibility under the act. Considerable numbers of undesirable people have been coming into this country, and we should have been better off if we had deported them. If we are to abide by the result of a trial there are sections in Canada where, as we know from past experience, the legal proceedings would be so protracted as to make it highly improbable that any undesirable person should be deported. We want to give these people short shrift. We have too many of the type who in the last ten years should have been deported on their arrival.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is not
at all a question of cowardice or of courage. Hon. gentlemen opposite are forever arguing that the courts are the proper authorities to settle disputes, and I am rather surprised that my hon. friends should take this attitude to-day. They seem to have more confidence in me than in the courts. I appreciate the
Immigration Act

compliment, of course, and I may assure the committee that I have never at any time stayed deportation upon report from the board that any individual was undesirable. There are however under section 41 a number of offences which in my opinion could better be dealt with by the courts. This provision was enacted at a time when the country was in a state of serious disorder.

It is not much better
now.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Well, I
still have authority to reject people at the boundary. I sympathize with the desire with which the provision was enacted, to prevent men from agitating the minds of others even though, in their view, legitimately. But on three different occasions attempts have been made to amend this section simply because it was felt to be unnecessary. It is considered advisable to put these particular crimes in the same category as others and let them go before the courts for decision.
Has the department acted upon any cases submitted to the authorities in the last few months?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Not since
I have been in the department.

Section 41 as it was
passed in 1919 and as it now stands creates certain offences which are not offences within part II of the Criminal Code.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would not say so.

If my hon. friend will analyse the provisions of part II of the code, in the light of the provisions in section 41, he will have no difficulty in arriving at the conclusion that there are, in that section, offences which are not contained in part II of the Criminal Code. I do not want to take up the time of the committee, for my absence should not be a reason for prolonging this discussion, but I do ask the minister to look at that carefully. My hon. friend from East Edmonton (Mr. Bury), who sits beside me, has gone over in detail all the sections of the Criminal Code, and I have looked over his memorandum. I certainly think section 41 does create offences that are not created by part II of the Criminal Code. Now, this proposed legislation repeals section 41. The new section provides that a man must have committed an offence against some section in part II of the Criminal Code before he can be dealt with by the minister. If, therefore, there are offences in section 41 that

are not covered in part II of the code, it follows that to that extent this legislation relaxes the supervision that we have been able to exercise over undesirables up to the present moment. I think it goes without saying that there has been in times past an organized effort in this country against the Dominion government and the governments of the provinces. As I came along on the train yesterday 1 read the daily papers from Winnipeg, and I observed that the mayor of that city has asked the citizens to unite for the purpose of putting down this communistic effort, and he names, for instance, an office building in the city of Toronto from which the objectionable literature is being sent out to various parts of Canada. The other day the members of the legal profession of Manitoba were invited by a gentleman from the United States who came to address them at Winnipeg to use their strongest efforts to prevent subversive propaganda that was now being circulated in his country and to a lesser extent in Canada.
I am wholly in sympathy with the idea that in this age it is perhaps a large power to leave with a board of inquiry to determine whether or not men are guilty of the offences in question. But once you have committed the matter to the courts-and as to that I am raising no objection-I submit to the minister that it is a 'lessening of the number of offences for which deportation is now possible, and to that extent this proposed legislation should not be passed. This is not the day to relax the arm of the law, this is not the day to lessen the authority of our officials to bring to account men who are deliberately endeavouring to destroy our institutions. I am wholly in accord with what my friend from Quebec said, that for the moment we are concerned about Canada alone, and not about any other portion of the British Empire. At the moment I am concerned with men who are circulating seditious literature and who are carrying on an active propaganda against organized government in the provinces and in this Dominion, and my regret is that in part II of the code there is no section that meets the cases mentioned in section 41.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Would my hon. friend enumerate those?

I do not want to be too lengthy. I will go over briefly the. memorandum prepared by my hon, friend from East Edmonton. Section 41 provides that:
Every person who by word or act in Canada seeks to overthrow by force or violence the government of or constituted law and authority in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland or Canada-

Immigration Act
I can readily understand the observation of hon. members that the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland can more or less take care of itself, and that for the moment we are concerned with Canada. Suppose all the words after the word "authority" were stricken out, leaving this part of the section: -or who in Canada defends or suggests the unlawful destruction of property or by word or act creates or attempts to create any riot or public disorder in Canada.
Now, riot is dealt with in the Criminal Code in part II, but threats of destruction of property by word are not dealt with in the part of the code as I read it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is wrong. Mr. BENNETT: Will my hon. friend give me the section?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 132 deals with
seditious words and so on, and if my hon. friend refers to Crankshaw's edition of the Criminal Code he will find there a number of cases in England, where the law is exactly the same as it is here. Everything that is referred to as coming under the offence of sedition, for instance, distributing or sending literature from Toronto, would be covered by the common law, and everything that has the effect of creating dissatisfaction as between different classes of the community has also been found to be sedition under the common law.
But the difficulty is that this is part II of the Criminal Code that the section deals with.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 132 is part II
of the Criminal Code.

It reads as follows:
(1) Seditious words are words expressive of a seditious intention.
(2)	A seditious libel as a libel expressive of a seditious intention.
(3)	A seditious conspiracy is an agreement between two or more persons to carry into execution a seditious intention.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

The difficulty is that
the section, as it now reads, places a limitation upon the provisions of section 41. because it provides that it must be for violation of the provisions of part II of the Criminal Code.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Section 41 has terms in
in that are not in the Criminal Code, as I have pointed out, and the very language used by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice shows that the common law excludes the operation of section 41.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I beg my hon. friend's
pardon. It is the common law that interprets section 132.

Then why do we not
say any criminal offences not provided for in the code and the common law.
The Criminal Code provides for that.

The criminal law is that body of criminal law which comes to us both by statute and by common law, and the provisions of the criminal law that come to us under the common law are not in the code. Section 41 this House is now asked to pass is the section that deals with part II of the Criminal Code. Unfortunately there is a series of offences that are offences against the common law, and we have not provided for them in section- 41.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh yes.

The Criminal Code
means just what it says, and criminal offences at common law, such as sedition, treason, conspiracy, and so on, are dealt with by the code; but it has been held that the old principles of common law with respect to the criminality of certain acts still prevail m this country. But all I suggest is that under this bill we are taking away the operation of the law against a number of offences because by repealing section 119 we are substituting the common law. Therefore if w(-propose to make the whole body of crimina law of Canada apply, that is, including the body of criminal law which is not part of the enactments of this parliament, contained in chapter 146-the Criminal Code of Canada we should provide by common law, or by part II of the Criminal Code, for such offences.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Does my
hon. friend suggest the insertion of the words " common law " in part II of the Criminal Code?
If my hon. friend the Minister of Justice is correct in his statement.
It would be laughed at.

The Solicitor General
says it would be laughed at. I say to him that within the four comers of the statute there is no provision for dealing with sedition at common law. If sedition at common law is an offence, the indictment will be drawn up against the peace of our said lord the king. Then will follow the description of the offence, not in violation of any section
Immigration Act

of this code but in violation of the common criminal law of this country, and unless you can name the section under which you frame an indictment and which will come within the sense of the common law, it is then an offence covered by section 41.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I still maintain that all offences coming under sedition are covered by part II of the Criminal Code, sections 132, 133 and 134. My hon. friend says the code does not refer to common law; certainly it does not, because it has always been found better to give the offence of sedition a wider meaning than its strict interpretation, and this applies in England as well as in Canada. I remember hearing the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) make a speech in connection with this matter in a very effective way.
In England, when they drafted the Criminal Code, the commissioners inserted a definition covering in part what is mentioned in section 41 of the Immigration Act, but the English parliament refused to accept that draft, preferring to leave the offence of sedition to be interpreted under the common law as has always been the practice. As I have said, it covers any offence which might create conflict between the subjects of His Majesty, between the classes of the community, or offences against the crown. The same thing happened in Canada; when our Criminal Code was drafted an effort was made to define sedition by inserting such words as these, but the parliament of Canada also declined to accept the draft, preferring to follow the British way of interpreting sedition, which has been the law in Canada up to the present time. Every one of the things my hon. friend has mentioned would come under the offence of sedition, and a man guilty of them would be convicted by a judge and jury.

But not under this section.
Mr. LAPOINTE. If my hon. friend will permit me to finish. I do not think there is anything to complain of in this legislation.
I am quite free to agree that under the circumstances which existed in 1919 when the law was enacted there was justification for the law, but apparently it has created a grievance; it has been offensive to various classes of labour-
What class?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Trades and Labour Council, for instance, and there is no better class of people in Canada than the labour unions. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. 
Cantley) says no, but I know better. I have been a member of the committee of the government which has received delegations from the Trades and Labour Council every year coming to make their recommendations, and this has been a thorn in the flesh of labour since 1919. They may be mistaken but they are afraid that it may work against them in some way, and have asked that an amendment be made making it clear that a man should be convicted before being deported. I really do not think there should be so much opposition to this piece of legislation.
May I ask the minister if he knows any case of hardship which has occurred under the provisions of the act during the last three or four years?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not.

Then why are we dealing with something under which no 'hardship has occurred? The act has been in force for some time and no hardship has been done. There are men in this country who should have been deported but who have been allowed to remain.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member for Pictou may be right; I do not know of any hardship being done. But on the other hand if the law were not used, if the circumstances did not necessitate application of the law, why keep it when it is abhorrent to an important part of our population?

The hon. gentleman says he knows of no case of hardship, and that the act was justified a few years ago. I would suggest to him that it might be well to ask those people who request a change to show that hardship has been done under the act before we remove a piece of legislation which safeguards the interests of this country. In my judgment there never was a time in the history of Canada, including the period directly after the war, when legislation of this kind was more necessary that it is to-day.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We are at peace to-day.

I inquired of the minister a few days ago, when this matter first came up, as to who were making the demands for this legislation. Since that time I noticed in the Toronto Saturday Night of June 5, 1926, a full page article in connection with the activities of the communists in North America and also in Europe. Reference is also made to the Department of Labour in Canada in connection with this matter, and great pains are taken to show that the Federation of Labour in the United

Immigration Act
States and in Canada is absolutely opposed to the principles advocated by communists. So I want it distinctly understood that in referring to these matters I am not casting any reflection on our labour unions. The minister says that in 1919 this legislation might have been necessary, and so far as I have been able to observe no fault has been found with the minister or his department in connection with those cases which have come before the officials in charge of this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.

For making a derogatory reference to the Union Jack at the May Day celebration in Winnipeg, Jack Gregg, who spoke on behalf of the Young Communist League, was deported, as were hiis parents and family.

I would further like to quote a statement made in this article to this effect:
The aims of communists the world over, and the close connection with Russia of Canadian communists, are clearly shown in the fifteenth annual report by the Department of Labour on "Labour Organization in Canada." On another page of this section there is a review of that publication. The section dealing with revolutionary labour organizations is especially pertinent to the subject of this article as it traces the direct connection between Canadian communists and the Red International of Labour Unions, which was founded in July 1921 through the efforts of a revolutionary body known as the Third (Communist) International, itself only organized at Moscow in 1919.
In the year that this legislation was enacted, this organization was formed in Moscow. It goes on:
The objective of the Third International, says the Department of Labour report, is to organize the working class for the overthrow of capitalism, the destruction of the bourgeois state and the establishment of the dictatorship of the proletariat. According to the theses of the Communist International, the trade 14011-261
unions represent the most important form of mass organization of the proletariat, and in order to propagate the communist doctrine in these bodies the Red International was established. The Canadian representative of the Communist International is the Communist party of Canada, which was formed on February 17, 1922.
Three years after this legislation was put on the statute book, this organization was organized in Canada, and the minister states that it is only by reason of the influence exercised by some of the friends of these people that complaints have reached the department. I wish the minister would pay some attention to the next paragraph.

speechtext: I said it may have been justified.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I trust the hon. member is not going to enter into a discussion of the Winnipeg strike.

No, Mr. Chairman, but statements have been made here this afternoon regarding it, and those of us who are attempting in any sense to represent labour have a right to answer general statements of this character.
I would just say that at that time the press reports were of such a character that they absolutely misled the general public as to what took place, and I do not much wonder that hon. gentlemen here, going upon the press reports, rather incline to take an altogether false view of what actually took place at that time. The hon. member for South Oxford, who has just spoken, used this phrase, and I think I should not have spoken again this afternoon had this phrase not been used: He spoke of giving these people "the dignity of a trial before a jury." Mr. Chairman, that is the reason a great many of us have been urging this legis-islation for some years. We be-
5	p.m. lieve that every man in this country ought to have the right of a trial by jury. We believe that it is the inherent right of people living in British lands that they should be given a fair trial. The design of the Immigration Act is to keep undesirable people out of this country, and with that I have every sympathy, but this act, on the contrary, permits the deportation of people from this country, not because they are undesirable in the Old Country, but because they have done something in this country that is said to be wrong. In this act we say, "Every person who by word or act in Canada-." Our position is that for crimes alleged to be committed in Canada there ought to be a fair jury trial, and that we ought not simply to allow departmental action with regard to the case. It is said that there has been no hardship with regard to this matter. I would point out again that in 1919, when the law was put on the statute books, a distinct effort was made to deport a number of Canadians to the Old Country without jury trial, and it was only because the common sense of the great masses of the people of Canada raised a protest 
against that kind of thing, that we did not have the deportation of a number of men. I should like to repeat what I said the other day, that among these men who were to be deported without trial was my colleague from North Winnipeg. Had this law been acted upon at that time, Mr. Heaps would have been returned to England without any trial by jury.
Hear, hear.

Hon. gentlemen
applaud. That shows the views they have upon su'ch a proceeding. Mr. Heaps eame before a jury and was acquitted. Now I ask, do you applaud? Those who talk about British institutions would have a man deported that a jury in this country had declared to be innocent! Talk about British loyalty-flag waving! It was not merely the labour people, but the British-horn people all over this country, those who had something of the spirit of British traditions, that protested against that kind of thing, and these men were not deported, but received jury trial.
Having that case before us, we feel very strongly that this kind of legislation ought to be wiped off the statute book. It is quite true that there are communist organizations in this country that are asking for the removal of this legislation, but it is also true that there are trades and' labour unions, even of the most conservative character, that are asking for the removal of this legislation simply on the ground that we believe that this has the effect of depriving certain groups of people, for certain alleged crimes, of that right to trial by jury which we were all taught in our school days was the right of every British subject. If it were simply a matter of keeping out people who were undesirable, I would have nothing to say, but I do urge that when people are permitted to come into this country and to reside here for a number of years, and subsequently do something in this country that is against our laws, let them be deported, but first let them be fairly tried before they are deported. That is the plea wre make, and I think if the hon. gentlemen who have objected could really understand what is involved in legislation of this character they could hardly ask that it be retained on the Statute books of Canada.

I would like to. ask the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre a question. He referred to a man by the name of Heaps who would have been deported from Winnipeg but for the fact that he claimed

subtopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Under the act as it stands it is not lawful for a superintendent of a hospital to order any narcotic drugs or to have them in his or her possession. The act is
very clear on that point; you can sell only to a doctor, a veterinary surgeon or a dentist. In this country there are many hospitals in which the superintendent is not a doctor, a veterinary surgeon, or a dentist; therefore, as I read the act, such a superintendent has no right to buy these drugs or to have them in his possession. In fact if a hospital has any narcotic drugs in its possession or in the possession of the superintendent, they are guilty of a criminal offence under paragraph (d) of section 4 of the act, which reads: Every person who has in his possession any drug without lawful authority, or manufactures, sells, gives away or distributes any drug to any person without first obtaining a license from the minister. . . shall be guilty of a criminal offence.
Section 16 of the act reads:
Without limiting the generality of paragraph (d) of section 4 of this act, any person who occupies, controls or is in possession of any building, room, vessel, vehicle, enclosure or place, in or upon which any drug is found, shall, if charged with having such drug in possession without lawful authority, be deemed to have been so in possession unless he prove that the drug was there without his authority, knowledge or consent, or that he was lawfully entitled to the possession thereof.
The superintendent of a local hospital who has opium or narcotic drugs in his possession within the meaning of this act is guilty of a criminal offence. It is unlawful for him to purchase the drugs. I do not know how the superintendent of a hospital can either purchase or be in possession _of drugs lawfully under this act.

subtopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The bill which is now under consideration does not affect the superintendent of a hospital. The superintendent is in exactly the same position after this bill is passed as he was before. The whole object of the section now under consideration is to oblige the retail druggist-it applies only to the retail druggist-if he dispenses narcotics even to a veterinary surgeon, or a physician, or a dentist, to have a written authority properly verified1.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understand that this bill was practically all passed in committee, a few days ago, with the exception of the preamble, and I desire now to move a slight amendment. During the conversations and debates on the automobile question it was represented to us that the automobile trade in Canada, in meeting competition in other countries, was somewhat at a disadvantage because of the higher selling price in Canada. Other countries have ruled that for customs purposes the duty should be on the basis of the fair market price in the country of origin. The automobile people said to us that they were unable to reduce the price because of the excise tax we impose, and I asked them, "Well, if I remove this excise tax to a degree will you give me a guarantee that you will pass that entire reduction on to the consumer?" I have under my hand a letter from the Automotive Industries of Canada dated June 5, 1926, which I desire to place on Hansard:
Hon. Jambs A. Robb,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir:
I have discussed with the Canadian manufacturers of motor cars the effect of the proposal to eliminate
rMr. Bennett.]
the 5 per cent excise tax on cars which are 50 per cent produced in Canada (or 40 per cent produced in Canada until April 1, 1927).
I am authorized to state on behalf of the following firms-
Ford Motor Company of Canada, Limited,
General Motors of Canada, Limited,
Dodge Bros., (Canada) Limited,
Willys-Overland Limited,
Durant Motor Company of Canada, Limited, Studebaker Corporation of Canada, Limited, Chrysler Motor Company,
that immediately such removal of excise tax is announced, the delivered price to the public, on the chrs which qualify for this exemption, will be reduced by the amount of the excise tax applying to such cars. This includes all the important manufacturers of passenger motor cars in Canada.
Yours very truly,
Automotive Industries of Canada,
T. A. Russell,
President.
It will be recalled that when the Prime Minister spoke, one month after the budget was delivered, the books had been closed and we were able to show a surplus of three and one-half million dollars more than when the budget was presented on April 15. We will lose some revenue by this amendment which I am proposing, but what the government loses the consumer will gain, so I propose to remove the excise tax on cars costing $1,200 and under.

I would like to ask the minister, before I make one or two remarks, whether I correctly understand the meaning of the amendment on hearing it read.
I take it that the luxury taxes are wiped out in regard to those automobiles of which a certain percentage is manufactured in this country.

speechtext: And other countries.

In countries

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, and other countries with which we have conventions. This is for automobiles costing under $1,200 only.

Well, Mr. Chairman, we have now another link in what has been found necessary in building up the fences which were destroyed. We had the spectacle the other night of the Minister of Customs, after referring to the privileges already given to the automobile manufacturers and dealers, particularly as regards parts, admitting that this sort of thing had to be done. The damage had been done and, of course, they wanted to make the damage good as much as they could. We are just now coming to that point where it is perfectly clear that what has been done must be undone, that something must be done in order to keep the Canadian workman working, and the way to do it is to have protection, not under the name of protection, but to have the remission of excise tax which will apply merely to machines made here, to machines made in the Mother Country and in the sister dominions, and in
other countries that enjoy the most favoured nation clause. But so far as the one place from which we have competition is concerned, namely the United States, the excise tax will continue. Well, I have no doubt that the government have found it absolutely necessary to do this. I have no doubt in the world that [DOT]they take this step regretfully, but it always goes the same way-it always must go the same way. When any government take a step absolutely in the dark affecting a large Canadian industry, sooner or later they realize that there is one claim that one section of the country has upon this Dominion, and that is the workingman. He must be looked after. Why, we had the same thing in connection with the agricultural industry. We had changes there, drawbacks, free duties, exemptions from the sales tax, and all that sort of thing, to keep the industry going. Now we are seeing the same thing in connection with the automobile industry, just exactly as was pointed out. I am not blaming my hon. friend for now discovering what he ought to have known so much sooner. I am not blaming him for this tardy recognition of what ought to be the first duty of government, namely, the question of a job for the Canadian workingman. That is all it was. It never had anything to do with the question of the manufacturer per se. The manufacturer per se, whether he be Ford, Canada, or Ford United States, has the market. The manufacturer, General Motors, whether it be General Motors, Oshawa, or General Motors, Detroit, or anywhere else, has the market. The difference was this:	In the one instance the
Canadian worker got the job; in the other, he did not. Therefore I do not blame my hon. friend for this belated recognition of what ought to be the very first consideration in any one of these fiscal questions.

speechtext: Yes. Therefore I do not anticipate that there will be a very great loss of revenue.

When the committee took recess at six o'clock I was pointing out what had happened, and we all know it. The government tried again their apprentice hand, without waiting for their newly-constituted tariff board to tell them what to do. They jump in and make just as big a mess of this as they did of the agricultural implement business. Just as they fixed up the agricultural implements, they are fixing up this matter. At the time t'he budget was brought down the opposition said that no proper care was being taken of the activities and the like of the Canadian worker. We were laughed at in certain quarters of the House. To-day, in order to keep the Canadian workman functioning, we have got to make a present of over a million dollars, a million and three quarters perhaps, or a million and a half, to the automobile business. We would not have had to make that present to keep them going if this matter h-ad been approached as we thought it should have been approached, temperately and properly, and not with a view to making a slash without knowing what was being done, just like so many elephants running amuck. Hon. members realize the justice of the simile. They heard about the elephant that went amuck and the damage he did and the cost of repairing it.
I was thinking of the crocodile.

A crocodile can do considerable damage as well. My hon. friend may have had an intimate experience with crocodiles. I leave that interesting question with him. But the fact is that we are today making contributions from the public treasury to keep going-what? To keep the factories going and to give employment to the automobile workers, and the government are convinced that they had to do it. They are not doing this for fun. They are not turning round and saying in effect, "Everything that 
has been said about this is true; we did not know what we were doing; we were making cuts that the business could not possibly stand." They are not doing that for fun. They have not turned round and put automobile parts and that sort of thing in some instances on the free list for nothing. They are not giving a discount of 25 per cent of the duty on automobile parts for nothing; they are not cancelling the luxury taxes on automobiles for nothing. They are doing it simply and solely because they find that they have made a mistake in connection with their budget announcement, and you know, Mr. Chairman, they are doing it in the light of very, very recent information. I wonder how often the government have said during this session that there were to. be no more amendments to the budget. I wonder how often my hon. friend has said that there will be no changes. This question of the luxury tax was brought to his attention and to the attention of the Minister of Customs, but absolutely nothing was to be done. They are not doing this lightly. They are doing it because they have either got to do it, or there will be to a large extent a removal of automobile activities from this country.
Now what have we been doing? Let us see what sort of tangled web we weave When we mix with something we do not know anything about. What have we done? We made a cut in the smaller automobile duties from 35 to 20 per cent, and made a cut in the more expensive automobiles from 35 to 271 per cent. I never said anything for or anything against the cut of 271 per cent in the more expensive cars. It is some time since I have gone into the cost of manufacture and some time since I knew what proportion was represented by Canadian labour of every dollar in that business, profits and the like, or how much is taken from the business for the purpose of looking after the country and the country's revenue. My recollection was, and my opinion would be, that 271 per cent was a sufficient duty on the more expensive automobile. The more expensive automobile has been helped by the refund of duties on the parts and by the free admission of materials not made in this country. But in the case of the other car, after all these weeks of uncertainty, all this talk and all this turning upside down of the business of the country, where are we? We had a duty of 35 per cent on the small automobile. Hon. gentlemen to my left who are particularly interested in the Ford oar received startling information as to how small a reduction could be secured for that car as a result

Special War Revenue Act
of the tariff changes and how much prices depend not upon tariffs, but upon business arrangements, patents and the like. They also learned how when shooting at the manufacturer through the tariff, they were looking up the wrong end of the gun and the kick they got from that end more than offset any slight advantage they got out of the right eni of it.
We have had all these weeks of uncertainty, for what? In the first instance there was a duty of 35 per cent upon the cheaper cars. To-day we are first taking off the luxury tax on the car imported into this country from countries whose production does not enter into competition with that of the Canadian manufacturer, taking off where it does not hurt, taking off where it is not needed for protection. Second, we have taken the luxury tax off the product of the Canadian manufacturer but we have left it on where the real competition comes in. When we practise protection, would it not be much better if we practise it honestly? When we speak about protection we should refer to our tariff. It would be ever so much better to keep Canada and the homes of our Canadian workmen functioning instead of shutting them up. We might as well be honest with ourselves and find out what we are doing. We take off that luxury tax from the Canadian car; we maintain it as against the United States car, and by so doing we raise the tariff of 20 per cent which we have to-day to 26 per cent and even more. That is calculated upon the wholesale value of the car in this country, so that really we are raising the tariff to 27 per cent in connection with the luxury tax. In that way we now have an additional protection of 7 per cent, not under the name of course, of protection, not a protection which can be read upon the pages of our tariff, but a devious protection through excise, a method of taxation which in the past has been a tax not for protection but merely for revenue. Over and above that we have further losses in our revenues made by 25 per cent rebates on raw material in some instances and in others free importation of raw material. To-day we have a result that will give a protection as I figure it out of about 30 per cent in connection with the smaller car. I admit it is very difficult to figure it out properly, but it is not far short of 30 per cent. When I talk about protection I mean the 27 per cent in connection with our tariff of 20 per cent and the luxury tax of 7 per cent. An equalizing of values of cost of production looks after the balance.
I did not understand what the hon. member said about a 7 per cent tax. Would he explain that?

There are two
sides to this question. Protection may be either direct and honest or indirect. We have a direct tariff of 20 per cent and we have an indirect tariff which on the full value of the $1,200 car will mean another 7 per cent in connection with the luxury tax which will be paid by the United States car coming in and which will not be paid by the Canadian manufacturer. That makes 27 per cent. As regards the difference between 27 and 30 per cent, that is not a question of protection one Way or the other; it is a question of reducing the cost to the manufacturer, but of doing so at the expense of somebody else's protection when we have a rebate of 25 per cent upon some parts and free importation of others that are required in the manufacture of automobiles. I may be slightly out in my calculation as to the 3 per cent, but I think it will be found to be a very reasonable percentage. On the other hand I admit at once that we shall get cheaper automobiles; we shall have a further large percentage of people of this country who will be able to buy automobiles. We shall have further traffic congestion and the like, but we shall get dearer other things. Something has to pay the tax; if you take it from the shoulder of one, you put it on the shoulder of another.
Economize.

The hon. gentleman says " economize." We have not had very much help from him in attacking the estimates this year. I hope he will suffer a change of heart and we shall be able to get a good deal of help from him later on. Be that as it may, we shall have cheaper automobiles, and to the people of the country who are interested in cheaper automobiles that will be a source of satisfaction. But we pay for this; we are paying for it from the country's revenues; we are paying for it by giving up revenues which we now have. We have before us an extraordinary spectacle. We have the government with its budget proposals, with its answers not week after week but at one time practically day after day that there would be no changes; that the government had stated its proposals and it was going to stand by them. On the other hand we have these changes. If this teaches us one thing it may be of some help to us. If it teaches us how little the House and the country can depend upon the word of
Special War Revenue Act

this government, perhaps all this fuss and turmoil have not been in vain. Can hon. gentlemen suggest anything that would be more instructive?
Again-but I despair of this thought-if the experience of the past two months plus the experience of the government in connection with what they did with regard to agricultural duties will really open their eyes and show them that they are entering on a difficult field when they make a snip here and a snip there, and that they should first know what they are doing before they try to do it, all the fuss and trouble of the past few weeks will not have been in vain.

Before the committee
rose at six o'clock the minister proposed an amendment to this bill. He also read a letter from an officer of the automotive industries organization, stating that if this tax were remitted the price would be decreased to the consumer. I have no reason to question the good faith of the automobile manufacturers' association, but I would ask the minister what steps he intends taking to remedy the situation in case the tax is not remitted as promised in that communication. The hon. member for West York said a moment ago that the remission of this tax would make a difference of 7 per cent altogether. I take it that the tax is applied to the wholesale price and if the manufacturers carry out what they propose in their communication, instead of the industry benefiting to the extent of 7 per cent, that advantage will be with the consumer. I do not think that the hon. member's criticism is altogether correct.

The basis on
which the luxury tax is assessed is the wholesale value of the automobiles manufactured in Canada, and comparing this with the American basis of cost the 7 per cent I have suggested will be found to be correct. There is a great difference in the basis of valuation.

If the excise tax applies to the wholesale price naturally this increases the price to the retailer, who must make a profit on the amount of his investment, including the tax, so that by the time the consumer is reached he has to pay the 7 per cent extra. In the case of cars of $1,200 and under the consumer ought to benefit to the extent of the 7 per cent in the event of the tax being removed. In the case of cars of $1,200 and under, imported from the United States, and bearing the excise tax, the con-

sumer naturally pays the 7 per cent, but so far as Canadian-made cars are concerned they save that extra cost.
I quite agree.

It is all right so long
as we understand each other.

There is a
saving to the consumer of that 7 per cent so far as cars from the United States are concerned. The consumer saves the 7 per cent at the expense not of the Canadian manufacturer but of the treasury.

The other evening, in
the course of his speech in regard to the duties on automobiles, the Prime Minister declared that in reply to the gentlemen who had come from the city of Oshawa to wait upon the government he had referred them to chapter 19 of the Acts of the Apostles. And when I heard the Minister of Finance this evening intimate to the House that he had changed his mind, that notwithstanding his violent protestations that there would be no amendments in the budget-oh, no! he stood by his guns-I could not help thinking of the incident related in the Scriptures of the traveller who journeyed from Jerusalem to Damascus bearing letters from the high priest. It will perhaps be in the memory of my hon. friend that on his way that traveller beheld a shining light, from which moment, dated his conversion. There was a cry, "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" Now, the automobile industry cries aloud to the Minister of Finance in somewhat similar language, "Why persecutest thou me?" And, having caught the vision, this Saul of Tarsus has now become Paul the Apostle-Saul of Tarsus who threw stones at the martyrs and denounced protection and all its works. But a short time ago he saw nothing but evil in all the activities of this persecuted industry, and now, with his sudden conversion into the apostolic Paul, he is preaching the great truth that the Canadian workman must be employed. An hon, member suggests the name Paul the Protectionist. Well, our newly converted apostle realizes that Canadian industry must be protected, and this is his gospel to-night.
I congratulate the Minister of Finance upon his assumption of this new role. Saul of Tarsus, as I say, is now Paul the Apostle. But what after all must be his excuses, not only to the House but to himself? I sent to the library just now for the Book to which the Prime Minister referred the representatives of the persecuted industry that cried

Special War Revenue Act
aloud to him and to the Minister of Finance and I cannot find very much in the passage he cited to suggest a solution to the problem which we must consider. It says that the Jews blasphemed his doctrine, which was confirmed by miracles. It occurred to me that .possibly this was what the Prime Minister had in mind; no doubt he was conscious of a miracle in the government's conversion. I congratulate the Prime Minister and his colleague. But, Sir, this country is more to be congratulated. There were those amongst us on this side of the House who believed that the very fabric of our industrial structure was likely to be destroyed by the tariff measures introduced into this House by the government-measures which, according to the Minister of Finance, were a concession to widespread sentiment in the country. That widespread sentiment, we contended, should not be given effect to unless it were found to be based upon sound economic reasons. Yet day after day and night after night, as the budget debate proceeded, the Minister of Finance asserted in his place that there certainly would be no changes in the tariff resolutions. The conclusion to which he had come was so sound that nothing could induce him to change it. Has the hon. gentleman suddenly beheld a great light? As the days have passed has some bright star illumined his path? It must be this. One of two things has happened: he was either wrong when he made the revision in the tariff which he did in his budget, thereby threatening the livelihood of Canadian workmen, or he was right in taking that course. If he was right, then he should yield to no pressure that may be brought against him, especially after his emphatic protestations that he would never give way. We on this side of the House ventured to believe that the Minister of Finance would yield.
I am sorry the right hon. gentleman who leads this party is not in his seat to-night: he would do justice to this occasion. It will be within the memory of everyone sitting here tonight that day after day as the House assembled, while the budget was being discussed, the leader of the opposition asked the Minister of Finance whether any changes were contemplated. While my hon. friend from West York was speaking a few minutes ago I turned over the pages of Hansard wherein I saw that my right hon. leader was quite insistent in putting this question to the Minister of Finance. Time and time again the same query was put: Are there to be any changes? And what was the reply? There was a stout assurance on the part of the
Minister of Finance that there would be no changes except with respect to procedure. There might be some trivial alterations in minor matters, but there would be no change at all in principle. Now, what about hon. gentlemen to my left? What about hon. gentlemen from the province of Saskatchewan who pounded the tops of their desks so lustily a few days ago? Where now are those hon. gentlemen? Where is the youthful member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) who, in thi6 reduction in the duties on automobiles, saw a new light in the fiscal firmament? Where is the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. McPhee), whose vociferation found expression not only in a noisy pounding of his deski but in vehement speech as well? Has he forgotten his most vociferous observations about the atrocious crime of being a young man? Where are all these gentlemen now? And then when I look down towards the leader of the Progressive party and see his calm benignant smile,, I realize that he has once more accepted, for the sake of the party, the measure that is now being introduced. But it has its pleasing side I recognize. The other evening the Minister of Customs tried to save the face of the Minister of Finance when he introduced his little measure looking towards the amelioration of the manufacturers, but when he found the House not disposed to take very kindly to it he withdrew the measure. It remained for the iron to enter into the soul of the Minister of Finance. He had to make the great choice. I am happy to say he chose what will benefit the Canadian workmen rather than acoept the worn-out policies and shibboleths of hon. gentlemen to my left. I think to that extent his - choice must be a matter of pride to all Canadians. Why, it is pleasing even to the heart of the gentleman from Maple Creek (Mr. Spence), who was so disturbed with respect to the steel duties as to send an advocate to appear before the tariff board. He too cheers as he realizes that the cause of the Canadian workmen has not fallen upon deaf ears. It is pleasing to think that the Minister of Finance has heard the voice; and, having heard it, we all welcome his conversion. You remember, it was not only his own countrymen who welcomed the conversion of Paul, it was also the Gentiles; and he rejoiced that he was sent to teach the Gospel not only to the Jews but to the Gentiles. So we on this side manifest our joy at the conversion of the Minister of Finance. It is a pleasing spectacle not alone to the Conservative party, but also to the Canadian people generally.
