In days gone by almost every member who sits to the left of the Speaker ventured to point out in the best way he could what the effect of the reduction of the tariff on automobiles would be. The other evening I ventured to point out, for instance, the effect of the tariff reductions on the agricultural implement industry. Some of my figures were questioned. I find now by looking at the Canada Year Book and the bulletin of the Bureau of Statistics that while in 1919 we had 88 establishments, in 1923 they had fallen to 67 and in 1924 to 63. In 1919 the number of employees was 11,036, in 1923 this figure had dropped to 7,792, and in 1924 there was a further reduction to 6,700. The value of products was $37,000,000 odd in 1919, in 1923 had fallen to $36,000,000, and in 1924 it was practically the same. Some objection was made to my figures with respect to imported goods, yet I find that for the eleven months ending February 1925-26 we imported duty-free $1,786,703 worth of rolled iron and rolled steel for the manufacture of agricultural implements and machinery which previously had been made in Canada by Canadian workmen. It is just that state of affairs which makes business in this country so uncertain. It is just the- condition we have been undergoing during the last six weeks that makes business men hesitate to put their money in new ventures. They wonder which industry is to be struck next, and when, after being struck, is the Minister of Finance again to be converted. This conversion cannot go on forever, you cannot have new conversions day after day. There are of course those who believe there is always a chance for the backslider to be reached and converted. But it is better not for us to undergo this uncertainty as to the tariff.
I put this to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance: What did he mean when he answered the right hon. leader of this party that there would be no substantial changes in his budget announcement? Did he mean it or did he not? If he meant it does he now say he was wrong; or was he right and has since yielded to pressure? If he was wrong, he should be prepared to say: We undertook to reduce the tariff to the point that meant unemployment to Canadian workmen, that meant ruin to Canadian industry, and now having found that to be the case we come back to this House and admit we were wrong. That is the right method for him to pursue. But what is the method pursued here to-night? I say first of all that every member of this House should have an opportunity to study the amend-

ment. It should be printed and in the hands of every member so he may understand what it means. Not until to-morrow will he have a chance to study it in Hansard.
iWhat does this amendment mean? If I understand it correctly, it means that an automobile brought in from the United States will be assessed upon the dtuty, as well as the cost, a tax of 5 per cent. That is, if you buy an automobile for $700 in Detroit-about which my friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) used to talk so long and learnedly-you will pay a duty which will now be 20 per cent, as I understand it; that is, $140, making a total of $S40; then upon that you will pay a tax of 5 per cent, or $42, making a total of $882 for this $700 car purchased in Detroit. That is the wrong against which my friend from Macleod used to inveigh. I, like others in this House, felt the duty was too high, but what the amount of the reduction should be I was not, neither was any member in this House, in a position to say. Why? Because the principle of protection is so far-reaching that if you touch it at one point you may disturb other industries in the most remote sections of the country, as happened in the case of the reduction of the duty on agricultural implements. How is that to be met? By taking off the oar manufactured in Canada the sales tax so that a Canadian car costing $900 which would have cost with the duty $945, is now to cost $900. That is the position. In other words, there is to be a duty of 5 per cent upon the car, and an extra duty of 5 per cent upon the car and the dhty. Now the duty is 20 per cent. Five per cent on 20 is one. So instead of having a reduction of 15 per cent in duty, there is a reduction of 9 per cent, and 9 only. That is what happens. Do not let us have any misunderstanding about that. There is a 6 per cent duty, because the sales tax of 5 per cent remains upon the American car, and the 5 per cent is charged against the duty as well as against the price of the car. The duty being 20 per cent, 5 per cent upon 20 is one, and 5 and 1 make 6, so that the duty which this resolution places upon American cars is 6 per cent. Therefore the reduction of 15 per cent that was heralded from one end! of the country to the other is now reduced to 9 per cent. I should like my hon. friend from Macleod to realize that-the duty is 9 per cent, not 15 per cent. These are facts.
For my part I am very glad that the Minister of Finance 'has done what he has done in the light of the knowledge he has obtained since he introduced this budget. Knowing as we did he must be convinced, he is now

Special War Revenue Act
convinced that 15 per cent reduction in the duty on small cars would wreck the automobile industry of this country. That is one of our most important industries. I was amazed on looking at the figures at the volume of business transacted1 and the number of people employed in it. During the last few years it has increased by leaps and bounds. I will not go over the amazing story because it has been recited so often in this House. But let it be remembered-and this is borne out by the investigations of the minister himself

that the tariff proposals made by this government have been injurious to Canadian industry and to Canadian workmen, and in nine cases out of ten. the government has had to modify them before they became law. To-day there is no man in this House and there is no man in the country who will not rejoice that the hon. minister has changed his mind. We told him he would have to. The right hon. leader of this party pointed that out to him. He said:	Before this debate finishes
you will be bound to do it, because you dare not destroy that industry. I do not believe the Minister of Finance would dare destroy it; I do not believe any responsible minister or any government would dare to destroy that industry in this country, and it is because they dare not destroy it that this industry is saved to-night. But for this new 6 per cent duty the manufacturers could not compete one single hour in the production of cars brought in here of a value up to $1,200. Without this legislation it is cheaper to-day to import cars into Canada than to manufacture them here. The manufacturers have told that to my hon. friend; it has been published in their journals broadcast throughout Canada; it is known everywhere now, and this government has at least had the courage to show signs meet unto repentance, to quote the Scripture as the right hon. Prime Minister desired. And the fruits meet unto repentance are these, that the 15 per cent reduction in duty which has been announced from one end of Canada to the other has resolved itself into 9 per cent; instead of being 35 per cent the duty is now 26 per cent, 20 per cent of the customs tariff and this additional 6 per cent, exclusive of drawbacks. Why not be frank about it; why not tell the people of Canada that you started in to reduce the duty on automobiles by 15 per cent, and then discovered that you were all wrong and that it is now reduced to 9 per cent?	-
But that is not all; in addition to that there are the rebates, and what are the rebates? I have not the skill or the complete
information which would enable me to work them out, but reading Hansard and applying my best knowledge, so far as I can ascertain it is fair to say that these rebates run all the way from 1J per cent to 3 per cent, 2 per cent at any rate as a minimum. My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) who has given' these matters consideration, says 3 per cent. Then, Sir, what have we? All that is left of this 15 per cent reduction which was broadcast from one end of Canada to the other, after the 6 per cent and the 3 per cent have been taken away, is 6 per cent.
Oh, oh.

Do not let us have any
misapprehension about it; let us look it over carefully again. The day the budget was delivered the duty was 35 per cent. It was reduced by 15 per cent, leaving 20 per cent. Last week you added a rebate, which is another 3 per cent; to-night we add another 6 per cent, and when these two are subtracted we find that the reduction of 15 per cent amounts in fact to a reduction of 6 per cent. That is the story. Now let us go out and tell that frankly to the people.
Hear, hear.

Oh, you members from
Saskatchewan 1 How you will go out and make the welkin ring; how you reduced the duty on automobiles 6 per cent! And you are not sure about that, for peradventure, if the rebates operate as they may, instead of 6 per cent it will be only 5 per cent. And then, as has been pointed out, how much will be lost in revenue? The figures given a moment ago were $2,900,000; the year before the amount was $1,750,000, so we have nearly a $3,000,000 loss in revenue. Perhaps this will be the peak of the reduction, and that being so it may be that this year the loss will not be as much. But money has to be found; it was the present Minister of Finance who said last year that the money had to be found, and mark you; every application of $5,000,000 to rural credits; every application of $5,000,000 for old age pensions and every application of $3,000,000 for the Hudson Bay railway means a corresponding load upon the taxpayer of this country, whether he pays it in automobile tax or in some other tax; it must be paid. That is the thing to remember.
Then, arguing as I do and appreciating the position of my hon. friend, why would it not be better to tell our people, " We promised you we would reduce the duty on automobiles by 15 per cent, but when we found sentiment a poor master in economic matters
Special War Revenue Act

and that facts are a more powerful guide we changed our minds and instead of reducing the duty 15 per cent we have just reduced it 6 per cent, and we are not quite sure of that; it may be 5 per cent, depending on the drawbacks." Why not tell them so frankly? Why, Sir, on every single tariff item touched by this government for sentimental reasons the experience has been exactly the same as that of to-night. My hon. friend suggests that it was done for votes, and not for sentiment. Well, a deluded people will in the end wake up.
Take milk bottles; you will remember what the government were going to do in 1922. The duty was then 20 per cent, 30 per cent and 32} per cent; they reduced it to 15 per cent, 25 per cent and 27} per cent. In 1922 we imported $12,658 worth of milk bottles, but last year we imported $36,904 worth, in eleven months. What does that mean? It means less employment for Canadian glass factories; less work for Canadian workmen, and more taxes to pay by those people left in this country because of the others who went to find work elsewhere. Take dairy tin hollow-ware and kitchen tin hollow-ware. The duty was reduced in 1922 from 15 per cent, 22}per cent and 25 per cent to 12} per cent, 17} per cent and 20 per cent. In 1922 we imported these goods into Canada to the value of $11,135, while in the eleven months of last year our imports amounted to $60,517:	In other words,
we imported $50,000 worth of new goods which workmen in other countries fabricated while Canadian workmen were idle. Then take the next item, stamped and coated products. The duty was changed in 1922, with what effect? In 1922 we imported $868,286 worth of these goods, while in eleven months of 1925-26 our imports amounted to $1,634,876. Take unbleached cotton fabrics; in 1921-22 the duty was reduced from 15 per cent, 22} per cent and 25 per cent to 12} per cent, 22} per cent and 25 per cent. In 1921-22 our imports amounted to 6,908,551 yards, but in eleven months of last year we imported 18,744,723 yards of these materials. That was the effect of the change in duty. Then take flax fabrics, unbleached. The duty was reduced on May 24, 1922 from 15 per cent, 22} per cent and 25 per cent to 12} per cent, 22} per cent and 25 per cent. In 1921-22 we imported 1,545,050 yards, while in eleven months of 1925-26 we imported 2,087,658 yards, and in the preceding year 2,524,701. Then there is harness and saddlery. On May 24, 1922 the duty was reduced from 20 per cent, 27} per cent and 30 per cent to 17} per cent, 25} per cent and 30 per cent. In

1921-22 our imports amounted to $89,395, while in the eleven months of 1925-26 their total value was $286,112.
What does all this mean? It means that that much less leather was fabricated in Canada; that much less tanning was done in this country; that much less work was done in our saddlery factories and so much less employment was to be found; it meant that that work had to be done in other countries, giving work to foreign people. That is the history of tariff legislation of hon. gentlemen opposite. Then we come to collars of cotton, linen and so on, and to incubators and brooders for fowl, about which we have heard so much. This tariff was changed in 1924 from 20 per cent, 27} per cent and 30 per cent to 10 per cent, 15 per cent and 15 per cent. In 1922-23 we imported $93,549 worth of incubators and brooders, while for the eleven months of 1925-26 our imports amounted to $156,868, These are the facts.
A great writer has said that the history of Liberalism is the history of experimentation, and I observe this: Whatever else may be said, nature at least is Tory-she works by evolution and not by revolution. We who sit on this side of the House realize that the experiments that have been made with the customs duties of this country, the experiments that have been made with incubators, with glass, with cotton fabrics, with woollen goods, all these experiments have resulted in one thing and one thing only- increased unemployment at home, increased employment abroad; increased imports, lessening production. That is what it means. The population of this country is barely steady. What has happened is just as I have indicated, and so to-night every thoughtful Canadian, every man in this country who reads this in the morning will realize that the government at last, after weeks of uncertainty, after weeks of denials, after weeks of stern repression of their own convictions, and despite the efforts that were made from well informed sources to convince them, have at last been convinced. At last they have realized that Canadian industry is better for Canada than American industry. At last they have realized that it is better to have thousands of men and women working in the factories of this country, in Toronto, Oshawa, Windsor and Ford, than have them working at Detroit, Chicago and Cleveland. Realizing that fact, I ask them to apply it not only to this particular industry, but to other industries that they have wrecked. The idle shops that are in Ontario, bring them back into activity, and renounce this fetish

Special War Revenue Act
to which you have so long paid tribute because you have been compelled to do it by my friends to the left. The time has come when you should no longer be compelled to worship strange gods, and we all know they are strange gods to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. His god, of course, is the god of protection for Canadian industry, but the strange god he has been compelled to worship within the last few weeks is the god of sentiment as expressed by the gentlemen sitting to my left who control this House. That is the position, and the time has come when I for one, like others, rejoice that Saul of Tarsus has become Paul the Apostle. I am sure that in reading the scriptures referred to by the Prime Minister we all alike have profited, but none so much as his own colleague the Minister of Finance, who reading the story with which I began my observations, of the journey of that great man from Jerusalem who saw a light and a great conversion on the way to Damascus, has himself during the last six weeks of tortuous walking, and incessant toil, with his face towards the light, blinded sometimes by the shibboleths of the faith of the gentlemen who sit to my left, but ever keeping his face towards the sun, at last seen the light, and that great conversion has come by which we welcome him now as Paul the Apostle of protection and of the Canadian workingman.

Is the information my hon. friend has just given of the same character that he gave some time ago when he stated that the Massey-Harris Company was employing more men in the United States than- in Canada, whereas at Batavia in the United States they are actually employing 800 as against 4,000 in Canada?

He did not say any such thing. I did not say that they employed more men in the United States; I said that the property in Canada was becoming more and more an assembling plant. I suggest that the hon. member for Acadia will stick to the truth in directing attention to any observations made by the hon. member for West Calgary.

speechtext:
Answering the last speaker
first, it occurred to me that had my hon. friend from West Calgary been as well versed in the Bible as he is in constitutional practice and the procedure of Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Disraeli, he would not have had to send to the library for the Bible. I 'have no fault to find with his quotation, except as to its application, and his application is all wrong, because from the evidence that has been 14011-262
produced in this House in the previous session and again this session the Canadian people have been crying out to the automobile manufacturers, ''How long, how long wilt thou persecute us?"
Wrong.

I had better hand the

read the first verses about Paul breathing out threatenings and slaughterings.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: They will pay the difference afterwards on this side.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It does not make any difference where they pay it. My hon. friend from West Calgary and my hon. friend from West York have forgotten that I hold in my hand a letter from the automobile manufacturers of Canada guaranteeing that they will pass this on to the Canadian people, and that the purchaser of a Canadian car will have all this reduction in the excise tax. My hon. friend from West York has said that we are making the same mess of the automobile industry that we made of the agricultural implement industry. That is really a compliment, because the manufacturers of agricultural implements in Canada are to-day, upon their own statements presented to their shareholders, in a better position than before we touched the tariff. I repeat that we have the promise of the associated automobile manufacturers of Canada, of all the manufacturers of automobiles in Canada-it will be found on Hansard to-morrow morning-that they will pass this excise reduction on to the Canadian purchaser, and I serve notice on them now, in the presence of my friends, that if they do not live up to that agreement we will find means of placing them in a position where they will have to do so, or meet competition of the world. I do not know that I have anything more to say upon
Special War Revenue Act

that subject. It would look as though everybody was satisfied with - these reductions, in view of the fact that they are going to be passed on to the consumer.
While I do not wish to enter upon another budget speech or upon a general discussion of the tariff-it is not the customs tariff that is under consideration now; that has 9 p.m. been disposed of-I would not like to sit down without answering the observations of the hon. member for West Calgary regarding the reductions this government has made in the dirties on milk bottles, glass, cotton fabrics and other products. The Dominion Glass Company, manufacturers of milk bottles, are to-day in a better position than they were prior to this government coming into office. They are making better dividends and employing more labour. Some of the cotton mills of this country are running rnigjht and day, and all of them are running on full time. If my hon. friend from West Calgary will look at the Financial Post of last week, he will find that Penman's are already preparing the way to hand out another melon to take care of their increased earnings. As to the Dominion Textile Company, my hon. friend will answer that they pay only five per cent, but they cut a melon three years ago; they split it into three; instead of five per cent, they are paying 15 per cent, and they have surpluses bigger than the year before. That is the condition of the industry generally throughout Canada.

Surely my hon. friend does not seriously argue that charging this tax against American manufacturers and forgiving the tax to the Canadian manufacturers does not operate in the protection' of Canadian industry. Surely he fully realizes, as everybody else does, that you can so tax as to give a benefit to your home producer without and apart from the customs tariff. He knows it. Will he say that a bonus is no help to your manufacturer? Will he say it is not a form of protection to your manufacturer and one of the most effective kinds of protection he can get? Surely it is idle to say that the protection of the Canadian manufacturer has not been increased by this very resolution. My hon. friend knows that that, and that only is the reason why it was introduced. He says it is a compliment to say the same thing that has happened here took place in connection with agricultural implements. Why is it a compliment? We were getting revenues which we have lost. We had to bedevil other taxes in connection with the agricultural industry. We had to cut them off the sales tax. We make concessions IMr. Robb.]
amounting to hundreds of thousands of dollars in order to do what has been done in connection with the automobile industry, and to-day we are making concessions again of hundreds of thousands, yes millions, in order to put back the automobile industry where it was. And you put it back just the same whether you give free material, whether you give rebates, whether you give it in the form of exemption from luxury tax, or the like; the effect is just the same as if you were to restore the duty. My hon. friend must know it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend again forgets that I have placed on Hansard a letter in which the automobile manufacturers agree to pass this on to the Canadian purchaser of automobiles. I said in introducing the measure that, looking into it carefully, we had discovered the automobile men were at a disadvantage in the export business. Forty per cent of their business is export. They were at a disadvantage in other countries because they were charged upon the fair market value in the country of origin. It is in their interest to reduce the price in Canada, because if 40 per cent of their product goes into other countries it will be better able to compete in those markets. I do not want to chide my hon. friend from West York with this, but why should he find any fault with my making certain amendments to my budget? I hold in my hand a record which shows that he himself on one occasion made some twenty-five changes in his budget. If he turns to the estimates of this year, page 60, he will find that we are providing SI,690,000 to correct some-well I would not say errors, but some of the grievances Canadian industry had against his government.

I am very glad my hon. friend referred to that matter. I was not in the House when the matter was up. My hon. friend is speaking now in connection with refunds of luxury taxes in connection with the time the luxury tax was taken off. All I cam say is that that matter was taken up when his predecessor, Mr. Fielding, was in power. He said he had gone over what had been done by the previous Minister of Finance, when he was asked to do the same thing, and he refused. It was brought up again next year, and the same thing was done. It was brought up again when, my hon. friend was in office, and he took the same position as his predecessor. Does he deny it? He cannot. He takes exactly the same position, that the right thing had been done. Last year again the same thing occurred, I said, "I do not object to what

Special War Revenue Act
you propose to do in connection with it" and I produced a memorandum in connection with what had taken place, and he said nothing was done. I supported it this year in the first instance, because prior to the last election and during the campaign the dealers who were interested in that rebate had a promise, not from my hon. friend but from other members of the government, that that tax would be refunded to them. After the election it was refused; it was said that there was no vote f,or it, and that certain recommendations would have to be made. They came to me and I said, "If you have been misled by the belief that you could place full confidence in the statements of governments, I would support your claim. If it be now said that the action was simply doing something I ought to have done, I say that my action had the endorsement of my hon. friend and Mr. Fielding. What was done this year was simply to make good the preelection promises of the government made for the purposes of election."
My hon. friend says I am not paying any attention to the 7 per cent mentioned in the letter. Of course I am. Everybody knows the full sum of that tax has always been added to the cost of the machine. It is always done-factory prices plus cost. I would like to know what would be done if the tax were not now taken off. Of course it will be taken off; but on the other hand, does anyone pretend that to the extent that that 6 or 7 per cent-I do not care which it is- the cost which the American manufacturer or the American competitor is put to, the cost which is held as against him and forgiven as against the other is anyone fatuous enough to think that is not protection? It is protection of a type that works very well. As a matter of fact, it is better for the trade. The position of the trade tojday is better in my view, safer and more secure, than it was before these resolutions were brought down.

I suggest to the Minister of
Finance that it is rather unfair to the committee to ask us to pass a long amendment such as is presented to-night without members of the House having a chance to read it. While the hon. member for West Calgary was relating the story of Saul of Tarsus becoming Paul the Apostle, I thought it would be appropriate if he would tell that story related by Christ in the New Testament about the judge and the importunate widow. Members who are familiar with the New Testament will remember that the judge gave in to this woman, not because he thought her cause was just, but because by her continual coming 14011-2624
she wearied him, and to get rid of her he gave her what she wanted. I think the judge in this case would be represented by the Minister of Finance and the importunate widow-I am not sure, but I think she is represented by some official of the automobile industries, backed up by the Conservative party, in this House.

The hon. member must
remember that in the beginning of the year the Ford company made very heavy reductions in all their lines of cars. They cut the price down as low as possible. The hon. member ought to refer to that.

I am sorry I have not the old prices. I could still show that the Ford company would have sufficient profits to pay handsome dividends on a capital of $7,000,000 all but $125,000 of which was made out of earnings of the company. In the face of these figures why should hon. gentlemen raise such a wail about what has been done to Canadian
Special War Revenue Act

industry and why, I adk the Minister of Finance, should it be necessary to grant to these men this additional protection which the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) figures at 6 iper cent? Personally I am not able to understand it. Of course I am glad to see the people of Canada getting cheaper cars but I do not like to see the treasury of this country depleted by $1,600,000 or $2,000,000. As I said when I first rose, this is a long amendment; the members have not had an opportunity of looking at it, and I do not see why we should not be given that opportunity.
Just a word in regard to the excise tax question. At the present time I am told that the manufacturers pay this excise tax on the wholesale value of the car, but they collect it from the consumers on the retail value. There is a difference of 1\ per cent between those two methods of paying the tax. The two questions I would like to submit to the minister again before I sit down are these: Why should the committee not have an opportunity to study this amendment before we pass it, and on what basis will the automobile manufacturers save us this excise tax-on the wholesale value or the retail value of the car?

support the position of the hon. member for Miacleod. We have heard this question debated for weeks and apparently a decision was reached. So far as I can judge from what we have heard to-night this decision is being decidedly modified.

Our friends across

Let me suggest to the minister what could be done under such an act, and why what we on this side suggest would be much more reasonable. This is a perfectly proper restriction. It seems to me that you cannot make the restrictions on the handling of narcotics too severe. I may be wrong in my understanding of it, but I think that the superintendent of a hospital, no matter how that superintendent requires the narcotics, whether on the order of the physician or any other way, should be obliged on occasion, or if required, to show exactly what has been done with the narcotic drugs supplied to that hospital. I do not understand that that is the law at present, but I do say that if it is not the law, the same restrictions that apply to the doctor in obliging him to tell what he has done with every ounce of narcotic drugs he has obtained ought to apply to the superintendent of a hospital. The penalties imposed upon those infamous characters-the most infamous that it is possible to find in any country-who peddle narcotic drugs round for the sake of gain, struck me as being too light. In the case of a person who is not a physician, who has acquired a drug in some underhand method and sells it to whoever will buy, I would, if I had the matter in my hands, sentence the offender to eight or ten years and a fine which would take from him every cent he had in the world. If after serving the first sentence he was found guilty a second time, I think he ought to be sentenced to hang by the neck until he is dead, because he is just as much a murderer as a man who stabs or shoots another. He is worse, because he is murdering by slow degrees; he is entitled to no consideration. When I read about how these infamous creatures have been handled by the courts, I say they have been dealt with altogether too leniently. The point is not so much as to how the superintendent of the hospital obtains the drug. You provide for that; it must be done through a doctor's prescription or order.
