Subject to the ratification of the present agreement as hereinafter stated in Article XII, the government of Canada will arrange for a mail, passenger and freight steamship or motor ship service to come into effect as soon as possible, and in any case within fifteen months after the date of the ratification of this agreement, between Canada, Bermuda, the Leeward islands, the Windward islands, Barbados, Trinidad and British Guiana, on the following lines:
1.	A fortnightly freight, passenger and mail service from Canadian ocean ports all the year round, calling eacii way at Bermuda, St. Kitts, Nevis, Antigua, Montserrat, Dominica, St. Lucia, Barbados, St. Vincent, Grenada, Tobago, Trinidad and Demerara.
2.	The vessels shall be of from 5,000 to 6,000 tons gross, capable of maintaniing an ocean speed of not less than 12 knots, and providing accommodation for 100 first-class, 30 second-class, and 100 steerage or deck passengers, and shall be provided with 'tween decks, and cold storage accommodation as required, but not less than 10,000 cubic feet.
Now dealing with that question of that competitive route, I ask the minister to tell us frankly whether there is any probability of any of these independent companies to which we have alluded, giving a service which will be adequate to the demands of these sections of the contract with the West Indies? I think not. In view of the additional competition which we now know there will be on that route, it will require a still larger subsidy from the treasury of the country in order to secure a new competing line under government direction to meet the demands of clauses 1 and 2 of article IX. Clause 3 of that article reads:
In addition to the foregoing the government of Canada will provide a fortnightly freight service with vessels of 4,300 tons or thereabouts dead weight, and a speed of about 10 knots, from Canadian river ports in summer and from Canadian ocean ports in winter calling at St. Kitts, Antigua, Barbados, Trinidad and Demerara.
It is possible that that particular freight service may be obtained in some way. I am so ignorant of it that I cannot speak decidedly, but I do not think there are in the government merchant marine at the present time boats that would adequately supply the freight service called for by clause 3. By making arrangements with some other freight line however, that service may be provided. But what is it going to cost? What is the estimate of the government as to the subsidy necessary to provide the service? If new steamships have to be built, as they may have to be, what will be the capital cost of their construction? The minister should not expect us to go it blind. We are all willing to make concessions to the British West Indies, but we should know what the cost of these concessions will be. We have already made, and parliament has voted, con-
[Mr. Cahan.l
cessions in the past, but we should have some estimate of the probable cost of these services.
Then there are some provisions in article X with regard to the reservation of freight space and passenger accommodation. Then article XIII has to do with another service which is likely to prove the more costly of the two. Article XIII reads:
The government of Canada undertakes to provide as soon as possible, and in any case within fifteen months after the ratification of this agreement as provided in article XVI, a fortnightly mail, passenger and freight service between St. Lawrence ports in summer and such Canadian ocean ports in winter as may be designated by the Canadian government, and calling both ways at Bermuda, the Bahamas, and Kingston, Jamaica, alternating with a fortnightly freight service between the said Canadian ports and Kingston, Jamaica, direct.
1.	Passenger steamers to be similar in size to those proposed for the eastern route, that is to say, from
5.000	to 6,000 gross tons, ocean speed 14 knots, accommodation for 100 first-class passengers, with 'tween decks, and refrigeration for about 70,000 stems of bananas, and also cold storage for Canadian meats, fish, butter, cheese and other dairy products from Canada to the colonies and for fruit, green vegetables, etc., from the colonies to Canada.
2.	Each of the freight steamers shall also have a speed of about 10 knots and refrigeration for about
50.000	stems of bananas.
3.	A steamer operating on a fortnightly schedule connecting with the steamers specified in Article XIII-1 shall be supplied by the government of Canada between British Honduras and Kingston, Jamaica, of about 1,000 tons, speed 10 knots, with accommodation for at least 20 first-class passengers, and cold storage.
I do not think the minister can suggest that any steamship company in Christendom proposes to perform this service under article XIII without a very large subsidy. In fact I would suggest to the minister that no subsidy parliament would offer would be sufficient to procure that service at the present time, and, the contract if ratified may necessitate the construction of steamers at the government's expense for the purpose of carrying it out.
With regard to the subsidiary service between Kingston, Jamaica, and British Honduras, it is only a ship of 1,000 tons with a speed of ten knots and accommodation for twenty first-class passengers, but I do not think any sane man would suggest that that sendee could be supplied without a subsidy, I know something of conditions in that country and I do not believe any sane steamship man is going to tender for that service, even though it is only a small service of 1,000 tons, without a considerable subsidy. Therefore we are in this position: we are asked to pass a bill ratifying an agreement, and under clause 6 of the bill the Governor in Council may make such orders and regulations as are deemed necessary to carry out the provisions

Canada-West Indies Agreement
and intent of the agreement. Am I right in inferring that clause 6 empowers the Governor in Council, without any further enactment by parliament, to subsidize these steamships or, if a subsidy will not procure the service, to build ships at an expense of, say $5,000,000, a reasonable amount for one service, or $10,000,000 for two services? Does that mean that the Governor in Council is now taking authority to make all the financial arrangements for carrying out the provisions of this legislation and the said agreement? The legislation is broad enough, and I suggest that it should not be passed by the committee until we have some clear idea of the capital cost and also of the annual expenditure. I would ask the minister, having had the information which is available to him: what is the capital cost of constructing ships with an adequate capacity and giving a quality of service such as is demanded under this agreement for the two main services and the subsidiary service to British Honduras?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I have already intimated,
the promised increased trade is such that we hope the subsidy required will be much less than we at first anticipated. I do not want to repeat, because I imagine my hon. friend was following me, I have already told him that the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company are carrying on a monthly service without any subsidy; that another company are prepared to put on a line of steamers plying direct to Canada.
Which service is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That will be on the western
service. A line of steamers is already plying between the British West Indies and the Pacific coast of Canada. We think the better way is to ratify the agreement in the hope that the promised increase trade will encourage shippers to go on that route with very little subsidy. I admit at once that it may be necessary, in order to meet the wishes of the different smaller islands, to subsidize a certain service to connect with some of these trunk lines for trans-shipment in the islands, but we are not going to ask parliament at this session to vote any more money than we have been voting for a number of years. Under this agreement, if it goes through, as regards subsidy and the promised steamship service Canada will be in no worse position than we were in under the arrangement of 1920. We shall be in this much better position, that owing to the reduction of Canadian tariffs and the tariffs of the West Indies, there will be a larger flow of trade to and from the West India islands.

The minister has not been
entirely frank with me. He has not met the clear objection that those services which are entirely independent of the government, which refuse any subsidy from the government, which refuse to come under the control or direction of the government, will be directly competing with the service which he is engaging to subsidize.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If we get the transportation
between Canada and the West India islands without subsidy, does the hon. member imagine that the West India islands, who are a party to this agreement and who under it will be compelled to pay for certain services, will subsidize another line? All they want is transportation to get the business.

But the minister knows that neither of the services projected are of the character, class and quality demanded by this agreement. He knows full well that this agreement will not be complied with by any of the services projected by any of these independent parties. He knows that this very competition necessitates a larger subsidy from the federal treasury in order to induce another competing line under the direction of and subsidized by the government to supply a service of the character, class and quality demanded by this agreement. The governments of the West India islands are not to be put off simply because some independent company comes in and supplies a second or third-rate service which does not comply with the terms of the agreement and does not fulfil the obligations that the government and parliament of Canada are undertaking in this legislation.
We are already making reductions in the tariff in favour of the West Indies, but the minister is very optimistic when he assumes that the increase of trade under those reductions is going to be so enormous as to supply two or three competing services. I know we had the figures in regard to the trade supplied by the minister, but anyone who knows the British West India islands knows that there is only so much trade and that even under these reductions that trade is not going to increase very largely in volume. I would ask the minister again: Will he give us some estimate of the cost to the government of building the ships necessary to carry out these two main services and the subsidiary one to British Honduras in case it becomes necessary for the government to build ships and to put them into those services? It is utterly useless to say that we are no worse off than under the 1920 agree-

Canada-West Indies Agreement
ment. The minister knows that we could not carry out that agreement; he knows that both the former government and his own found it impossible to do so. It was impossible to supply ships of the quality, character and class demanded by that agreement. Why therefore put our necks in the noose again before we find out whether we are now in a position to live up to the agreement, and what the capital cost will be if we build ships of our own-ships which in any ease will undoubtedly run at a heavy loss-or in the event of our having to subsidize other steamship companies to assume the service. We ought to have clear information on these points.

An important part of
the West India agreement is the provision that there shall be a steamship service of certain specifications. The ships shall be of a stated size and speed, with a specified amount of cold storage facilities. That is an important condition in the treaty. I understand from the minister that it is proposed to supply the service in part through the old steamship company which previously operated.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not necessarily. I said they
were carrying on the service now.

That part of the service will be performed by the old line, and in addition to that the Canadian merchant marine will operate between this country and the West Indies. Now it has always been considered of high importance that the steamship sendee shall consist of larger and speedier boats, properly equipped with cold storage. Is that true of the Canadian merchant marine? 1 understand that these boats are not up to the requirements in speed, size or accommodation. If this service is to be performed in part by the Canadian merchant marine will these boats meet the requirements called fo*-in the treaty? The minister might inform us on that point.
This question occurs to me: Will the West Indies be satisfied with the service which the minister has suggested to be carried out by the Canadian merchant marine? The committee would like to hear what the minister has to say in this regard. But whether the West Indies are satisfied or not, I am afraid that we shall not get the improved service which we counted upon and which is essential if we are to develop a proper trade. I have been looking through the bill, but I have not been able to find the section in reference to the option of calling at United States ports. I understand there is a section making it optional for ships to call at United States ports either coming or going. While this may

not affect the general principle of a preference being given to freight coming to Canada, it is nevertheless very Objectionable, in that it interferes with the policy, which is supposed to have been kept in view, of furthering the development of trade through Canadian ports. There is a possibility that in view of this option, United States ports may be made use of. I know that representations have been made to the minister from different boards of trade protesting against this clause, and we shall be glad to hear what he has to say, if he still adheres to the provision making the use of American ports permissive.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
When we invited tenders we
put in this provision:
In addition to the calls specified above, tenders may be submitted for either or both services or any part thereof including calls at one port in the United States in either or both directions.
That was inserted with the idea that possibly we might secure a somewhat lower bid, while steamers would be able to stop at one of the United States ports and pick up passengers. The tenders received were not accepted by the government, and there is no provision in this bill for calls at United States ports.

The tenders are based
on this bill.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, but in the bill itself there is no reference to United States ports. My hon. friend (Mr. Cahan) has stressed the importance of submitting to parliament an estimate of what the service is going to cost. The tenders to which I have referred were called for in order that the government might know approximately what the service would cost, and I think hon. gentlemen will agree with me that it is not in the public interest to advertise what those tenders were which the government deemed too high. We shall have fifteen months in which to determine what service can be provided and whether or not it will be mutually satisfactory to Canada and the West Indies. If any vote is needed for the subsidy we shall be obliged to come to parliament, and parliament will have the power either to reject or to accept any such vote. My hon. friend (Mr. MacLaren) points out that boards of trade have protested against any calling at United States ports. As I have already indicated, we are not pressing that provision. It was included in the tenders only for the sake of obtaining information. Certain boards of trade protested against some aspects of the agreement, but there are other boards of trade that have strongly urged us to put the matter through. Before I sit down let me quote a couple of

Canada-West Indies Agreement
communications under my hand. The first is from the Toronto Board of Trade and is dated March 20, 1926:
At a meeting of the executive of this board held yesterday the new trade agreement between Canada and the West Indies was discussed. It was the unanimous opinion of the committee that it was of the utmost importance that as all of the islands interested had approved of the agreement, it should be ratified by the parliament of Canada with the least possible delay. It was particularly gratifying to learn from the press last evening that you had brought the matter forward in the House yesterday, and that the recommendation of the government, through the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, that the parliamen ratify the agreement, was so favourably received by both sides of the House. This action is most commendable and we sincerely trust that no time will be lost in completing whatever further procedure is necessary to ratify the agreement and advise the various West India islands accordingly, so they may be assured of the sincere desire of the Dominion of Canada to co-operate with them in getting the best possible results in our mutual interests from the operation of the agreement.
The communication is signed by Mr. Wilson, the president. I have also a letter from the Montreal Board of Trade directed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce on June 16, 1925:
Steamship communication. Satisfactory and successful steamship services are dependent on favourable tariff arrangements and resultant increased business; our recommendations therefore in regard to the steamship communication should be consideraed accordingly.
Now we have by reduction of our tariff encouraged more business with the West Indies, and the West Indies have encouraged more business from Canada. That is why today the steamship companies are coming to the government and saying, We are prepared to put on this service as soon as the agreement is ratified. I think the government might well be trusted to find out how far these steamship companies will go in providing a service to the extent that will meet with the approval of the different West India islands. I repeat, before going into the additional expenditure the government must come to parliament, and we have fifteen months to do it.

Is it not a fact that by
ratifying this agreement not. only are the government and parliament bound, but the honour of the country is irrevocably bound to carry out its terms.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No more than we were bound in 1920.

I am not talking of the breach of faith in 1920, which was complained of so much and gave rise to a great deal of discussion. W'e do not want another breach of faith. If parliament is bound by this agreement, it will not be bound any more
than when that breach was made; but now, knowing that the government of Canada declared it was impossible to carry out the terms of that agreement, knowing that that is what caused the breach of faith on the part of the Canadian government and the Canadian people, we should know exactly what we are doing now. We are pledging the honour of parliament to carry out the terms of this agreement to the full. The government cannot complain that they entered into the agreement with lack of knowledge; they have had ample opportunity and had their eyes opened by the previous breach of faith on the part of this country-a breach of faith for which I am not blaming the hon. gentleman. Therefore we should consider tha/t fact now when we are pledging ourselves to carry out this agreement. What good is it to say that within twelve months, that is, within another session, the government will come down to the House, and parliament may then be called upon to vote the necessary supplies to carry out the agreement, say $10,000,000 on capital account and $1,000,000 or $2,000,000 to provide for the annual deficit? Parliament next session is in honour bound to ratify whatever sum the hon. gentleman may ask for to carry out the agreement, because to-day we have pledged our faith to carry it out to the full. The hon. gentleman says, But let us wait for a year or fifteen months; we have not to put on the new steamers before that time. Well and good. Will he suggest that the Royal Mail Company or the other independent steamship company have announced that without any subsidy from the government they are entering upon the freight and passenger business for one service oi the two and a half services-because it is a sort of two main services and one subsidiary? He knows that neither the Royal Mail nor the other company to which he referred has the slightest intention of placing in the service steamships of the character, class and quality required under this agreement, and he knows just as well as he sits in his seat to-night that the British West Indies, after having been fooled once and having received formal encouragement as to the class and character of this service, will not be satisfied with the inferior service which these independent companies propose.
The hon. gentleman says he has received two tenders both of which he has rejected. Did he receive tenders for the two main services and for the subsidiary service? I do not know; he knows, but he has never told us. The general impression of the public is that no tenders were received whatever for one of the main services, or if it was re-

Canada-West Indies Agreement
ceived that the cost was so appalling there was no prospect of the government accepting it. Now the hon. gentleman can tell us at once if he received any tenders for the two main services. Did he receive a tender for the subsidiary service from Jamaica to Honduras? If so, now that those tenders have been rejected, why should we not know in round figures what was the aggregate of the tenders received? That will give parliament some idea of the financial obligations which we are undertaking and of the amount we will be called upon to vote at the next session of parliament in order to implement this statutory pledge and demonstrate the good faith of Canada towards the British West India governments.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to answer for the minister as to the cost of the service, but it seems to me that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George is simply putting up a bogey man to be knocked down. As a member of the committee which negotiated with the representatives of the West Indies, I found no feeling of such a terrible breach of faith as he speaks of on the part of the Canadian government in not supplying the full service under the 1920 agreement. Hon. gentlemen who came from the West Indies deplored of course that the service was not quite what had been hoped for, but they did not charge the Canadian government at all with any breach of faith. They pointed out that by the negotiations of past governments trade had been increased. Our imports from the West Indies have grown from $9,000,000 in 1913 to $24 000,000 in 1921, and our exports have increased from $5,000 000 to $18,000,000 under the service that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George claims was so inadequate. They did point out to us that they wanted a somewhat better service. We all realized that it is difficult to obtain boats of a suitable class for that particular service. Only boats of eighteen-foot draft can be used on account of the bar that has to be crossed at Demarara, and such boats are not easy to secure. But I think the House should view the matter in a veiy broad sense. Practically every business man who has seen our trade increase with the West Indies between 1913 and 192(1, and realizes that the total trade of the West Indies with other countries is $90,000,000, feels that is will be easy to develop our trade to the $30,000,000 mark. It is easy to imagine 100 per cent increase. Supposing by a diversion of the trade bananas are brought in through Canadian ports, supposing we do (Mr. Cahan.]
double our trade with the West Indies, I think the minister is perfectly justified in asking parliament to trust him. He has knowledge which he has not revealed to me, and which I think it would be unfair to ask him to reveal to the House, and although I cannot speak authoritatively for him, I believe from what I know of the negotiations there is every reason to expect that the increased volume of business with the West Indies will decrease the cost of the subsidies.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George speaks of national honour. I do not believe, Mr. Chairman, there is going to be any loss of national honour whatsoever under this agreement. I believe it is going to be possible to provide the service required, for the reason that the trade will be there to justify it. We have been endeavouring for some years to divert Canadian money to the British West Indies as a winter resort. A good deal of Canadian money goes to Florida and California, but the West Indies contain delightful spots in which to spend the winter months, as we all know. If anything like a reasonably good passenger service is provided there is every reason to hope that there will be many more Canadians travel to the West Indies than go at present. Speaking calmly, as a member of the committee, I have every reason to assure the House that, from my knowledge of the negotiations, the members of the West India delegation hold no grievance against either the late government or this government because of the service of 1920. We did the best we could; the service was not what it should have been but, Mr. Chairman, I think every member of the House will admit that the trade did increase enormously even with the service we gave. With the advantages of trade which have been given by both sides it is surely reasonable to suppose the trade will increase, and that because of the increase the Minister of Finance will have no difficulty whatever in supplying the service provided for under this contract.

I wish
to say a few words in support of the position taken by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), whose remarks were referred to by the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm) as a bogey. If the hon. member will carefully read this agreement into which we are now asked to enter he can come to no other conclusion than that it is a most serious and vital question with which to deal. If he will read clause 9 referred to by the hon. member for St.

Canada-West Indies Agreement
Lawrence-St. George he will see why members of this House should take great care as to the way in which this treaty is accepted.
This treaty demands that we establish a fortnightly passenger and mail service from Canadian ocean ports all year, calling at certain ports in the West Indies. Then paragraph 2 says the vessels shall be of from 5,000 to 6,000 gross tons, capable of maintaining a speed of not less than twelve knots per hour and providing accommodation for one hundred first class, thirty second class, and one hundred steerage or deck passengers. Does the hon. member for North Bruce think that is an easy thing to agree to? Does he think this government would be wise to undertake to build such vessels?

We do not have to
build them.
This is the agreement.

We have to provide
them.
That is true, but if we enter into a definite agreement with the West Indies we must carry it out.
We will carry it out.

In addition to all that in paragraph 3 it says:
In addition to the foregoing the government of Canada will provide a fortnightly freight service with vessels of 4.300 tons or thereabouts dead weight, and a speed of about ten knots, from Canadian river ports in summer and from Canadian ocean ports m winter-
Calling at a number of places. Then article XIII goes on in the same way. There is apparently no end to the promises made by this government in this connection. If we are going to carry out these promises we must expect to spend an enormous sum of money, and the member for St. Lawrence-St. George has merely asked the Finance minister to give us a reasonable estimate of the amount of money which will be expended. If he does not care to do so surely it is a wise thing to ask him to place on record the amount of money asked by those who have tendered for this service? I certainly support the hon. member in his request.
Will the hon. gentleman permit a question? If he were Minister of Finance and received some tenders would he like to give in advance to those tendering an idea of what he expected to pay?

The minister has asked for and received certain tenders. Is it unfair or unreasonable to ask that the members of this House as well as
the Minister of Finance should have access to those tenders?
It is very unfair.

Should we not know the
amount, without knowing who the tenderers are?
We should know the amount, and we would then have some idea of the cost of this treaty.

There seems to be a fair
approach to unanimity of opinion as to the desirability of developing this trade. Speaking for myself I heartily approve of any reasonable effort to stimulate trade between Canada and the West Indies. This particular treaty is one of the things I have urged in the House for many years as a desirable step in our trade development. The minister will also recall that I often pleaded with him for the development of trade with other sections of the empire, and I hope he will find it possible to take those matters up now. There is, of course, some apprehension in the minds of some who have spoken with regard to the cost, and I have no hesitancy in saying that so far as it is reasonable the minister should, and I am sure will, be desirous of satisfying that anxiety or curiosity. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has asked the minister to uncover the tenders he received, and I confess that I see some difficulty facing the minister in so doing. I think W'e should assist the minister as much as we can in this regard, and if the minister were to uncover these tenders here-which would mean to everyone-
Will you allow me to interrupt? I did not ask that; I asked for a general statement of the aggregate cost, based upon these tenders.

I think what my hon.
friend asks is not unreasonable, but I am now arguing rather from the minister's point of view. I can see a difficulty, and I think perhaps there is a way out. It would be unfair to ask the minister to uncover these tenders, because the ultimate result would be to prejudice his efforts to bargain for better terms from other sources, or even from the same sources. If it were possible to satisfy the demand of my hon. friend as to the round figures without uncovering these tenders, that

Canada-West Indies Agreement
I think might be conceded. I was sitting here thinking the matter over pretty carefully, not only to-day, but I have thought this agreement over pretty carefully for some months, and I was going to suggest to the minister that he might as the Minister of Finance and on his responsibility as a minister give to the House some general assurance in the matter. I realize that it is difficult for him to pledge himself definitely to any maximum figure. It is very hard to adk a government to tie its hands to any fixed amount; that may be difficult. On the other hand, I think the House is entitled to some assurance from the government to which parliament could hold the government afterwards. In other words, the government ought to take some responsibility, and the minister, I know from his past record and from my acquaintance with him, has never hesitated to take responsibility where he felt he could properly do so. I gather from his words that he might be able to give to the House an assurance that would meet fairly all the demands and still leave himself free to carry on negotiations with these various interests that he must approach and deal with in order to give full effect to the treaty.
I would like to say this, Mr. Chairman, for my own part. This treaty is of very, very great interest to the western section of Canada. To the eastern section we know that it is important. We have developed in the last six years a trade running from about $5,000,000 to $17,000,000, and in one year it ran to $22,000,000, which is quite an important factor. But there has been very little development of trade from the Pacific coast largely because during all the years of the war there was no traffic through the canal at all through lack of tonnage, and subsequent to the war, up to three or four years ago, the value of tonnage was so high as to make it unprofitable. But if I am not mistaken, from correspondence I have had recently, the minister is assured of some service from the Pacific coast. If we get that service I can say this from my knowledge of the trade, that it will open up an opportunity for a great expansion of trade from the western section of Canada 12 m. which I hope in time will parallel the development from the eastern section. All of this is of value, something that I think we ought to strive to secure.
So my general feeling towards the treaty is one of encouragement and support, and I would again suggest to the minister-I do not do it in any spirit of "riticism or obstruction-that perhaps he could give to us some measure of assurance as to the limitation-shall I say? 
-of the cost of these services. I think if we could receive that, there might be fair unanimity of opinion regarding the advisability of the passage of the agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That looks like a fair compromise.

If I did not misunderstand the minister when this matter was up before, he made some objection then to giving to the House the figures as to the cost of the service until the tenders were opened, and until he had reached some decision in regard to the matter. I take it that he has reached a decision, and I do not quite see how his hands are going to be tied or he is going to be hurt very much if, having made up his mind that the tenders were too high and that he is not going to accept them, he should tell the House the figure that he will not accept. Giving the figure would only intimate to the people who are likely to tender for the service that the service cannot be entertained at that price.
In regard to another point, I understood the minister to say that he had fifteen months in which to negotiate and1 make up his mind. I do not so understand it. As I read the contract, the government have fifteen months after ratification in which to provide the steamship service. I assume that we will ratify the agreement now. But the boats have to be provided, and if we are going to keep faith with the West Indies, the boats must be in active service within fifteen months. The minister and everybody else in the House knows that you cannot take eight or ten boats of this character down off a shelf. It is going to take months, the large portion of a year, to build those ships. The ships are of a character not to be picked up. They are of shallow draft, of a certain size and a certain speed. Contracts have to be made with shipowners who are prepared to go into the market and contract for the ships, and then they must *have them built and in service within fifteen months to comply with the terms of the agreement.
I am rather surprised that the hon. member for North Bruce should inform the committee that there was no great feeling in the West Indies in regard to the character of the service we have had in the last few years. My information, and from what I have seen of the West Indies and of West India people up in the Maritime provinces, is quite the contrary. We ourselves, as a matter of fact, were ashamed of the service. That is the real fact, and any Canadian who has travelled on those boats should have been

Canada-West Indies Agreement
ashamed of the service. They were four old discarded boats that the Royal Mail Company was running down to South America
fifteen years ago. They were dirty. We shall never get any great volume of West India tourist traffic with boats of that character. Are we going to break faith with the people of the West Indies again?
I take it that it is not honourable on the part of this country to enter into a contract such as this, and with our tongue in our cheeks say:	We have fifteen months to decide, and then we will see whether we will put on this service or not. If we are going to ratify the treaty, let us do it in good faith; let us carry out our obligations. If we do not intend to face the cost, let us say so now; let us tell our cousins in the West Indies that we are not prepared to meet the cost. But for the Lord's sake do not now sign another contract with no intention of eanying it out. I was hopeful that we would have a large tourist trade from this country to the West Indies. The senior member for Halifax is not at all sanguine in regard to the outcome of the treaty. He ought to know better than I do. but I know this, that without first-class boats it is impossible, and to keep on the route boats of the character we have had is simply impossible, a disgrace to this country, and an insult to the people with whom we have made the contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I was proceeding to say in
answer to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, there might be a possibility of compromise if we were to make a commitment on behalf of the government that we would enter into no additional subsidy without the approval of parliament, that any contract we make will be subject to the approval of parliament. We will ask parliament this year for the usual vote of $340000, but we may vary the wording of the vote-I have not looked at it lately-so that we shall not be confined to one company.
Answering further my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre, I had a letter from a firm in Vancouver advising me that they were putting on this service, but unfortunately the letter has been mislaid and I have not got it here to-night, but as I recall the letter, the following statement which appeared in a western newspaper is correct:
Bright trade prospects in the Caribbean, resulting from the consummation of a treaty between Canada and the West Indies, have induced the Canadian Transport Co. Ltd., to establish a direct steamship service, between Vancouver and other Pacific coast ports to Port-of-Spain, Trinidad, and other ports in the islands, as inducement offers.
The service, to be known as the Vancouver-West Indies Line, was inaugurated on April 23 with the departure of the S.S. August from Vancouver, the next sailing to be in June, the company announces. Present plans call for a sailing every six weeks or as often as the volume of cargo offering demands.
Agents for this company at Port-of-Spain will be Messrs. Furness, Withy and Co. Ltd.
I repeat that we will not enter into any obligation or any commitment. It will be made subject to the approval of parliament. I agree with all my hon. friend from Pictou has said, and I know that the service was not satisfactory. That is why we did not accept the tender at one time to increase the cost of this service from these people. But it is fair to the Royal M-ail Steam Packet Company to say that they have carried on that service for some time at the request of the Dominion government. They were ready to quit. They were not satisfied with the service. But as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Bruce a moment ago, the increased trade has induced other companies to come along, and the government believe we will be able +o obtain service at a lower cost than previously estimated. But my hon. friend is wrong in one thing. I hope I did not say that we have fifteen months to decide; I said that we had fifteen months to provide the service. The hon. member from Vancouver Centre has taken proper ground: if we give the figures now it is an invitation to other tenderers to come up nearer to them. I think it is better in the interest of Canada that these figures should be left in the department. If necessary we will invite other tenders and consult our friends of the West India islands, who were a party to this agreement and who must provide a percentage of the subsidy. If the increased trade will encourage the shipping firms to put on, a service that will be satisfactory to Canada and the West India islands, why should we pay a large subsidy to others to compete with them?

I certainly understood the minister to say

and I think he did say it, but I accept his explanation-that the House had fifteen months to decide. I understand he thinks differently now. The point so far as the Royal Mail is concerned is that the boats will not meet the expectations of our people or the people in the West Indies.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We admit that.

So that the talk about
those boats is to my mind out of the question. Now to provide a service of boats

Canada-West Indies Agreement
of the class asked for, 5,000 to 6,000 tons, with a speed of 12 to 14 knots, is going to run into a lot of money. It will have to be a special class of boat.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How much will' the cost be?
Eight or ten millions. I hope we will get them. I would like to see the service inaugurated, but it will not be inaugurated except at a much greater cost than the minister has in mind.
A capital expenditure of ten million dollars at the least.

The hon. member for Pictou misunderstood me. I did not say the people of the West Indies were not complaining about the West India service. I said the delegation which came here did not consider the lack of service as a breach of honour. They realized that the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company were doing the best they could. They were willing to keep on the service year by year at the request of the government, and they realized that something had to be done to justify a better service. But after negotiations were over they left with the feeling that the volume of trade between the West Indies and Canada, with the concessions offered to Canada by the West Indies and the concessions offered to the West Indies by Canada, would justify the establishment of a better service. I was pointing out that the stand taken by the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George, that we were being accused of a breach of faith, was hardly justified. It was admitted that while the boats were not good they were as good as could be expected for the volume of trade offered.

I did not say the commissioners who were here in their negotiations with the government openly stated that there had been a breach of faith with regard to the 1920 agreement. They were here to negotiate; they were met by commissioners who told them it was practically impossible for the government to carry out the 1920 agreement, and they accepted that statement. They then sat down and negotiated this arrangement, the assumption being-and I think the hon. member who has just spoken will admit it-that this was an agreement that would and could be carried out by the government in good faith, if approved by the Canadian paifisi-ment. I was referring to the West Indian people. I know the West Indies; I have been there time and again. I see their journals, and I know that throughout the West Indies, in the public press, the suggestion has been

made that there had been a breach of faith on the part of the Canadian government in respect to the 1920 agreement. I was not referring to the officials who were negotiating. Here we are ratifying the agreement, and its ratification, we undertake to provide, either by subsidy, by purchase or by construction, the ships required to perform this service. When we do that we are bound in honour to carry it out, because we have entered into it with our eyes open. It is not a proper reply to the House to say that the capital expenditure of $10,000,000 required to build those Ships or to purchase them will be provided for in a measure which may be accepted or rejected by the House. If the minister comes down next year with a provision for a capital expenditure of $10,000,000 for that purpose and tells us that that is the only practical way in which we can carry out the agreement, we cannot refuse him the money. We have already voted, or we are bound in honour to vote at a subsequent session of parliament, the entire amount required; if the minister says it is necessary to construct these ships at a cost of $10,000,000 we are bound to vote that amount. We may criticize him a bit, but, so far as parliament and the public and the government of the West Indies are concerned, we are bound to vote the money. We should not commit ourselves without having a reasonable idea as to what the cost is going to be.
With reference to making tariff concessions to the West Indies and receiving certain concessions in return therefor, this treaty agreement has general approval, but the whole country is looking to ascertain what the cost will be, the ancillary cost, the additional cost of providing this steamship service. The Minister of Finance read some resolutions passed by the Montreal Board of Trade last year. I think there have been some subsequent communications from the Montreal Board of Trade dealing with the matter, in which they said they are anxious to trade with the West Indies, that they were hoping for an increase of trade with them, but that they wanted to know what the capital and the annual cost of securing that trade was going to be. In the Maritime provinces we have a number of men who are not Liberals nor Conservatives, not confined to one party or the other, who are engaged in the West India trade. They understand that trade, and if you talk to any one of them he will tell you that this proposition should be accepted or rejected according to the cost of this steamship service which the government is bound to carry out. The whole issue before

Canada-West Indies Agreement
parliament and the country as to whether the treaty should be ratified or not depends upon the cost of carrying out the treaty after it is ratified. I fully realize, as every hon. member must, that once the treaty is ratified we are committed to the entire cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend seems to be
well posted in discussing costs. How does he arrive at this figure of $10,000,000 that he is repeatedly quoting?

I have asked different competent men as to what the cost would be of providing a steamship service. In Montreal there are a dozen men who can look at the specification of the service and tell you within a few dollars at least the cost per tonnage of the ships to [DOT]'supply that service. If you ask any of them they will tell you that if you cannot get the ships by a reasonable subsidy, it will cost about $10,000,000 in capital expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is to
build a completely new fleet?

To build ships to carry
passengers to perform the service in addition to supplying by other means a large part of the freight service. There are many men who understand the shipping business who doubt very much whether you can get ships for both of those services by means of a subsidy.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How much subsidy?

I do not know; I am not
in a position to say. The hon. gentleman knows, and that is the information I am asking him to give the committee. My information is-and he has not told me whether it is correct or not-that he could not get a tender for one of the services for any subsidy whatever. Is that right or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend is right as
regards one company. I am satisfied now that he is fairly well posted.

All I can say is that I
have not been in communication directly or indirectly with any company that has tendered, but there are a large number of people interested who know generally the facts. If it is true that no company of British steamship men could be found to make a tender to carry out the more expensive service-

My
hon. friend is misinterpreting the remarks of my colleague. The minister said that one company would not tender for both services, but there was a tender for both services.

I did not understand him
so. I would like to have that statement from the hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There was a tender for both
services.

I will take back the statement. I know now, and the committee knows, but was it not really the government subsidiary company, the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, that tendered for both services? Was it a private and independent company that tendered? Let us be fair to the committee in this matter. My information from competent shipping men is that no independent company-that was the term I used or intended to use-tendered for one of those services. It is true the government has a tender from the Canadian merchant marine, but that tender implied that at the cost of the government the ships would be built or purchased to carry out that service. Let us have the facts fairly. If one of those tenders was from the government's own service, a branch of the government-because the Canadian government merchant marine is simply a branch and under the control of the government in every way-they must have before them the actual facts of the cost of building the ships to carry out that service. Why not tell us? The government are not making a breach of faith with some independent concern.

Why
does the hon. member want to know?

Because to-day we are being asked to commit ourselves to the entire expense necessary to provide the ships; we are being asked to-day to pledge parliament to provide subsidies necessary to carry out the other service if it is carried out by subsidy. We are now undertaking, without any adequate knowledge of the cost, to provide the money when the money bills are brought down to provide for these services over a term of years. What is the position of hon. members? It is a matter of utter indifference to hon. members from the west; it does not mean one dollar to Saskatchewan.
Saskatchewan is a part of the Dominion of Canada as much as any other province.
It does not mean a dollar to the trade of Saskatchewan.

Does the hon. member
want to get into a quarrel with us?

No.
