Canada-West Indies Agreement
Let us express our own opinions and the hon. member can express his.
I am saying thalt this sendee does not mean one dollar of additional value to any of the products of Saskatchewan at the present time.

We believe
Saskatchewan is a part of Ganada and anything that helps any part of Canada indirectly helps Saskatchewan. We have never taken any narrow, selfiA view and we do not like to have a narrow, selfish view placed in our mouths by the hon. member.
I commend the spirit of the hon. member. The position is this, that this is a service which is voted particularly for the benefit of the eastern provinces.
Not at all.
Does the hon. member realize that the preference on butter and flour is vital to Saskatchewan?
I venture to say that not one hundred pounds of Saskatchewan butter will go over those lines to the West Indies.
Why should so much Saskatchewan butter be exported to Great Britain?

I am prepared to discuss the matter of butter with my hon. friend, because I know something about it. This is being promoted for the advantage of the trade of the eastern provinces, and if it is going to cost as large an amount as may be reasonably anticipated for one of those services, there is a great deal of hesitation on the part of members from the eastern section of Canada to give it support.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Suppose it cost 18,000,000 to provide the service and a subsidy was required commensurate with that investment, would it be too much to pay for the service?
I would think it would be the most ridiculous thing in the world to vote it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am speak-ng not of the investment itself, but of the subsidy that would be required. We are paying now $340,000. It would not entail a very much greater expenditure if we went even to the extent of paying one-half the interest on the cost.
There are two alternatives. If you provide capital expenditure necessary for these services you have an investment of $10,000,000 which will not return one dollar in income.
Why?
Because it cannot earn one-half of the amount required as interest upon capital.

How
do you know?

I know from conversations I have had with people who do know, and I am putting it forward as an intelligent opinion. I am asking the hon. gentleman as a member of the government to give us facts to the contrary. We want to know. We are not going to vote in support of this blindly, without knowing just what the facts are. We' are not going to vote in favour of a capital expenditure of $10,000,000 and an annual deficit of a million and a half. The government comes to the House to-night and asks parliament to sanction an annual loss of a million and a half, and it has not the facts to furnish in support of its position. The minister cannot produce one fact in contradiction of what I say. But he hopes to bluff the House into committing itself now to this huge capital expenditure and this considerable annual deficit. We are entitled to have some definite assurance that this capital expenditure to which we are now asked to pledge ourselves will be fairly compensated by a prospective increase in the trade.

My hon. friend is either in favour of the treaty or he is not; and notwithstanding all his casuistry in discussing the subject I gather that he is not in favour of it. If he is not, then why does he not say so frankly, instead of evading the issue and suggesting all sorts of difficulties that do not occur to the mind of any other hon. gentleman? What is the situation? Here is a considerable portion of the British Empire which has been trading with the United States, and which now desires to do business with this country. Both the Mother Country and other parts of the empire are anxious to have all British tropical products sold here, marketed in Canada directly instead of through the United States as at prseent. The hon. gentleman comes forward now and declares that while a great number of people are in favour of the treaty he and other hon. gentlemen opposite want to know what were the tenders that were submitted to the government in connection

Canada-West Indies Agreement
with the steamship service. He has had conversations with a lot of imaginary people who have told him what the construction of these vessels would cost. Now the government called for tenders and in the case of one service the subsidy was so surprisingly low that I am satisfied the House would accept it without question. In regard to the other service there was only one tender and for an amount which the country need not be afraid of for a moment. My hon. friend pictures a situation in which the government will spend $10,000,000 to provide the necessary service to carry this inter-empire trade, *wherein we shall be able to supply from our products such things as the West Indies require and which at the present time they secure from the United States, giving them in return certain favoured treatment. Does any hon. gentleman think that any sound business man would consider it wise for the government to disclose the details of the tenders which have been received? Surely the government would be ill-advised if they did anything of the kind. All these fears which the hon. gentleman has expressed tonight are conjured up purely in his own fancy. The proposition before the House is quite simple: either we want to trade with this portion of the empire, or we do not. If hon. gentlemen are not in favour of the treaty, let them say so. We have no desire to impose any onerous burden on the country for the purpose of providing proper steamships, and there is no ground for the fears of hon. gentlemen. We believe that we can secure tenders from people who are prepared to furnish steamers of the right type for a reasonable subsidy and we ask the House to confirm the treaty.

The government has already asked for tenders and has received some which are deemed unsatisfactory. The minister asks what the cost of the fleet will be. May I ask him in turn how many steamers he thinks it will require to maintain the service? Will it be eight or ten?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
You will find that in the
agreement.

I do not find the number of boats mentioned in the agreement; I find merely a reference to a fortnightly service. How many boats will maintain the service adequately? That, I submit, is a fair question.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Three or four on the eastern service and two passenger and four freight boats on the western.

The two small 1,000 ton boats can be picked up easily, but the others are not in existence to-day and they will have to be provided. Whether the government themselves will provide these boats or whether they will be built by private capital is not very material to the case except that in one case the country will be committed to a further expenditure in connection with steamship property. And that I do not believe any of us want. There are three items that must be met; (1) insurance; (2) depreciation, and (3) interest on cost. Taking the second first: depreciation on such a fleet would be at least 5 per cent, which would write off the cost of the vessels in twenty years. Less than this would not suffice. Then insurance would run to between 5 and 10 per cent. Suppose we put it at 6 per cent- and it certainly will cost more than that. It may be observed in passing that one of the boats which the company had while in the service becarqe a total loss, so that the insurance is low and is bound to be a considerable item. The least that you could expect shipping people to look for on their investment would be 5 per cent by way of interest. Here, therefore, you have three items of 5 per cent each-all low estimates-or a total of 15 per cent. The minister wants to know what the fleet will cost. I do not know, but I am certain it will cost $6,500,000 and probably $10,000,000. But assuming the capital cost to be $6,500,000-[DOT]

The
cost varies according to where the ships are built.
Not a great deal.
Yes.

I do not care where you build them. They may be built a trifle cheaper in Germany, but there would not be very much difference in the cost. I am satisfied there would not be a difference of 10 per cent. Now, the mercantile marine have no boats of their own to put on this service, and if that organization is to take up the service they must therefore go into the market and acquire boats either by purchase or by long term time charter. If therefore we put the cost at $6,500,000 it means that in respect of the three items I have mentioned, insurance, depreciation and interest at 5 per cent each, we shall have an annual charge of something like $1,000,000. And, as I say, these items are all too low. You could not, for example, induce capital to invest in that class of shipping on 5 per cent, nor would you

Canada-West Indies Agreement
be able to get insurance at that rate. These items will therefore exceed a million annually. I do not believe the freight and other revenue, in the first few years at all events, would be sufficient to meet the cost of operation. It is difficult to eee how the minister is going to get tenders for ia service of this kind at a yearly cost of less than $1,000,000. If he does, he is to be congratulated.
The Minister of National Defence wants to know if we on this side of the House are in favour of the treaty or against it. I am in favour of it, but before committing himself every reasonable and intelligent man wants to know what it will cost. That is all we ask of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend appears to be
a shipping man who is well posted. I suppose he would be willing to admit that the subsidy paid should be in proportion to that trade we are doing with the West Indies? Would that be a fair proposition?
I presume you will have to pay a subsidy to provide the ships for the service.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But suppose we pay a subsidy in proportion to the amount of trade, would that be a fair way of measuring it?
I suppose it would. You majr pay too much.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In 1900 we paid a subsidy to
the firm of Pickford & Black-I suppose my hon. friend knows that firm?
It is a very good firm.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
It is not the same kind
of service, and conditions are not similar to what they were in 1900. I am not saying a million dollars is too great; all I want to find out is what the service is going to cost.
I have made an estimate; the minister makes none. He comes back at me and asks what the ships will cost. I ask him how many will be required for the service. He says he does not know, at least he would not care
[Mr. Cantley.J
to decide. I say the cost of the vessels to meet that service will be between $6,500,000 and $10,000,,000, and he cannot run them for less than 15 per cent.

Mr. Chairman, I
have been more or less associated with the West Indian trade for a long number of years. As a matter of fact, I think my firm
inaugurated not only the steamer sendee from Halifax to Jamaica, but also from Halifax and St. John to what is called in the contract the eastern group of islands. At its inception the sledding was hard, it was very difficult to obtain cargoes and to operate the boats at a profit-in fact they were not operated at a profit. The cargoes were largely of fish, lumber and some other products, which were shipped to the West Indies on consignment, and payment was made by the shipment back of the products of the West Indies, chiefly molasses and sugar. It was a sort of barter trade. The introduction of steamers developed that trade, and later on tariff concessions were made in what might be termed a trade treaty between Canada and the West Indies. That led to a very considerable increase of business, and at the present time Canada is supplying the West Indies with the bulk of the staple commodities used there, such as flour, lumber and fish. The fish were always supplied from the Maritime provinces, I think chiefly from Halifax and from Lunenburg, Yarmouth and other southern shore ports of Nova Scotia. Recently the West Indies gave the same tariff advantage to Newfoundland as to Canada, and at the present time our market in the West Indies for fish is absolutely destroyed so far as the Maritime provinces are concerned, for the reason that Newfoundland ships its higher grade fish to the markets of the Mediterranean and the cullage to the West Indies in large quantities.
I take no objection to the treaty except in one or two points, which I shall refer to later. Anything that will tend to increase the trade of Canada with other countries on a fair and equitable basis I heartily endorse. But I may say that the eastern group of islands is supplied to-day by Canada with 99 per cent of the flour which they consume. That being the case, what possibility is there of an increase in that business, which is one of the our most valuable lines? All the lumber they require of the kind produced in Canada is now supplied by us. As regards manufactured articles, Great Britain stands in the same tariff relation as Canada, and to

Canada-West Indies Agreement
my mind the possibility of increasing our export of manufactured goods to the West Indies is limited.
So far as imports from the West Indies are concerned, my information is that to-day and for some considerable time past Canada has been receiving all the sugar that our refiners require of that grade. Therefore the reduction in the duty on sugar I believe was quite unnecessary. It was made at a cost of from $300,000 to $400,000 a year to the treasury of this country. I repeat that we are to-day receiving all the West India sugar we can consume; the same thing applies to molasses, and a reduction in the tariff will not add to our importations from that country. What eles we can get from there I know not, and I think anyone will find it difficult to mention any product which can be brought from the West Indies to Canada in large quantities and which we are not already getting. So I do not look for the increase in trade because of this treaty and this steamship service which the Minister of Finance thinks will come.
So much for the treaty, and I might here say that had the government stopped with the treaty no one would have found fault or criticized. But they went further and undertook to provide, with a small assistance in the way of a subsidy from the West Indies, a steamship service. The government did that in the dark, so to speak; a busines man would have first estimated the cost of such a service and carried on negotiations intelligently with some idea of the cost of subsidy if it were to be done that way, or if not, with some idea of the cost of construction and the cost of operation. If that had been done parliament would know exactly what we were being asked to contribute to this service. I view that part of the treaty as on a par with the absurd, unbusinesslike proposition which was before this House last year, the so-called Petersen contract. I know that proposition was regarded by many hon. gentlemen opposite as an unbusinesslike proposition, and I believe the same thing applies to this part of this treaty. It has already been said here to-night that parliament is asked to ratify an agreement the cost of which no one knows, and at which we cannot arrive.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Does my
hon. friend argue that because of the cost we should not enter into the treaty? There seems to be the utmost assurance in the minds of two or three hon. gentlemen opposite that the cost is prohibitive and that therefore we should not have a treaty at all. We cannot have the
treaty unless we have the ships, and it must therefore naturally follow, according to hon. gentlemen opposite, that it is a very bad piece of business to go into the treaty.
Does my hon. friend think it neeesary to have all these ships?

Is it customary in making treaties of this kind to couple up steamship services, and to commit the country to large expenditures for such services? I do not think you can find anywhere a treaty which binds the parties to provide steamship service, and that is what I take exception to. Besides all) that, this proposed service is extreme to a degree. The service to the eastern group, that is to Jamaica, is such that no one would tender on it, notwithstanding what the Minister of Finance has told us. He says they have had an offer for this service, but I am informed that the suggestion is that the merchant marine might do it, and that the cost would be so and so. There was no tender at all for that service, which goes to show that steamship owners are not prepared to make themselves rediculous by offering that service at a price which they know would be almost laughed at. The ships for either group are not afloat; they have yet to be built. The merchant marine ships are unsuitable; I challenge contradiction when I say there is not one of those ships qualified to perform the service required.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Does my
hon. friend say there is too much service provided in the treaty?
There is too much service provided in the treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have not
heard that argument before.

That is my judgment, and I think if you will take the record of exports and imports and go minutely into the traffic you will find far too much service provided. Especially is that the case with regard to the Jamaica service.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Are there
not five vessels operating at the moment, three on one service and two of the merchant marine?

At present there
are six vessels operating on the eastern route, two government vessels and four privately-

Canada-West Indies Agreement
owned. There is another point; you propose putting on a government service which will probably drive off the private services being operated to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Then there are eight vessels operating at the moment?

They are operating at the moment and have been operating for years. Now government competition comes in and interferes with the private interests. We all know that the government can operate at a heavy loss and drive private interests to the wall. That is the situation with regard to the Jamaica service, and I submit that if this proposed service is to be maintained it will cost Canada millions annually; the traffic is not there. It is all very well to say what we should have; the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley). condemns the Royal Mail Steam Packet ships, saying they are dirty and finding other faults with them. I can tell this House that the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company have been ashamed of that service for years; they have come repeatedly to this government asking that they be allowed to improve that service, which is not creditable to them and is a disgrace to the country. I take issue with the hon. member when he says those ships are dirty and badly run. Only the other day a friend of mine went with his wife from Ottawa to the West Indies in one of these ships; they were perfectly satisfied, had a very delightful trip and enjoyed it very much. The ships are well run and well kept, but they are slow and their passenger accommodation is antiquated. We all admit that and no one knows it better than does the company.

Is it not a fact that there
are no ships in existence to-day which can fulfil the terms required by the treaty in respect of the Jamaica service?
Then Americans do not go there in the summer?

No, that is what I say. There is another point. Our friends to the south, with their West India trade extending over years and years, have never considered it worth their while to put on passenger ships, such as are called for here, between New York and the West Indies, and they have 120,000,000 people and all the nearby large cities like New York and Boston to get traffic from. Then to what extent can Canada expect to support such a line of steamers? I do not know that it is of any great advantage to Canada to carry a few hundred or a few thousand people to the West Indies. They simply spend their money there and then come back home broke, and I do not see any great advantage to us in doing that. So that as far as the passenger part of the steamship service is concerned, I do not look upon it as of any great value.

Canada-West Indies Agreement
Is there any reason why freight should not be carried both to and from the West Indies during every month of the year?
There are times when the ships will come up with clean holds, with not 100 tons of cargo in them. That is occurring now, and always has occurred.
It would not occur if the treaty was in effect.

It occurs under the present treaty. These ships will come north trip after trip during the off season with not 100 tons of cargo. There is no question about that at all; that is the experience. Take the cargo returns of your own merchant marine, and you will see that that is the case with them. It is the case with all the services that have been operating down there all these years.
As I si_-d before, I have no objection to the treaty, bat I do seriously object to the government considering for one moment the operating of steamers of their own down to the West Indies. The experience of the merchant marine is sad indeed, and to add to that grief and sadness is something that should not be. Not one of the merchant marine boats is fit to put on that route, and other boats from outside will have to be provided. I have heard it suggested that these boats can be altered, that cold storage can be installed, and the engines and this, that and the other thing be changed. My answer to that suggestion is simply this: From Land's End to the north of Scotland and from east to west across Great Britain you will not find a single steamship owner who would consider such a suggestion as that. They would never for one moment think of adding expenditure to ships of that age and of that speed. It is money thrown away. Here we are with the ships of the merchant marine; they will have to go through their No. 2 survey presently, and what will they be then? Eight or nine or ten year old ships, worth not any more than the government has sold its other ships for during the past year, about $10 per dead ton. In my judgment the sooner they are sold the less expense they will be to the country. Those ships are not fit to put on the West India service. They will not fill the requirements, and therefore the whole eight or ten ships, or whatever may be required if the government takes up this service, will have to be procured from outside. The experience of the merchant marine, it seems to me, does not justify the investment by this country of any more capital in steamers.

I do not understand the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite. They have all been protesting that they are in favour of the treaty, and yet they have all been arguing about the one thing necessary to the treaty, namely, the maintaining of steamship communication to the West India islands. You cannot have trade with islands situated as the West Indies are in relation to Canada unless steamship accommodation is provided, and arrangements have been made by which all parties will contribute to that end. The committee will agree that it would not be in the interests of this country to make public the tenders that have been received. I am free, however, to say this, that the tenders that have been received for both services, which we have declined believing that we can get lower tenders, are for amounts well under $1,000,000.
Is it not a fact that one of the tenders received was from the Canadian merchant marine?

My
hon. friend need not ask that question of me, because if we are going to state to the House who tendered and all that kind of thing, there will be no use asking for new tenders. Everybody who has to do with business agrees to that. Hon. members are either in favour of the treaty or they are not. That is the crux of the situation. I want to reiterate the remark I made earlier, that I regard the connection of the Mother Country and the situation of the West Indies to-day in relation to the empire as very important, on account of the increasing trade of the United States, and our endeavour here to provide communicatons on lines closer to us and to the empire is of the greatest possible interest to us. I would ask hon. members who say they are in favour of the treaty and do not want to give the steamship communication with the West Indies to realize where they stand. This government do not propose to spend one dollar more than they have to in order to provide the necessary communication. What interest have we in increasing that amount? Tenders have been called for, and in a general way we have indicated what the total expenditure in the way of subsidy would be. We believe we can get it for a less subsidy, and if hon. gentlemen are in favour of the treaty we as a government ask them to trust us to see that this service is provided at the lowest possible cost to Canada.

I do not think my hon. friend's attitude, so far as the op-



Canada-West Indies Agreement
position is concerned, is quite fair. I would like to point out the position he is putting us in to-day, which is the result of the government's inaction and delay. Here is an agreement entered into last summer; we are dealing with it nearly a year later; the government do not know what it means, and yet we are told that unless we immediately fall over to the government, and accept everything they say and do, we are against this treaty. It is not fair. With the situation as it stands at present it may well be that the government cannot very fairly give out the tenders which have been received, particularly when they think they are too high, and when they are going to try to run one against another. But that is the situation the government is creating. It is not the opposition. The government held these things back all these months. They entered into an agreement last summer, and they have done nothing towards furthering it until the House has been in session for months. Now they expect the House to deal with it. What the opposition say is perfectly true. They are in favour of the closest trade arrangements that can be made with the West Indies. We are keenly alive to what the Minister of National Defence has said, to the fact that there has been altogether too much American penetration there; we have idly sat by and allowed them to get in. I do not think it is too late for us to get our share. But there is a little more in it than that. What has been said by hon. members on this side as to the attitude of the West India islanders is perfectly correct. I have been down to the West Indies since the former agreement was entered into, and I know what they think about it. They consider that Canada fell down on the contract of 1920, and so she did. There is no question about it, and that contract still stands. The West India islands are in a position to-day to practically ask for the service, whether this agreement is put through or not. The contract is there. They are still in a position to enforce it.
It has been pointed out that to-day we are doing a great deal in connection with the flour trade in the West Indies. Well, we are. We practically have that trade. One of the things necessary in connection with this agreement is to hang on to that trade, to give us some service which will make sure that the troubles which occurred there and the dissatisfaction which existed, is not going to become such as to compel us to lose that trade. At the present time we have a very favourable trade showing in connection

with flour, and we are very deeply interested in that commodity. We are all in favour of the treaty, but we would like to be in a better position to know what we are doing. One thing said by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Black) gave me some concern; he said we were calling for a much better service under this treaty than New York, with its enormous business, required. If that be correct, I should think it was very extravagant to say the least. When I was in Jamaica, as I recollect it, we had a weekly service with a boat of 5,000 tons, and a weekly service also during the passenger season of boats almost as large again. They were very excellent boats; we had both kinds. My idea of the service which was required was one which would enable us to do business with the islands. We have not got it today. I would like a service which would provide cold storage, but not necessarily a palatial passenger service. Some of the boats going down to Jamaica are very expensive boats. I should think they would be at least 7,500 tons. But we do not want that palatial steam service. We want a service with proper cold storage which would look after our banana business, which would enable us to increase that business and which would release our fruit trade from the grip of the present trust in connection with citrous fruits. We think that is all that is necessary, and I hope that is all that is being done. I hope we are not putting on a service which will give a better passenger service than is given to New York. Much as I am in favour of the trade, I never look for large earnings in connection with the passenger service. What we are interested in is the biggest volume we can get of the traffic of the West Indies going through our own ports and not through the United States. We want to get our freight and commodities at first cost, and we want to increase the trade of our ports. On the other hand we want to see to it that they get just as much of our freight as possible in return. That is what we are after, and not the passenger business.

The hon. member for
Antigonish (Mr. Macdonald) cannot confound me with his casuistry as to whether or not I am in favour of the treaty. My position is clear. I am anxious to do everything possible to. preserve the most friendly relations with the West Indies. I do it, not because Great Britain regards it as our duty to do it, but because we are associated with the West Indies as a part of the empire. But I am not prepared to pay too high a price

Canada-West Indies Agreement
for trading with the West Indies, and I want to know what price I am called upon to pay before voting in favour of the bill.
I have a suggestion to make, and I say it is a fair one. Every tariff concession which Canada proposes to make under the agreement with the British West Indies, and which purports to be made under the clauses of this bill, have already been made by a previous tariff bill which has passed this chamber and which undoubtedly will be ratified by the Senaite and approved by His Excellency. Therefore every concession which we are called upon to make in the way of tariff reductions has been made in such a way as to open our market to the West Indies to the fullest extent demanded by them. We have still fifteen months in which to provide a steamship service. I would suggest to the Minister of Finance that the fair way to deal with the House and the country would be to withdraw this measure and to hold it over until another session. In six or seven months more the House will necessarily meet again and by that time he will be able to ascertain definitely the cost by way of steamship subsidy and the capital expense for steamships to carry out the agreement. In the meantime the British West Indies cannot complain; they have access to our markets under the other measure to the fullest extent possible, and they have certain new services proposed by way of competition for their freight. Why not hold this measure over until parliament meets again and then tell us the cost? If it is at all reasonable I think we on this side of the House will be prepared to vote ratification of the agreement. If it runs up into a capital expenditure of ten or even eight million dollars with an annual deficit of one to one and one-half or even one and three-quarter million dollars, I for one am going to oppose it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: The statement made by the Minister of Finance dealing with the Jamaica service is, as we now know, from an estimate made not by any independent shipping company but by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is not going to put any words into my mouth. I said nothing of the kind.

That is the only fair inference from what has been said to-night. From my seat in the House and knowing full well what certain of the facts are, I say that the hon. gentleman dare not rise in his seat and deny the statement I have made.

Who
told the hon gentleman?

It is not necessary that I
should say who told me. The hon. member need not attempt to draw a red herring across the trail. Neither the Minister of Finance nor the Minister of National Defence dare say that a tender was made for that service by any independent company.

The
gentleman who is trying to draw a red herring across the trail is the hon. member who thinks he can get information from the government as to who the tenderers are, which information we do not propose to give.

There is not a single ship in the Canadian merchant marine that can fulfil the terms of that contract. The ships are

not in existence on the high seas to-day in Great Britain or the United' States or Germany that can fulfil those services.
Has the hon. member before him Lloyd's Register to give him that information?

That is not necessary. Everyone knows it. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Black) has so stated and no one can deny his statement. That being the fact I appeal to the Minister of Finance, who has charge of the bill, that his statement is not based on an intelligent investigation of the facts or on such information as the government may rely upon in giving assurances to the House as to what the ultimate cost will be. I suggest in all fairness to the committee that the bill should be held over until the next session of parliament when we should have full information about the matter, because passing this to-night and binding parliament to all future appropriations will not put the project ahead for one hour of what it would be if it were passed in March or April of next year.

This is rather unseemly procedure. The minister who has the matter in charge sits in bis seat and the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has been trying to extract information which the minister has been refusing for hours to give to the committee. I think the country and the House may well be alarmed by any trade treaty that this government may make, in view of the treaties which they have made since 1921, I can mention three: the first with France, one with Italy and another with Australia. As a result of these three treaties there has been a loss of upwards of $20,000,000 in trade balances. I think this treaty should stand over for a little further consideration in view of the refusal of the government to give reasonable information to hon. members who have been asking for it to-night and who have discussed the question intelligently in a manner indicating that they know exactly what they are talking about. The minister sits in his place and asks questions trying to obtain information, without giving any to the committee. This is absolutely unfair and a most unusual attitude for any government to take. This

matter might well stand over at least until to-morrow for further consideration. It is now half past one o'clock in the morning, and the government has sat here for hours, refusing to give reasonable information repeatedly asked for by those' who understand the question better than members of the government do. I refer to these other treaties for the reason that while the government profess to be on the lookout for wider markets for Canadian producers they have been in fact losing trade for the people of this country through every treaty they have entered into since coming into power.
Has the minister further considered the effect the treaty will have on the sugar beet growers of Canada? This question is of interest to my constituents.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That question was fully discussed in the budget and I tried to satisfy my hon. friend, with what success I do not know, that the sugar beet growers would not be in any worse position than they were before. As a matter of fact they will be better off inasmuch as the market is now stabilized for the period of the agreement.

I do not agree with the minister; on the contrary, their market has been undermined. However, will the minister promise to allow the sugar beet growers to appear before the tariff board and present their claim for reasonable protection against the raw sugar producers of the West Indies?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the sugar beet growers ot Canada want to appear before the tariff board there will certainly be no objection.
Do I understand that if the board recommend an increase in the duty this will be agreeable to the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Surely my hon. friend does not expect me to commit myself to any finding the board may make.
